questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company fine-tuned a model in Amazon Bedrock on its equipment repair manuals, which it keeps in Amazon S3. The manuals run to thousands of pages. Each release changes many pages, and releases come out on any weekday, with no fixed schedule.
After the last release, the assistant still gave the old repair steps. The team ran a new fine-tuning job on the updated manuals, and some answers still mixed old and new steps.
Technicians now need two things. Each answer must follow the latest release from the day it comes out, and it must name the manual file it came from.
Which design change meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
A company fine-tuned a model in Amazon Bedrock on its equipment repair manuals, which it keeps in Amazon S3. The manuals run to thousands of pages. Each release changes many pages, and releases come out on any weekday, with no fixed schedule.
After the last release, the assistant still gave the old repair steps. The team ran a new fine-tuning job on the updated manuals, and some answers still mixed old and new steps.
Technicians now need two things. Each answer must follow the latest release from the day it comes out, and it must name the manual file it came from.
Which design change meets these needs?

options.text: Run a new fine-tuning job on the full set of manuals after each release, and switch the application to the new custom model when the job ends.
Create a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases on the manuals bucket, start an ingestion job after each release, and return the citations with each answer.
Create a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases on the manuals bucket, start an ingestion job each Sunday night from an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule, and return the citations.
Keep the fine-tuned model, and add the full text of every procedure that changed in the latest release to the system prompt of each request.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases on the manuals bucket, start an ingestion job after each release, and return the citations with each answer.
A knowledge base keeps the manual text outside the model. At question time, the knowledge base finds the chunks that match the question, and the model writes the answer from them. So a new release reaches the answers as soon as the knowledge base holds it. Each time files in the data source change, the data source needs a sync. The sync is incremental: it processes only the files that were added, changed or deleted. The release step starts the sync with the StartIngestionJob API right after it uploads the new manuals. The RetrieveAndGenerate response includes citations, and each one holds the Amazon S3 location of its source file, so the answer can name the manual.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.1.1: "Create comprehensive architectural designs that align with specific business needs and technical constraints"
Example: "integration patterns"

Sources:

  • Sync your data with your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base

  • RetrieveAndGenerate (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Using universal targets in EventBridge Scheduler

INCORRECT: Run a new fine-tuning job on the full set of manuals after each release, and switch the application to the new custom model when the job ends.
Fine-tuning trains a model on labeled examples, so it performs better on a specific task. It fits when the model must learn a task, a format or a style. Here, the need is current facts with a named source. The team already ran a new job on the updated manuals, and some answers still mixed old and new steps. A fine-tuned model answers from what it learned in training, so it has no source file to point to.

INCORRECT: Create a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases on the manuals bucket, start an ingestion job each Sunday night from an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule, and return the citations.
This design has the right parts. A scheduled sync fits content that changes on a fixed day, for example a price list that changes every Sunday, and EventBridge Scheduler can call StartIngestionJob as a universal target. Here, releases come out on any weekday. A release on a Monday would reach the answers only after the Sunday night sync, six days later. Technicians need each release from the day it comes out.

INCORRECT: Keep the fine-tuned model, and add the full text of every procedure that changed in the latest release to the system prompt of each request.
Adding a few changed facts to the system prompt is a simple fix when a change is small. Here, each release changes many pages, and the manuals run to thousands of pages. Every request would carry a large part of the manuals, and that part would grow with each new release.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company plans to add a contract summarizer to its legal portal with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Leadership approves a production budget only after a proof of concept shows two results. The summaries must match the quality of the summaries that the company's lawyers write. Each summary must also arrive fast enough while a user waits for it.
The team has 200 past contracts, each with a summary that a lawyer wrote. Nobody knows the production load yet. Until leadership approves, the company may not reserve model capacity or promise to pay for it, and it pays only for the requests that the team sends.
How should the team run the proof of concept?
questions.promptText:
A company plans to add a contract summarizer to its legal portal with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Leadership approves a production budget only after a proof of concept shows two results. The summaries must match the quality of the summaries that the company's lawyers write. Each summary must also arrive fast enough while a user waits for it.
The team has 200 past contracts, each with a summary that a lawyer wrote. Nobody knows the production load yet. Until leadership approves, the company may not reserve model capacity or promise to pay for it, and it pays only for the requests that the team sends.
How should the team run the proof of concept?

options.text: Create Provisioned Throughput with a commitment term for the model, run the 200 contracts through it, compare each summary with the lawyer's summary, and read the response time of each request.
Call the model on demand from a test script with the 200 contracts, compare each summary with the lawyer's summary, and read InvocationLatency in Amazon CloudWatch.
Create a batch inference job for the model, run the 200 contracts through it, compare each summary with the lawyer's summary, and read the total run time of the job.
Run an automatic model evaluation job with the built-in Gigaword dataset for text summarization, read its accuracy score, and read InvocationLatency in Amazon CloudWatch.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call the model on demand from a test script with the 200 contracts, compare each summary with the lawyer's summary, and read InvocationLatency in Amazon CloudWatch.
With on-demand use, the company pays for the input and output tokens of each request, and it reserves no capacity. So the proof of concept costs only the 200 test requests, and nothing keeps running after the test. The test script sends each contract to the model in the same way that the portal would. The team compares each summary with the summary that a lawyer wrote, which measures quality on the company's own contracts. For speed, the InvocationLatency metric records the time from when a request is sent to when the last token is received. That is how long a user waits for a full summary.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.1.2: "Develop technical proof-of-concept implementations to validate feasibility, performance characteristics, and business value before proceeding to full-scale deployment"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock"

Sources:

  • Amazon Bedrock pricing
  • Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock
  • Monitor bedrock-runtime inference using CloudWatch metrics

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput with a commitment term for the model, run the 200 contracts through it, compare each summary with the lawyer's summary, and read the response time of each request.
Provisioned Throughput reserves a level of throughput for a model, measured in model units, at a fixed cost. With a commitment term, the team cannot delete it before the term is over, and a longer term gives a lower price. It fits a steady production load that the team knows well. Here, nobody knows the production load yet. Until leadership approves, the company may not reserve model capacity or promise to pay for it, and a commitment term is that kind of promise.

INCORRECT: Create a batch inference job for the model, run the 200 contracts through it, compare each summary with the lawyer's summary, and read the total run time of the job.
A batch inference job reads many prompts from files in Amazon S3, generates the responses asynchronously and writes them to S3. It fits large jobs where nobody waits for an answer, and it would show the quality of the 200 summaries. But the total run time covers the whole batch. It does not show how long one user waits for one summary in the portal, and that is the second result that leadership asks for.

INCORRECT: Run an automatic model evaluation job with the built-in Gigaword dataset for text summarization, read its accuracy score, and read InvocationLatency in Amazon CloudWatch.
An automatic evaluation job scores a model on a task type in a repeatable way, with no person reading the outputs. It is a good way to compare models on a general task. With a built-in dataset, the job sends the prompts of that dataset to the model, not the company's contracts, so its score says little about how the model summarizes these contracts. Leadership wants proof on the company's own contracts, compared with the summaries that its lawyers wrote.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company has five product teams that call foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. They run two chat assistants, a document summarizer and two content writers. Each team reviewed its design with its own checklist, and the checklists do not match. No one owns or updates the checklists.
The architecture board wants every workload reviewed in the AWS Well-Architected Tool against the same best practices for the risks these workloads share, such as prompts that users misuse, answers that the model invents, and the choice of foundation model. AWS must keep these practices current, not the company. The board also wants to track the fixes that each team makes.
What should the architecture board do?
questions.promptText:
A company has five product teams that call foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. They run two chat assistants, a document summarizer and two content writers. Each team reviewed its design with its own checklist, and the checklists do not match. No one owns or updates the checklists.
The architecture board wants every workload reviewed in the AWS Well-Architected Tool against the same best practices for the risks these workloads share, such as prompts that users misuse, answers that the model invents, and the choice of foundation model. AWS must keep these practices current, not the company. The board also wants to track the fixes that each team makes.
What should the architecture board do?

options.text: Apply the Machine Learning Lens from the lens catalog to each workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.
Apply a custom lens built from the teams' checklists to each workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.
Apply the Generative AI Lens from the lens catalog to each workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.
Apply the AWS Well-Architected Framework lens, which the tool applies by default, to each workload, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Apply the Generative AI Lens from the lens catalog to each workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.
The lens catalog holds official lenses that AWS creates for the AWS Well-Architected Tool and keeps up to date. The Generative AI Lens holds best practices for applications that use foundation models on Amazon Bedrock. It covers the choice of model, checks on user prompts that try to make the model do a task it should not do, and guardrails and retrieval that reduce incorrect answers. Every team applies the same lens, so every workload answers the same questions. The review shows the risks of each workload, and its improvement plan tracks the fixes.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.1.3: "Create standardized technical components to ensure consistent implementation across multiple deployment scenarios"
Example: "AWS WA Tool Generative AI Lens"

Sources:

  • Lens Catalog for AWS WA Tool
  • Generative AI Lens, AWS Well-Architected Framework
  • Machine Learning Lens, AWS Well-Architected Framework

INCORRECT: Apply the Machine Learning Lens from the lens catalog to each workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.
The Machine Learning Lens is also an official lens in the catalog. It covers machine learning workloads such as classification, fraud detection, forecasting and recommendation engines. It fits teams that build and train their own models for tasks like these. For generative AI workloads, the lens itself points to the Generative AI Lens. These teams call foundation models, and the risks that the board lists, such as misused prompts and invented answers, come from that kind of workload.

INCORRECT: Apply a custom lens built from the teams' checklists to each workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.
A custom lens holds a company's own pillars, questions and best practices. It fits rules that only the company can write, such as its own governance needs. Here, the board wants best practices that AWS keeps current, and no one owns or updates the checklists. A lens built from them would keep their gaps, and someone in the company would have to maintain it.

INCORRECT: Apply the AWS Well-Architected Framework lens, which the tool applies by default, to each workload, and track the fixes in each workload's improvement plan.
The AWS Well-Architected Framework lens applies to every workload by default. It covers general best practices for reliable, secure, efficient, cost-effective and sustainable systems, so it is the right base for any workload. The board wants best practices for the risks that foundation model workloads share, such as misused prompts, invented answers and the choice of model. The Generative AI Lens extends the Framework to cover these.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a shared generative AI platform on AWS. Product teams build workloads on it with Amazon Bedrock, and each new workload gets a review in the AWS Well-Architected Tool.
In every review, the team answers the same AWS Well-Architected Framework questions about the shared platform, for example how identity, logging and network access work. The answers differ from team to team, although the platform is the same for all of them. The platform team owns the platform design, and it wants every new review to start with its answers to these questions. Each product team still answers the questions about its own workload.
Which approach should the platform team use?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a shared generative AI platform on AWS. Product teams build workloads on it with Amazon Bedrock, and each new workload gets a review in the AWS Well-Architected Tool.
In every review, the team answers the same AWS Well-Architected Framework questions about the shared platform, for example how identity, logging and network access work. The answers differ from team to team, although the platform is the same for all of them. The platform team owns the platform design, and it wants every new review to start with its answers to these questions. Each product team still answers the questions about its own workload.
Which approach should the platform team use?

options.text: The platform team creates a custom lens with its own platform questions, shares the lens with the teams' accounts, and each team applies it to new workloads.
The platform team creates a profile with the business context of the platform, shares the profile with the teams' accounts, and each team adds it to new workloads.
The platform team answers the platform questions in its own workload, shares that workload with the teams' accounts as Contributor, and each team copies the answers.
The platform team creates a review template with its answers to the platform questions, shares the template with the teams' accounts, and each team defines new workloads from it.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The platform team creates a review template with its answers to the platform questions, shares the template with the teams' accounts, and each team defines new workloads from it.
A review template holds pre-filled answers for Well-Architected Framework and custom lens questions that many workloads share. The platform team writes its answers to the platform questions once. It shares the template with other accounts, or with an organization or organizational unit, and each product team defines its new workload from the template. Every review then starts with the same platform answers, and each team still answers the questions about its own workload.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.1.3: "Create standardized technical components to ensure consistent implementation across multiple deployment scenarios"
Example: "the AWS Well-Architected Framework"

Sources:

  • Review templates in AWS WA Tool
  • Custom lenses for workloads in AWS WA Tool
  • Using profiles in AWS WA Tool

INCORRECT: The platform team creates a custom lens with its own platform questions, shares the lens with the teams' accounts, and each team applies it to new workloads.
A custom lens adds a company's own pillars, questions and best practices. It fits when the company needs questions that the Framework does not ask. Here, the platform questions already exist in the Framework. The problem is the answers. A lens only adds questions for each team to answer, so the answers can still differ.

INCORRECT: The platform team creates a profile with the business context of the platform, shares the profile with the teams' accounts, and each team adds it to new workloads.
A profile describes the business context and the goals of a workload. The tool then shows a prioritized list of the questions and risks that matter for that context, which helps a team focus its review. A profile fills in no answers, so each team would still answer the platform questions in its own way.

INCORRECT: The platform team answers the platform questions in its own workload, shares that workload with the teams' accounts as Contributor, and each team copies the answers.
Sharing a workload gives other accounts access to that one review, either read-only or as a Contributor who can update its answers. It fits when several people work on the same review. Here, each product team needs its own new workload, and the share gives that workload no answers. Each team would type the answers in by hand, and answers typed in by each team are the reason the reviews differ now.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company's support assistant runs two AWS Lambda functions. The answer function calls a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock to write each answer. The tone function rewrites each answer with a custom model. The team built this custom model from the same foundation model with replies from its best agents, because prompt instructions did not give the company's tone.

The Amazon Bedrock console now shows the foundation model as Legacy, with an end-of-life date a few months away in every AWS Region. A newer version of the same model is Active and supports the same customization.

Both functions must keep working after that date, and answers must keep the company's tone.

Which actions should the team take?

Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company's support assistant runs two AWS Lambda functions. The answer function calls a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock to write each answer. The tone function rewrites each answer with a custom model. The team built this custom model from the same foundation model with replies from its best agents, because prompt instructions did not give the company's tone.
The Amazon Bedrock console now shows the foundation model as Legacy, with an end-of-life date a few months away in every AWS Region. A newer version of the same model is Active and supports the same customization.
Both functions must keep working after that date, and answers must keep the company's tone.
Which actions should the team take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Create a new Provisioned Throughput for the current custom model, and change the tone function to call the custom model through it.
Test the Active model version with the assistant's own prompts, and change the model ID in the answer function to that version.
Test the Active model version with the assistant's own prompts, and change the model ID in the answer and tone functions to that version.
Copy the current custom model to another AWS Region, and change the tone function to call the copy in that Region.
Run a fine-tuning job on the Active model version with the team's training data, and change the tone function to call the new custom model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Test the Active model version with the assistant's own prompts, and change the model ID in the answer function to that version.
A Legacy model is scheduled for retirement. The team can still use it for now, but it should move to an Active model before the end-of-life date. On or soon after that date, the model is no longer available in any AWS Region, and requests to it fail. The move does not happen on its own. The team updates its own code, so the answer function calls the new version by its model ID. Amazon Bedrock lets a team test a new model version in the console or with the API first. A test with the assistant's own prompts shows whether the newer version still writes the answers that the team needs.

CORRECT: Run a fine-tuning job on the Active model version with the team's training data, and change the tone function to call the new custom model.
The tone comes from a custom model, and that custom model was built on the Legacy model. So the tone function also depends on the model that retires. Fine-tuning trains a model with labeled examples, here the replies of the best agents, so the model learns what output to give for each input. A Legacy model accepts no new fine-tuning jobs, so the new custom model must come from an Active model. The team runs the job on the Active version with the same replies, and the tone function then calls the new custom model. Custom models should move to an Active model as soon as their base model becomes Legacy, and the move should end before the end-of-life date.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.4: "Implement FM customization deployment and lifecycle management"
Example: "lifecycle management to retire and replace models"

Sources:

  • Model lifecycle (Legacy)

  • Customize your model to improve its performance for your use case

  • Copy a model to a Region

INCORRECT: Create a new Provisioned Throughput for the current custom model, and change the tone function to call the custom model through it.
Provisioned Throughput gives a custom model dedicated compute capacity and guaranteed throughput, and it is a common way to run a custom model under a steady load. It does not change the model underneath. After a foundation model becomes Legacy, a team cannot create new Provisioned Throughput for a custom model that was built on it. Even capacity that already exists would still serve a custom model of the Legacy model, and the team must leave that model before the end-of-life date.

INCORRECT: Test the Active model version with the assistant's own prompts, and change the model ID in the answer and tone functions to that version.
Moving a feature from a custom model to a newer base model is a good choice when the base model does the job with instructions alone. The team then has no custom model to maintain. The answer function part of this option is right, but the tone function part is not. The team built the custom model because prompt instructions did not give the company's tone. A base model has not learned from the replies of the best agents, so the tone function would lose the tone that answers must keep.

INCORRECT: Copy the current custom model to another AWS Region, and change the tone function to call the copy in that Region.
Copying a custom model to another AWS Region fits a team that needs the model where another application runs. The lifecycle state of a model can differ by Region, but here the end-of-life date applies in every AWS Region. The copy is the same custom model, built on the same Legacy model, so the tone function still depends on the model that retires.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company fine-tunes a model every month and hosts it on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. A pipeline registers each new version in SageMaker Model Registry after it passes the offline tests.
The last version passed every offline test. After the release, all users moved to the new version at once, and the endpoint returned errors and slow responses for many live requests. An engineer rolled back by hand, and it took hours.
For the next release, the team wants a new version to reach only a few users first. It also wants the endpoint to go back to the old version with no person involved when errors rise.
Which changes should the team make to the release process?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company fine-tunes a model every month and hosts it on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. A pipeline registers each new version in SageMaker Model Registry after it passes the offline tests.
The last version passed every offline test. After the release, all users moved to the new version at once, and the endpoint returned errors and slow responses for many live requests. An engineer rolled back by hand, and it took hours.
For the next release, the team wants a new version to reach only a few users first. It also wants the endpoint to go back to the old version with no person involved when errors rise.
Which changes should the team make to the release process?
Select TWO.

options.text: Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses canary traffic shifting, and set a baking period after the first part of the traffic moves.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses all at once traffic shifting, and set a baking period after all of the traffic moves.
Add Amazon CloudWatch alarms on the error and latency metrics of the endpoint to the auto-rollback configuration of the blue/green deployment.
Add Amazon CloudWatch alarms on the error and latency metrics of the endpoint that notify the on-call engineer through an Amazon SNS topic.
Raise the accuracy threshold in the condition step of the pipeline, so that fewer new versions pass the offline tests and reach the endpoint.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses canary traffic shifting, and set a baking period after the first part of the traffic moves.
A blue/green deployment starts a new fleet, the green fleet, next to the old blue fleet. With canary traffic shifting, SageMaker AI first sends one small part of the traffic to the green fleet. During the baking period, CloudWatch alarms watch the green fleet. If no alarm fires, the rest of the traffic moves, and a final baking period follows. So a bad version reaches only a few users.

CORRECT: Add Amazon CloudWatch alarms on the error and latency metrics of the endpoint to the auto-rollback configuration of the blue/green deployment.
The auto-rollback configuration lists the CloudWatch alarms that SageMaker AI watches during the baking periods. The team creates these alarms on the endpoint's metrics before the deployment starts. If any of them fires, SageMaker AI sends all traffic back to the blue fleet by itself. This replaces the manual rollback that took hours.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.4: "Implement FM customization deployment and lifecycle management"
Example: "rollback strategies for failed deployments"

Sources:

  • Use canary traffic shifting

  • Deployment guardrails for updating models in production

INCORRECT: Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses all at once traffic shifting, and set a baking period after all of the traffic moves.
All at once traffic shifting is a real deployment guardrails mode. It moves all traffic to the green fleet, and alarms watch it during the baking period, with automatic rollback. It fits a release where a short problem for every user is acceptable. The team wants a new version to reach only a few users first, and this mode sends every user to it at once, as the last release did.

INCORRECT: Add Amazon CloudWatch alarms on the error and latency metrics of the endpoint that notify the on-call engineer through an Amazon SNS topic.
An alarm that notifies an engineer is a standard way to learn about a problem fast. It still leaves the rollback to a person. The last manual rollback took hours, and the team wants the endpoint to go back to the old version with no person involved.

INCORRECT: Raise the accuracy threshold in the condition step of the pipeline, so that fewer new versions pass the offline tests and reach the endpoint.
A stricter offline gate helps when bad versions show their problems in offline tests. The last version passed every offline test, and its problems appeared only with live requests. A higher threshold would still let such a version through, and it does not change how a release reaches users or how it rolls back.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company fine-tunes Amazon Nova models in Amazon Bedrock on conversation records from partners. Partner systems upload JSONL files to an incoming prefix in an Amazon S3 bucket at random times. A customization job can start at any time and reads its data from the training prefix.
Bad records have made jobs fail. Every bad file opened without errors in a JSON reader, but some conversations started with the assistant, or had two user turns in a row. Each file must be accepted or rejected within seconds of its upload. Partners fix a rejected file and upload it again, so they need it back exactly as they sent it.
Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company fine-tunes Amazon Nova models in Amazon Bedrock on conversation records from partners. Partner systems upload JSONL files to an incoming prefix in an Amazon S3 bucket at random times. A customization job can start at any time and reads its data from the training prefix.
Bad records have made jobs fail. Every bad file opened without errors in a JSON reader, but some conversations started with the assistant, or had two user turns in a row. Each file must be accepted or rejected within seconds of its upload. Partners fix a rejected file and upload it again, so they need it back exactly as they sent it.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that parses each line of the file as JSON, and moves the file unchanged to a rejects prefix or to the training prefix.
An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that checks the turn order of each conversation, removes the records that fail, and writes the other records to the training prefix.
An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that parses each line of the file as JSON, removes the records that fail, and writes the other records to the training prefix.
An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that checks the turn order of each conversation, and moves the file unchanged to a rejects prefix or to the training prefix.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that checks the turn order of each conversation, and moves the file unchanged to a rejects prefix or to the training prefix.
In fine-tuning data for Amazon Nova, each record holds a messages array with the roles user and assistant. The first turn comes from the user, the roles take turns, and the last turn is the assistant's response. The bad files broke this rule while they were still valid JSON. Amazon S3 invokes the Lambda function with an event that names each new object, so the check starts when the file arrives. The function reads every record and checks the order of the roles. Then it moves the whole file, unchanged, to the rejects prefix or to the training prefix. Clean files reach the training prefix, and a partner gets a rejected file back as it was sent.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.1: "Create comprehensive data validation workflows to ensure data meets quality standards for FM consumption"
Example: "custom Lambda functions"

Sources:

  • Prepare data for fine-tuning text-to-text models

  • Preparing data for multimodal fine-tuning (Amazon Nova User Guide)

  • Process Amazon S3 event notifications with Lambda

INCORRECT: An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that parses each line of the file as JSON, and moves the file unchanged to a rejects prefix or to the training prefix.
A JSON check is a fast first step, and it catches files where a line is broken or cut off. Moving the whole file also gives a partner the rejected file exactly as it was sent. But every bad file here opened without errors in a JSON reader. The problem sits inside the records: conversations that start with the assistant or have two user turns in a row. This check passes those files, and the jobs still fail.

INCORRECT: An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that checks the turn order of each conversation, removes the records that fail, and writes the other records to the training prefix.
Dropping bad records and keeping the good ones is a common way to clean data that a company owns. The check itself is the right one. But the partners fix a rejected file and upload it again, so they need it back exactly as they sent it. This design changes the file and keeps no rejected copy, so a partner never learns which file failed.

INCORRECT: An S3 event invokes an AWS Lambda function that parses each line of the file as JSON, removes the records that fail, and writes the other records to the training prefix.
Removing the lines that do not parse is a quick way to clean a file that a company owns, when some lines are cut off. Here the JSON check misses the real problem, because every bad file opened without errors in a JSON reader. The conversations in the wrong order pass the check and reach the training prefix. The design also changes the file, and partners need a rejected file back exactly as they sent it.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
An engineering company keeps an archive of large scanned drawings in Amazon S3. Before a model in Amazon Bedrock can answer questions about the drawings, each drawing must become text plus image crops of its parts.
The company must use its own open-source vision model, which it trained on its own drawing symbols. The model runs in a container image in Amazon ECR, needs a GPU, and takes several minutes for each drawing. The step runs once for the whole archive and then once a week for new drawings. Nothing may keep running between the runs.
Where should the team run this step?

An engineering company keeps an archive of large scanned drawings in Amazon S3. Before a model in Amazon Bedrock can answer questions about the drawings, each drawing must become text plus image crops of its parts.
The company must use its own open-source vision model, which it trained on its own drawing symbols. The model runs in a container image in Amazon ECR, needs a GPU, and takes several minutes for each drawing. The step runs once for the whole archive and then once a week for new drawings. Nothing may keep running between the runs.
Where should the team run this step?

options.text: Send each drawing to Amazon Textract from an AWS Lambda function, and write the detected text and tables for each drawing to Amazon S3.
Run an Amazon SageMaker Processing job with the company's container image on GPU instances, and have it read the drawings from Amazon S3 and write the results to S3.
Host the company's container image on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with GPU instances, send each drawing to it, and delete the endpoint after each run.
Send each drawing to Amazon Bedrock Data Automation from an AWS Lambda function, and write the structured output for each drawing to Amazon S3.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run an Amazon SageMaker Processing job with the company's container image on GPU instances, and have it read the drawings from Amazon S3 and write the results to S3.
A processing job runs a script or a container on instances that SageMaker AI launches for the job. It reads its input from Amazon S3, writes its output to S3, and releases the instances when it finishes. The team can bring its own container, so the job runs the company's model, and it can use GPU instance types. No caller waits for a response, so each drawing can take several minutes. Nothing runs between the weekly jobs.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "SageMaker Processing"

Sources:

  • Data transformation workloads with SageMaker Processing
  • Custom Inference Code with Hosting Services
  • What is Amazon Textract?

INCORRECT: Send each drawing to Amazon Textract from an AWS Lambda function, and write the detected text and tables for each drawing to Amazon S3.
Amazon Textract detects typed and handwritten text in documents, and it extracts forms and tables. It fits scanned business documents such as reports, records and tax forms, with no model for the team to run. Textract uses its own pre-trained models. The company must use the vision model that it trained on its own drawing symbols.

INCORRECT: Host the company's container image on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with GPU instances, send each drawing to it, and delete the endpoint after each run.
A real-time endpoint runs the company's own container on GPU instances, and deleting the endpoint after each run stops the charges between runs. It fits requests that need an answer quickly. The problem is the time per request. The container of a real-time endpoint must respond to each request within a short, fixed number of seconds. Each drawing takes several minutes, so the requests fail before the model finishes.

INCORRECT: Send each drawing to Amazon Bedrock Data Automation from an AWS Lambda function, and write the structured output for each drawing to Amazon S3.
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation uses generative AI to turn documents, images, video and audio into structured output. It fits teams that want managed extraction with no model of their own to run. Like Textract, it runs its own models. The company's drawing symbols need the vision model that the company trained, in its own container.

questions.promptText:
A company records its support calls and sends each recording to Amazon Transcribe in a batch job. An Amazon Bedrock model then writes a short summary from each transcript. The company keeps every transcript as the official record of the call. The record must show each part code the way the company writes it, for example KT45R.
Many summaries name the wrong product, because the transcripts spell new product names and part codes in the wrong way. The products are new, and nothing is written about them yet, apart from a short list of the terms.
Which change fixes these terms in the transcripts?

options.text: Train a custom language model in Amazon Transcribe on the text of the company's product manuals and support articles, and add it to each job.
Create a custom vocabulary in table format in Amazon Transcribe with each term as it is spoken and as it must be written, and add it to each job.
Train a custom language model in Amazon Transcribe on the transcripts of the company's past support calls, and add it to each job.
Create a custom vocabulary in table format in Amazon Transcribe with each term as it is spoken, with letters and numbers as words, and add it to each job.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a custom vocabulary in table format in Amazon Transcribe with each term as it is spoken and as it must be written, and add it to each job.
A custom vocabulary teaches Amazon Transcribe specific words that it does not render well, such as brand names, acronyms and other domain terms. That is the problem here: the terms are known, and the list is short. In table format, two columns matter. The Phrase column holds the term as it is spoken. It cannot contain digits, so the numbers are spelled out as words, and each spoken letter gets a period after it. The entry for KT45R is "K.T.-four-five-R.", with a period after the R too. The DisplayAs column holds the term as it must be written in the transcript, and it can contain digits, so the output shows KT45R. The vocabulary corrects the transcript itself, so the stored record and the summary both get the right terms.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "AWS Transcribe"

Sources:

  • Creating a custom vocabulary using a table

  • Improving transcription accuracy with custom vocabularies and custom language models

  • Custom language models (Amazon Transcribe Developer Guide)

INCORRECT: Train a custom language model in Amazon Transcribe on the text of the company's product manuals and support articles, and add it to each job.
A custom language model learns how words are used in context. It trains on a large amount of text from the domain, and manuals, articles and technical reports are good training text when accurate transcripts do not exist. Here, the products are new and nothing is written about them yet. The only text is a short list of terms, and a list gives the model no context to learn from.

INCORRECT: Train a custom language model in Amazon Transcribe on the transcripts of the company's past support calls, and add it to each job.
Accurate transcripts are the best training text for a custom language model, because they match how people really speak in the calls. The important word is accurate. The company's past transcripts come from the same jobs that spell the product names and codes in the wrong way, so a model trained on them learns those wrong spellings. The products are also new, so most past calls never mention them.

INCORRECT: Create a custom vocabulary in table format in Amazon Transcribe with each term as it is spoken, with letters and numbers as words, and add it to each job.
This is the right feature, and for a brand name without digits, this row is enough, because the DisplayAs column is optional. The problem is the part codes. When the DisplayAs column is empty, Amazon Transcribe uses the contents of the Phrase column in the output. The Phrase column cannot hold digits, so each code comes out with its numbers spelled as words. The official record must show KT45R, with the digits.

For a question about an order, the model's response stops with a request to use the lookup tool, and the request carries an ID.
The application runs the tool, which returns the order details as JSON. The application keeps the model's response. Right after it, the application adds the order details as a second message from the assistant, and calls Converse again. The call fails. The tool itself works and returns the right data.
How should the application send the tool output to the model?
questions.promptText:
A company builds an order assistant with the Converse API and Claude Sonnet in Amazon Bedrock. Each request includes a tool definition for an order lookup tool, which an AWS Lambda function runs. For a question about an order, the model's response stops with a request to use the lookup tool, and the request carries an ID.
The application runs the tool, which returns the order details as JSON. The application keeps the model's response. Right after it, the application adds the order details as a second message from the assistant, and calls Converse again. The call fails. The tool itself works and returns the right data.
How should the application send the tool output to the model?

options.text: Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add a user message with a document block that holds the order details as a text file.
Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add a user message with a toolResult block that holds the order details and the same toolUseId.
Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add a user message with a toolResult block that holds the order details, the same toolUseId and the status error.
Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add the order details as text in the system field of the next Converse request.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add a user message with a toolResult block that holds the order details and the same toolUseId.
When the model wants a tool, its response is an assistant message with a toolUse block, and the stop reason is tool_use. The block holds the tool name, the input and a toolUseId. The application keeps that assistant message in the conversation. Then it builds a user message with a toolResult block. The toolResult carries the same toolUseId, so the model knows which request the output answers, and the order details go in its content as JSON. The next Converse call sends the whole conversation, and the model writes its answer from the result.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.3: "Format input data for FM inference according to model-specific requirements"
Example: "conversation formatting for dialog-based applications"

Sources:

  • Call a tool with the Converse API

  • ToolResultBlock (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Converse (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

INCORRECT: Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add a user message with a document block that holds the order details as a text file.
A document block adds a file to a user message, such as a report or a spreadsheet that the user wants the model to read. It fits when a user shares a document. Here, the model asked for a tool, and its request carries an ID. A document block has no toolUseId, so nothing in it answers that request. Tool output goes back in a toolResult block.

INCORRECT: Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add a user message with a toolResult block that holds the order details, the same toolUseId and the status error.
This is the right block in the right message. The status field tells the model whether the tool worked, and the value error is for a tool that failed, for example a lookup that found no order. The error tells the model that the tool did not work, so the model can react to the failure. Here the tool worked and returned the right order details. With the status error, the model gets the data together with a message that the lookup failed.

INCORRECT: Add the model's response message to the conversation, then add the order details as text in the system field of the next Converse request.
The system field gives the model instructions or context for the whole conversation, such as the task or the persona of the assistant. It fits text that applies to every turn. The order details answer one tool request, and the model asked for them with an ID. Text in the system field is not linked to that request. Tool output goes back to the model in a toolResult block inside a user message, with the same toolUseId.

The assistant said that 2 pounds weighed more than 1.5 kilograms. The team told the model in the system prompt to convert all values first, but the same orders still gave different results on different runs.
Auditors must see the exact values behind each answer. New orders arrive all day, and the assistant must use each one within a minute.
Which change should the team make before the prompt is built?

A company's order assistant uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to compare orders from three systems. Two systems write the day and the month of a date in opposite order. Amounts use a comma or a period as the decimal mark, and weights come in pounds or kilograms.
The assistant said that 2 pounds weighed more than 1.5 kilograms. The team told the model in the system prompt to convert all values first, but the same orders still gave different results on different runs.
Auditors must see the exact values behind each answer. New orders arrive all day, and the assistant must use each one within a minute.
Which change should the team make before the prompt is built?

options.text: An AWS Lambda function converts the dates, amounts and weights in each record to one standard format with fixed rules, and stores the converted record.
An Amazon Bedrock model call converts the dates, amounts and weights in each record to one standard format, and stores the converted record.
Amazon Comprehend detects the dates, amounts and weights in each record, and the application stores the detected values next to the original record.
An AWS Glue ETL job converts the dates, amounts and weights in each night's records to one standard format with fixed rules, and stores them in Amazon S3.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An AWS Lambda function converts the dates, amounts and weights in each record to one standard format with fixed rules, and stores the converted record.
A Lambda function runs code that the team writes, and it fits data processing that must run as each event arrives. Here the code applies fixed rules. It reads each date in the pattern of its source system, it reads each amount with the right decimal mark, and it converts every weight to one unit, for example kilograms. The same record always gives the same result, because the rules do not change from run to run. The function stores the converted record, so auditors can see the exact values behind each answer. The model then compares values that are already in one format.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.4: "Enhance input data quality to improve FM response quality and consistency"
Example: "Lambda functions to normalize data"

Sources:

  • What is AWS Lambda?
  • GENPERF02-BP02 Optimize inference parameters to improve response quality
  • Entities (Amazon Comprehend Developer Guide)

INCORRECT: An Amazon Bedrock model call converts the dates, amounts and weights in each record to one standard format, and stores the converted record.
A model call can rewrite text in a new format. It fits free text, where the formats vary too much for fixed rules. Here the formats are known: three source systems, each with its own pattern. Foundation models are non-deterministic, and inference settings help reduce this variation. The team already saw the same orders give different results on different runs when the model converted the values, and a separate model call converts them in the same way.

INCORRECT: Amazon Comprehend detects the dates, amounts and weights in each record, and the application stores the detected values next to the original record.
Amazon Comprehend finds entities in text, such as dates and quantities. It fits documents where the values are hidden in sentences and must first be found. Comprehend returns each entity with its type and its text as written. So a date keeps the order of day and month from its source system, and a weight keeps its unit. The model still has to convert the values, and the problem stays.

INCORRECT: An AWS Glue ETL job converts the dates, amounts and weights in each night's records to one standard format with fixed rules, and stores them in Amazon S3.
A Glue ETL job with a scheduled trigger applies fixed rules to many records at once. It fits data that people use the next day, such as a daily report. Here, new orders arrive all day, and the assistant must use each one within a minute. A nightly job converts an order many hours after it arrives.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A law firm keeps its signed contracts as files in Amazon S3, and the contract records, such as client, status and end date, in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. Staff update the records all day.
Its new assistant uses a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. Lawyers ask what clauses mean in their own words, such as whether a client can leave early without a fee. They also ask for lists, such as one client's active contracts that end this quarter. A list must miss no contract that fits and must show each status as it is at that moment. The database team must approve every query before it runs.
Which components should the firm add?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A law firm keeps its signed contracts as files in Amazon S3, and the contract records, such as client, status and end date, in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. Staff update the records all day.
Its new assistant uses a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. Lawyers ask what clauses mean in their own words, such as whether a client can leave early without a fee. They also ask for lists, such as one client's active contracts that end this quarter. A list must miss no contract that fits and must show each status as it is at that moment. The database team must approve every query before it runs.
Which components should the firm add?
Select TWO.

options.text: A tool in an AWS Lambda function that calls the Retrieve API on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases that holds the text of the contract files.
A tool in an AWS Lambda function that runs one of a few fixed SQL queries on the RDS database with the model's values and returns all matching rows.
A tool in an AWS Lambda function that runs a SQL query that the model writes for each question on the RDS database and returns the rows.
An AWS Lambda function that writes each changed record as a text file to the contract bucket and starts an ingestion job, so each Retrieve call can also return records.
A metadata file with the client, status and end date from the RDS record next to each contract file, and a Retrieve filter on these fields for list questions.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A tool in an AWS Lambda function that calls the Retrieve API on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases that holds the text of the contract files.
A knowledge base splits the contract files into chunks and stores an embedding of each chunk in its vector store. An embedding stands for the meaning of a text. The Retrieve API turns the question into an embedding too, and it returns the chunks that are closest in meaning. So a question about leaving early without a fee finds the right clause, even when the contract uses other words, such as "termination". The model does not call the tool itself. When the model asks for this tool, the application runs the Lambda function and sends the chunks back to the model as the tool result. Each chunk carries the location of its source file.

CORRECT: A tool in an AWS Lambda function that runs one of a few fixed SQL queries on the RDS database with the model's values and returns all matching rows.
List questions need exact answers: every contract that fits, with its status as it is now. Results from a search by meaning can vary, so they do not suit exact lists or counts. A SQL query on the RDS database returns all rows that meet its conditions, from the data as it is when the query runs. The tool holds a few fixed queries, for example the contracts of one client, with one status, that end between two dates. The model sends only the values, such as the client name and the dates. So every query that runs is one that the database team approved in advance, and the list shows the records that staff just updated.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.1: "Create advanced vector database architectures specifically for FM augmentation to enable efficient semantic retrieval beyond traditional search capabilities"
Example: "Amazon RDS with Amazon S3 document repositories"

Sources:

  • Use a tool to complete an Amazon Bedrock model response

  • Build a Text-to-SQL solution for data consistency in generative AI using Amazon Nova

  • Sync your data with your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base

INCORRECT: A tool in an AWS Lambda function that runs a SQL query that the model writes for each question on the RDS database and returns the rows.
When the model writes the SQL for each question, the design is called text-to-SQL. It fits analysts who ask new questions that no fixed query covers, and like the fixed queries, it reads the current records. But here the database team must approve every query before it runs. A query that the model writes at the moment of the question is new each time, so nobody can approve it in advance.

INCORRECT: An AWS Lambda function that writes each changed record as a text file to the contract bucket and starts an ingestion job, so each Retrieve call can also return records.
Writing database records into a knowledge base as text fits record data that people search by meaning, for example case notes. It fails both needs of the list questions here. A changed record reaches the knowledge base only after the data source is synced, and staff update records all day, so a status can be out of date when a lawyer asks. A search also returns only the chunks that are closest to the question, up to a maximum number of results, so a list can leave out contracts that fit.

INCORRECT: A metadata file with the client, status and end date from the RDS record next to each contract file, and a Retrieve filter on these fields for list questions.
A metadata file adds attributes to one file in the data source, and a filter in the Retrieve call keeps only the chunks whose attributes match. This fits attributes that rarely change, such as the practice area of a contract. Here the status changes all day, and a changed metadata file reaches the knowledge base only with the next sync, so the filter can use an old status. A filtered search also returns no more results than the call allows, so a long list can still leave out contracts that fit.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
An online store runs a shopping assistant with a model in Amazon Bedrock. The assistant finds products with a vector search in Amazon OpenSearch Service, and each search returns up to ten products. Each product document in the index also holds the price and stock, which a job copies each night from an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Prices and stock change many times an hour, so answers show old prices and sold-out items. In a load test, writing these changes into the index slowed searches for all users, whether one by one or in groups. The table holds several million products, and each answer may add only a few milliseconds.
How should the assistant get the current price and stock?
questions.promptText:
An online store runs a shopping assistant with a model in Amazon Bedrock. The assistant finds products with a vector search in Amazon OpenSearch Service, and each search returns up to ten products. Each product document in the index also holds the price and stock, which a job copies each night from an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Prices and stock change many times an hour, so answers show old prices and sold-out items. In a load test, writing these changes into the index slowed searches for all users, whether one by one or in groups. The table holds several million products, and each answer may add only a few milliseconds.
How should the assistant get the current price and stock?

options.text: Keep price and stock in each product document, and update the documents from a DynamoDB stream through a Lambda function as each change happens.
Keep price and stock in each product document, and update the documents from a DynamoDB stream through a Lambda function in batches of changes.
After each search, run a Scan with a filter on the returned product IDs against the DynamoDB table, and add the current values to the prompt.
Leave price and stock out of the index, and read them for the returned product IDs from the DynamoDB table with one BatchGetItem request.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Leave price and stock out of the index, and read them for the returned product IDs from the DynamoDB table with one BatchGetItem request.
The vector search finds products by meaning, and it does not need the price or the stock to do that. So these two values can stay in one place only: the DynamoDB table, which already receives every change. After the search returns the product IDs, one BatchGetItem request reads those items by their primary keys, and the application adds the current price and stock to the prompt. No price change writes to the index, so searches stay fast. BatchGetItem uses eventually consistent reads by default, and the application can ask for strongly consistent reads when the latest value must count.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.1: "Create advanced vector database architectures specifically for FM augmentation to enable efficient semantic retrieval beyond traditional search capabilities"
Example: "Amazon DynamoDB with vector databases for metadata and embeddings"

Sources:

  • BatchGetItem (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference)

  • Process DynamoDB records with Lambda

  • Scanning tables in DynamoDB

INCORRECT: Keep price and stock in each product document, and update the documents from a DynamoDB stream through a Lambda function as each change happens.
A DynamoDB stream records the changes to the items in a table, and a Lambda function can copy each change into the index. This keeps the index current, and it fits values that change a few times a day, such as a product description. Here prices and stock change many times an hour. The load test showed that writing these changes into the index slows searches for all users.

INCORRECT: Keep price and stock in each product document, and update the documents from a DynamoDB stream through a Lambda function in batches of changes.
Lambda can read a DynamoDB stream in batches, and a batch window lets it gather records for a set time before it runs. So the function writes groups of changes instead of one change at a time. Fewer, larger writes help when the number of write calls is the problem. Here the load test showed that the writes slowed searches whether they came one by one or in groups, and prices change many times an hour, so the index would still take writes all day.

INCORRECT: After each search, run a Scan with a filter on the returned product IDs against the DynamoDB table, and add the current values to the prompt.
A Scan reads every item in a table, and a filter applies only after the read, so the Scan uses the same read capacity with or without the filter. It fits a job that needs the whole table, such as an export. The table holds several million products. A Scan for ten products reads all of them for each answer, and each answer may add only a few milliseconds.

questions.promptHtml:
An airline keeps its aircraft maintenance manuals in Amazon S3 and searches them through a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Each manual holds many procedures. A procedure starts with a line such as "Procedure 12:", and it holds numbered steps and a warning box. Procedures run from half a page to several pages.
Mechanics got steps without their warning box, because the current chunks split procedures in the middle. Each procedure must now be exactly one chunk. The documentation team owns the manual files, and the files in the bucket must stay as they are published. The team wants to keep the knowledge base's own ingestion jobs.
Which chunking setup meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
An airline keeps its aircraft maintenance manuals in Amazon S3 and searches them through a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Each manual holds many procedures. A procedure starts with a line such as "Procedure 12:", and it holds numbered steps and a warning box. Procedures run from half a page to several pages.
Mechanics got steps without their warning box, because the current chunks split procedures in the middle. Each procedure must now be exactly one chunk. The documentation team owns the manual files, and the files in the bucket must stay as they are published. The team wants to keep the knowledge base's own ingestion jobs.
Which chunking setup meets these needs?

options.text: Use fixed-size chunking with no overlap, and add a custom transformation Lambda function that adds the procedure title to each chunk as metadata.
Use hierarchical chunking with a parent chunk size larger than the longest procedure, so each small child chunk returns with its full parent chunk.
Use fixed-size chunking with a maximum chunk size larger than the longest procedure and no overlap, so each chunk is large enough for any procedure.
Use no chunking, and add a custom transformation Lambda function that splits each file into chunks at the first line of every procedure.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use no chunking, and add a custom transformation Lambda function that splits each file into chunks at the first line of every procedure.
A custom transformation Lambda function adds the team's own logic to the ingestion job of the knowledge base. For chunking logic that the built-in strategies do not offer, the team chooses no chunking and gives the knowledge base a Lambda function that holds the chunking logic. The knowledge base writes the files to an intermediate S3 bucket, and the function reads them there. The function starts a new chunk at each line such as "Procedure 12:", so each procedure, with its steps and its warning box, becomes one chunk. The manual files in the source bucket stay as they are, and the knowledge base still runs its own ingestion jobs.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.1: "Develop effective document segmentation approaches to optimize retrieval performance for FM context augmentation"

Sources:

  • Use a custom transformation Lambda function to define how your data is ingested

  • How content chunking works for knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Use fixed-size chunking with no overlap, and add a custom transformation Lambda function that adds the procedure title to each chunk as metadata.
A built-in strategy can work together with a custom transformation Lambda function. The knowledge base cuts the chunks first, and then the function adds chunk-level metadata, such as the title of the procedure. This fits documents where the chunks are already right and only need more information for search and filters. Here the chunks themselves are the problem. Fixed-size chunking ends each chunk at a set number of tokens, so a procedure can still be split between two chunks. A title in the metadata does not move that border.

INCORRECT: Use hierarchical chunking with a parent chunk size larger than the longest procedure, so each small child chunk returns with its full parent chunk.
Hierarchical chunking creates small child chunks inside larger parent chunks. A search finds the child chunks, and the knowledge base replaces them with their parent chunks, so the model gets more context. This looks like a good fit, but the parent chunk size is a number of tokens. A parent chunk ends when it reaches that size, not when a procedure ends. So a parent chunk can start in the middle of one procedure and end in the next one.

INCORRECT: Use fixed-size chunking with a maximum chunk size larger than the longest procedure and no overlap, so each chunk is large enough for any procedure.
Fixed-size chunking cuts the text into chunks of a set number of tokens. It fits documents with a flat structure, such as short notes of similar length. A chunk ends when it reaches the size, wherever that falls in the text. Procedures here run from half a page to several pages. A chunk sized for the longest procedure holds several short procedures together, and each border between chunks still falls at a token count, not at the first line of a procedure.

An AWS Lambda function reads batches of article texts from an Amazon SQS queue, and it calls the model once for each text. When one call fails, the function returns an error for the whole batch.
Each failure now makes the function embed every text in the batch again, and embedding costs have risen. Most failures are short errors, and the failed text works on the next try. The queue receives thousands of texts each hour, and the team must keep the current batch size to process them in time.
Which change stops the extra embedding calls?

Each failure now makes the function embed every text in the batch again, and embedding costs have risen. Most failures are short errors, and the failed text works on the next try. The queue receives thousands of texts each hour, and the team must keep the current batch size to process them in time.
Which change stops the extra embedding calls?

options.text: On the event source mapping, set the batch size to one, so each failed call sends a single text back to the queue.
On the event source mapping, turn on ReportBatchItemFailures, so the function returns the IDs of the failed texts and the other texts leave the queue.
On the source queue, add a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue, so a text that fails several times moves out of the source queue.
On the source queue, raise the visibility timeout to several times the function timeout, so each batch has time to finish before its texts return.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: On the event source mapping, turn on ReportBatchItemFailures, so the function returns the IDs of the failed texts and the other texts leave the queue.
By default, when the function returns an error for a batch, every message in the batch becomes visible in the queue again, including the texts that the function already embedded. So the next invocation embeds them again. ReportBatchItemFailures turns on partial batch responses in the event source mapping. The function catches each failed call and returns the message IDs of those texts in a batchItemFailures list. Only these messages become visible again, and the next invocation embeds just the texts that failed. The batch size stays the same.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.2: "Select and configure optimal embedding solutions to create efficient vector representations for semantic search"
Example: "Lambda functions to batch generate embeddings"

Sources:

  • Handling errors for an SQS event source in Lambda

  • Creating and configuring an Amazon SQS event source mapping

INCORRECT: On the event source mapping, set the batch size to one, so each failed call sends a single text back to the queue.
A batch size of one gives each text its own invocation, so a failure affects one text. It fits a queue with few messages, where a large batch brings no benefit. Here, the queue receives thousands of texts each hour. The team must keep the current batch size, or the function cannot process the texts as fast as they arrive.

INCORRECT: On the source queue, add a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue, so a text that fails several times moves out of the source queue.
A dead-letter queue collects messages that fail many times, such as a text that the model rejects on every try. It keeps such a message from coming back again and again. Here, most failures are short errors, and the failed text works on the next try. Each failure still sends the whole batch back, so the texts that worked are embedded again.

INCORRECT: On the source queue, raise the visibility timeout to several times the function timeout, so each batch has time to finish before its texts return.
The visibility timeout hides messages while a function works on them. A longer timeout helps when messages come back before a batch is done, for example when the function is throttled. Here the batch ends with an error, and all of its messages come back after the timeout. A longer timeout changes when they come back, not which ones.

A company runs a support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. An AWS Lambda function calls the Retrieve API on its existing knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The team keeps this knowledge base and its vector store. Before any chunk reaches a model, the function checks each chunk against the user's contract in a separate contract system. Then it builds its own prompt and calls the Converse API.
Questions with two or three parts return chunks for only one part. When the team asked for more chunks, the extra chunks covered the same part. Questions with one part, even ones that name a part number, get the right chunks.
Which change retrieves chunks for every part of a question?

options.text: Change the function to call RetrieveAndGenerate with QUERY_DECOMPOSITION in its orchestration configuration, and move the function's own prompt instructions into the generation prompt template.
Change the function to add a reranker model to the reranking configuration of its Retrieve call, so the chunks that fit each part of the question rank first.
Change the function to set overrideSearchType to HYBRID in the vector search configuration of its Retrieve call, so the search also matches the exact words of the question.
Change the function to ask a small model to split each question into sub-questions, call Retrieve once for each sub-question, and merge the chunks without duplicates.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Change the function to ask a small model to split each question into sub-questions, call Retrieve once for each sub-question, and merge the chunks without duplicates.
This is query decomposition, done inside the function. The small model turns one question with three parts into three short questions. Each Retrieve call then searches for one part, so each part gets its own results. The function merges the results and drops the chunks that come back twice. The order of steps stays the same: the function still gets the chunks first, checks them against the contract system, and writes its own prompt for the Converse call.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.5: "Develop sophisticated query handling systems to improve the retrieval effectiveness and result quality for FM augmentation"
Example: "Lambda functions for query decomposition"

Sources:

  • Configure and customize queries and response generation

  • KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Improve the relevance of query responses with a reranker model in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Change the function to call RetrieveAndGenerate with QUERY_DECOMPOSITION in its orchestration configuration, and move the function's own prompt instructions into the generation prompt template.
This option turns on the query decomposition that the knowledge base offers. The setting belongs to RetrieveAndGenerate, so the function must move to that API. That is a good choice when the knowledge base may build the answer itself. Here it breaks the order of steps. RetrieveAndGenerate retrieves the chunks and passes them to the model in the same call. The function can no longer check each chunk against the contract system before a model sees it.

INCORRECT: Change the function to add a reranker model to the reranking configuration of its Retrieve call, so the chunks that fit each part of the question rank first.
A reranker model scores the chunks that the search returned and puts them in a new order. It helps when the right chunks are in the results but rank too low. Here they are not in the results at all. When the team asked for more chunks, the extra chunks still covered the same part. A new order cannot add chunks that the search never returned.

INCORRECT: Change the function to set overrideSearchType to HYBRID in the vector search configuration of its Retrieve call, so the search also matches the exact words of the question.
Hybrid search combines a search on meaning with a search on the raw text. It helps most with keyword searches, for example a question that names a part number. The scenario says that questions with one part, even ones with a part number, already get the right chunks. So the search itself works well. The problem is that one search for a question with three parts returns chunks for only one of them.
