Which design should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A company's support assistant searches a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Before each search, one AWS Lambda function changes the question in three steps. A model in Amazon Bedrock translates it into English, the function expands internal acronyms from a glossary table in Amazon DynamoDB, and a second model call rewrites the question for search.
Sometimes a step fails with no clear error. New log lines now show which step failed, but a retry still runs all three steps, and each model call costs tokens.
The team needs a retry of the failed step alone, a record of each step's input and output, and no search before all three steps succeed.
Which design should the team use?

options.text: An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state that invokes the current function, and a Retry field on that state for the errors of any step.
An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state for each step, and a Retry field on each state for the errors of that step.
An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state that invokes the current function, and a Catch field that sends the original question to the search.
An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state for each step, and a Catch field on each state that passes the question to the next step unchanged.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state for each step, and a Retry field on each state for the errors of that step.
Step Functions runs each step as its own Task state. The translation and the rewrite can call the model through the Step Functions integration with Amazon Bedrock. The glossary step can run in a small Lambda function that reads the DynamoDB table. When a state reports an error, its Retry field runs that state again, and the steps that already worked do not run again. So a retry costs tokens only for the model call that failed. In the execution details of the Step Functions console, the team can read the input and the output of each state, which gives it a record of each step for each question. The search comes after the three states, so a question reaches the search only when all three steps succeed.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.5: "Develop sophisticated query handling systems to improve the retrieval effectiveness and result quality for FM augmentation"
Example: "Step Functions for query transformation"

Sources:

  • Handling errors in Step Functions workflows

  • Viewing execution details in the Step Functions console

  • Invoke and customize Amazon Bedrock models with Step Functions

INCORRECT: An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state that invokes the current function, and a Retry field on that state for the errors of any step.
A Retry field on one state that runs the whole function is a simple way to add retries to existing code. It fits a function that does one task. Here the function holds three steps. When the rewrite fails, the retry runs the translation and the glossary step again, and their model calls cost tokens again. The team needs a retry of the failed step alone.

INCORRECT: An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state that invokes the current function, and a Catch field that sends the original question to the search.
A Catch field sends the workflow to a fallback state when a state fails and its retries do not help, for example to search with the original question. This keeps an assistant answering when a preparation step is optional. Here, no question may reach the search before all three steps succeed. A question in another language, with its internal acronyms, would reach the search.

INCORRECT: An AWS Step Functions workflow with one Task state for each step, and a Catch field on each state that passes the question to the next step unchanged.
One state for each step gives a record of each step, and a Catch field on each state keeps the workflow moving after an error. It fits steps that the process can skip. Here, the failed step would not run again. The question would reach the search with a step missing, for example with the acronyms still in it, and the team requires all three steps to succeed.

questions.promptText:
A company has five agent teams. Each team wrote its own code to search the same vector index in Amazon OpenSearch Service. Each team filters and ranks the results in its own way, so the same question returns different chunks in each agent.
Two of the agents run outside AWS and have no AWS credentials. All agents reach their other tools through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with an OAuth token. The search team wants to change the search logic in one place, for example to add a filter, and every agent must use each change with no agent redeployed.
Which design gives every agent the same search?

options.text: One Lambda function for each team's search code, each added as a target of the AgentCore Gateway, which every agent calls as a tool through its MCP client.
One Lambda function for each team's search code, which every agent calls directly with the Lambda Invoke API and the AWS SDK.
One Lambda function that holds the search code, which every agent calls directly with the Lambda Invoke API and the AWS SDK.
One Lambda function that holds the search code, added as a target of the AgentCore Gateway, which every agent calls as a tool through its MCP client.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: One Lambda function that holds the search code, added as a target of the AgentCore Gateway, which every agent calls as a tool through its MCP client.
AgentCore Gateway turns Lambda functions and APIs into tools that agents can use through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The team adds the search function as a gateway target, with a tool schema that names the tool and its input fields. Every agent already connects to the gateway with its MCP client and its OAuth token, so it can find this tool and call it like its other tools. All agents now run the same search code, so the same question returns the same chunks. When the search team changes the function, every agent gets the new logic on its next call, and no agent is redeployed.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.6: "Create consistent access mechanisms to enable seamless integration with FMs"
Example: "Model Context Protocol [MCP] clients for vector queries"

Sources:

  • AWS Lambda function targets

  • Core concepts for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

  • Invoke (AWS Lambda API Reference)

INCORRECT: One Lambda function for each team's search code, each added as a target of the AgentCore Gateway, which every agent calls as a tool through its MCP client.
A gateway can have many targets. It puts the tools of all its MCP targets, such as Lambda functions, in one tool list, so every agent sees every tool. With one function for each team, every agent, including the agents outside AWS, has one way to reach the search. This fits teams that must each keep their own search logic. Here the problem is that logic. Each function still filters and ranks in its own way, so the same question still returns different chunks. A change to the search would also have to reach five functions, not one place.

INCORRECT: One Lambda function for each team's search code, which every agent calls directly with the Lambda Invoke API and the AWS SDK.
One function for each team gives each team one place for its own search code, and a direct call with the AWS SDK fits agents that run on AWS with an IAM role. Here the problem is the search logic itself. Each function still filters and ranks in its own way, so the same question still returns different chunks. Two agents also run outside AWS and have no AWS credentials, so they cannot call the functions with the Invoke API.

INCORRECT: One Lambda function that holds the search code, which every agent calls directly with the Lambda Invoke API and the AWS SDK.
One function puts the search logic in one place, and a direct call fits agents that run on AWS with an IAM role. The Invoke API requires permission for the lambda:InvokeFunction action, and that permission belongs to an AWS identity. Two agents run outside AWS and have no AWS credentials, so they cannot call the function this way.

Users now see a different name and tone in each feature, although the answers stay on topic and pass every content check. The team wants one role text for all features, and each feature must still add its own task details. How should the team make every feature use the same role text?
questions.promptText:
An online shop's AI assistant has five features. An AWS Lambda function serves each feature and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. Each function keeps its own copy of the assistant's role text, and the copies no longer match.
Users now see a different name and tone in each feature, although the answers stay on topic and pass every content check. The team wants one role text for all features, and each feature must still add its own task details. Prompt writers, who do not change code, must test each change to the role text with the model before users see it.
How should the team make every feature use the same role text?

options.text: Create one prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with the role text in its system prompt and a variable for the task details, and have every function call a version of the prompt.
Add a word filter that blocks the other assistant names to one Amazon Bedrock guardrail, and have every function apply that guardrail to its Converse requests.
Put the role text in one Lambda layer that every function includes, and have every function add the text from the layer as the system prompt of its Converse requests.
Add denied topics for replies that do not match the role text to one Amazon Bedrock guardrail, and have every function apply that guardrail to its Converse requests.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create one prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with the role text in its system prompt and a variable for the task details, and have every function call a version of the prompt.
A prompt in Prompt Management can contain a system prompt and variables in double curly braces, such as {{task_details}}, that the caller fills in. Each function calls Converse with the ARN of a prompt version as the model ID and passes its own task details in the promptVariables field. So every feature uses the same role text, and each feature still adds its own task details. Prompt writers open the prompt in Prompt builder in the console, enter test values for the variables, and run the prompt with the model. Their changes stay in the working draft, and the functions keep calling the version that they name, so users do not see an untested change. When the writers are satisfied, they create a new version for production.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.1: "Create effective model instruction frameworks to control FM behavior and outputs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to enforce role definitions"

Sources:

  • Create a prompt using Prompt management

  • Converse (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Test a prompt using Prompt management

INCORRECT: Add a word filter that blocks the other assistant names to one Amazon Bedrock guardrail, and have every function apply that guardrail to its Converse requests.
With a word filter, a guardrail blocks exact words and phrases in prompts and in model responses, for example the name of a competitor or profane words. A word filter fits an assistant that must never use certain words. Here each feature uses its own name and tone, and the team wants one role text for all features. A filter can block a reply that uses another name, but the filter gives the assistant no name and no tone. The user sees a blocked message in place of the answer, and the tone still changes from feature to feature.

INCORRECT: Put the role text in one Lambda layer that every function includes, and have every function add the text from the layer as the system prompt of its Converse requests.
Lambda layers are .zip file archives with code or data, such as configuration files, that many functions share. One layer can keep one copy of the role text for all five functions. Lambda has no tool that runs a new role text with the model and shows the answer. To try a change, someone must publish a new layer version, attach it to a function, and invoke the function with a test event. That changes the setup of a function, which is developer work, and the prompt writers do not change code.

INCORRECT: Add denied topics for replies that do not match the role text to one Amazon Bedrock guardrail, and have every function apply that guardrail to its Converse requests.
Denied topics in a guardrail block subjects that are not wanted in an application, for example investment advice in a banking assistant. They fit an assistant that starts to answer questions about subjects that it must avoid. Here the answers stay on topic and pass every content check. The problem is the name and the tone of the assistant, and a guardrail that blocks content does not set a name or a tone.

Last month, an outage in that Region stopped the applications in both Regions, because none of them could load a template. Teams overwrite a template file when they change it, and auditors now want the text of every past template kept. A change to a template must reach every application with no extra step for the teams.
Which features should the team add to the template repository?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company keeps its prompt templates as text files in an Amazon S3 bucket. Many applications load a template from the bucket each time they call a model in Amazon Bedrock. The applications run in two AWS Regions, but the bucket sits in one of them.
Last month, an outage in that Region stopped the applications in both Regions, because none of them could load a template. Teams overwrite a template file when they change it, and auditors now want the text of every past template kept. A change to a template must reach every application with no extra step for the teams.
Which features should the team add to the template repository?
Select TWO.

options.text: Use AWS CloudTrail data events for the template bucket as the audit record, so auditors can see each call that writes to a template file.
Set up S3 Same-Region Replication from the template bucket to a second bucket, so each template change is copied to it automatically.
Turn on S3 Versioning for the template bucket, so each overwrite of a template keeps the earlier text as an older version.
Move the templates into Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, and create a new prompt version each time a team changes a template.
Set up S3 Cross-Region Replication from the template bucket to a bucket in the second Region, so each template change is copied to it automatically.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on S3 Versioning for the template bucket, so each overwrite of a template keeps the earlier text as an older version.
S3 Versioning keeps several versions of an object in the same bucket. When a team overwrites a template, the new text becomes a new version, and the earlier text stays in the bucket.

A delete adds a delete marker instead of removing the text. So auditors can read and restore every past template. Replication also needs versioning on both the source bucket and the destination bucket, so the team turns it on in both.

CORRECT: Set up S3 Cross-Region Replication from the template bucket to a bucket in the second Region, so each template change is copied to it automatically.
Cross-Region Replication copies objects from one bucket to a bucket in another AWS Region, automatically and asynchronously. Each change to a template reaches the second bucket with no step by the teams.

Replication copies only new and changed objects, so the team copies the templates that are already in the bucket once, with S3 Batch Replication. The applications in each Region then load templates from the bucket in their own Region. An outage in one Region no longer stops the applications in the other Region.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.3: "Implement comprehensive prompt management and governance systems to ensure consistency and oversight of FM operations"
Example: "Amazon S3 to store template repositories"

Sources:

  • Replicating objects within and across Regions

  • Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning

  • Requirements and considerations for replication

INCORRECT: Use AWS CloudTrail data events for the template bucket as the audit record, so auditors can see each call that writes to a template file.
CloudTrail data events record the operations on the objects in a bucket, such as PutObject and DeleteObject. As an audit record, they fit auditors who must see each call that wrote to the templates. These auditors want something else: the text of every past template. A data event describes the call, and it does not hold the text that an overwrite replaced. So after an overwrite, the earlier text is gone. S3 Versioning is the feature that keeps it.

INCORRECT: Set up S3 Same-Region Replication from the template bucket to a second bucket, so each template change is copied to it automatically.
Same-Region Replication copies objects to another bucket in the same Region. It fits copies between production and test accounts, or logs that many buckets send to one bucket. Both buckets sit in the Region that failed last month, so the same outage would stop both copies.

INCORRECT: Move the templates into Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, and create a new prompt version each time a team changes a template.
Prompt Management keeps prompt versions, and each version is a snapshot for production use. It fits prompts that applications call through Amazon Bedrock, with the text kept for every version. But a prompt is a resource in one AWS Region, and its ARN names that Region. An outage in that Region would again leave the applications in both Regions with no template.

How should the team change the prompt?
questions.promptText:
A company reviews marketing drafts with Claude Sonnet in Amazon Bedrock. Each prompt holds the review instructions, the company's style guide, three example reviews and the draft, all in one block of plain text.
Two problems appear. Some reviews copy whole sentences from the example reviews. Other reviews list rules from the style guide as mistakes in the draft. The example reviews were added last month, because reviews written from the instructions alone came out in the wrong layout.
How should the team change the prompt?

options.text: Put the instructions, the style guide, the example reviews and the draft each in its own XML tags, and name these tags in the instructions.
Put each example review in its own example tags, and keep the instructions, the style guide and the draft together in one block of plain text.
Remove the example reviews from the prompt, and describe in the instructions, in words, the layout that a good review must follow.
Move the review instructions to the end of the prompt, after the draft, and leave the instructions, style guide, examples and draft in one block of plain text.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Put the instructions, the style guide, the example reviews and the draft each in its own XML tags, and name these tags in the instructions.
XML tags mark the important parts of a prompt, and they are a common practice with Claude models. Here each part gets its own tags, for example <instructions>, <style_guide>, <examples> and <draft>. The instructions then name the tags. For example: review the text in the draft tags against the rules in the style guide tags, and use the examples for the layout. The model can now tell which text is an example, which text is a rule and which text it must review. This fixes both problems and keeps the examples that the layout needs.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.5: "Enhance FM performance to refine prompts iteratively and improve response quality beyond basic prompting techniques"
Example: "structured input components"

Sources:

  • Prompt templates and examples for Amazon Bedrock text models
  • What is a prompt?
  • Design a prompt

INCORRECT: Put each example review in its own example tags, and keep the instructions, the style guide and the draft together in one block of plain text.
Example tags around each example are a good practice with Claude models, and they help the model tell the examples apart from the rest of the prompt. That fixes the copied sentences. But the style guide and the draft still sit together in one block, so the model still cannot tell a rule from the text that it must review. The second problem stays.

INCORRECT: Remove the example reviews from the prompt, and describe in the instructions, in words, the layout that a good review must follow.
A layout described in words avoids copied text, and it works when the model follows the words well. Here the team added the example reviews because reviews written from the instructions alone came out in the wrong layout. Without the examples, that problem comes back, and the style guide problem stays.

INCORRECT: Move the review instructions to the end of the prompt, after the draft, and leave the instructions, style guide, examples and draft in one block of plain text.
Putting the instruction at the end of a prompt often gives better results, and it helps when a long prompt makes the model lose the task. Here the model does the task, but it mixes up the parts of the prompt: it copies sentences from the examples, and it reviews rules from the style guide as if they were part of the draft. In one block of plain text, nothing shows where the examples and the style guide end and where the draft begins. A new order adds no borders, so both problems stay.

After each draft, a check step tests every rule. The step returns only pass or fail, and editors fix the drafts that fail.

The prompt lists all 15 rules with examples, but some drafts still fail. When the team ran the same prompt again for a failed draft, the new draft often broke the same rule.

Only descriptions that fail the check may use extra tokens. The workflow can make only a fixed number of model calls for each description.

Which parts should the workflow include?

Select THREE.
questions.promptText:
A company uses an AWS Step Functions workflow and a model in Amazon Bedrock to write product descriptions. Each description must pass 15 brand rules, such as a word limit and rules about tone. After each draft, a check step tests every rule. The step returns only pass or fail, and editors fix the drafts that fail.
The prompt lists all 15 rules with examples, but some drafts still fail. When the team ran the same prompt again for a failed draft, the new draft often broke the same rule.
Only descriptions that fail the check may use extra tokens. The workflow can make only a fixed number of model calls for each description.
Which parts should the workflow include?
Select THREE.

options.text: In each round, a model call receives the original prompt again, and it writes a fresh draft that goes to the next check.
In each round, the check step returns the list of broken rules for the draft, in addition to the pass or fail result.
A Choice state ends the loop when no rule is broken or when the round count reaches a limit, and it publishes the last draft on the product page.
In each round, a model call receives the draft together with the list of broken rules, and it rewrites the draft before the next check.
Starting with the first draft, three model calls in each round write three drafts in parallel, and the workflow keeps the draft with the shortest list of broken rules.
A Choice state ends the loop when no rule is broken or when the round count reaches a limit, and it flags a draft that still fails for review.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In each round, the check step returns the list of broken rules for the draft, in addition to the pass or fail result.
With this change, the check becomes the evaluator of a feedback loop. An evaluator reviews each draft against a rubric, and here the rubric is the 15 brand rules. Code in an AWS Lambda function can test a simple rule, such as the word limit, and a model call can judge tone. Today the check returns only pass or fail. The list tells the next step which rules the draft breaks, and an empty list means that the draft passes. The check already runs for every draft, so the list adds no model call.

CORRECT: In each round, a model call receives the draft together with the list of broken rules, and it rewrites the draft before the next check.
The refine part of the loop sends the model its own draft together with the rules that the draft broke, so the model knows what to change. Running the same prompt again gave the model no such information, and the new draft often broke the same rule. Only drafts that fail the check reach this step, so only those descriptions use extra tokens.

CORRECT: A Choice state ends the loop when no rule is broken or when the round count reaches a limit, and it flags a draft that still fails for review.
A Choice state adds conditions to a workflow. Step Functions checks the conditions in order and goes to the state that belongs to the first true condition. Here one condition ends the loop when the list of broken rules is empty. Another condition ends the loop when the round count reaches the limit, so no description goes past a fixed number of model calls. The States.MathAdd intrinsic function can add one to the round count in each round, without a Lambda function. A draft that still fails goes to the editors, as failed drafts do today.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.5: "Enhance FM performance to refine prompts iteratively and improve response quality beyond basic prompting techniques"
Example: "feedback loops"

Sources:

  • Evaluator reflect-refine loop patterns

  • Choice workflow state

  • Intrinsic functions for JSONPath states in Step Functions

INCORRECT: In each round, a model call receives the original prompt again, and it writes a fresh draft that goes to the next check.
Running the same prompt again is a common way to recover from a random failure, because a new draft may pass by chance. The team already tried this approach, and the new draft often broke the same rule. The prompt tells the model nothing about the mistake, so the model tends to repeat the mistake.

INCORRECT: A Choice state ends the loop when no rule is broken or when the round count reaches a limit, and it publishes the last draft on the product page.
Publishing the last draft after a fixed number of rounds fits content where a small mistake is acceptable, such as internal notes. Here each description must pass all 15 brand rules, and editors fix the drafts that fail. A draft that still breaks a rule after the last round must go to the editors, not to the product page.

INCORRECT: Starting with the first draft, three model calls in each round write three drafts in parallel, and the workflow keeps the draft with the shortest list of broken rules.
When the budget allows extra model calls, a workflow can write several drafts in parallel and keep the best one, which can raise quality. This option writes three drafts in every round, starting with the first draft. So the workflow makes three model calls for the first draft of every description, even when one draft would pass the check. Only descriptions that fail the check may use extra tokens.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs four flows in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows, one for each support channel. Each flow starts with a prompt node that sorts each message into one of eight topics. Each flow defines this prompt inline, with its own copy of the text, the model and the inference settings.
The last fix changed the text, the model and the temperature, and it reached only two flows. The flows now sort the same message in different ways. Each channel team owns its flow and releases it when it chooses. The team built the flows with no code and wants to keep them that way.
How should the team make the sorting prompt one shared part of every flow?
questions.promptText:
A company runs four flows in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows, one for each support channel. Each flow starts with a prompt node that sorts each message into one of eight topics. Each flow defines this prompt inline, with its own copy of the text, the model and the inference settings.
The last fix changed the text, the model and the temperature, and it reached only two flows. The flows now sort the same message in different ways. Each channel team owns its flow and releases it when it chooses. The team built the flows with no code and wants to keep them that way.
How should the team make the sorting prompt one shared part of every flow?

options.text: Store the prompt text in an Amazon S3 object, and add an S3 retrieval node to each flow that passes the text to the inline prompt node.
Merge the four flows into one flow with one prompt node that holds the text, model and settings, and add a condition node that sends each message to its channel's steps.
Create the prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with its text, model and settings, and set the prompt node in each flow to use that prompt.
Keep the inline prompt node in each flow, and create a new flow version and an alias for each flow after every fix to the prompt.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create the prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with its text, model and settings, and set the prompt node in each flow to use that prompt.
Prompt Management stores prompts that many workflows can reuse. A prompt there holds the template text, the model and the inference settings, such as the temperature. A prompt node in a flow can define its prompt inline, or it can use a prompt from Prompt Management. When all four prompt nodes use the same prompt, the text, the model and the temperature are kept in one place. The flows no longer hold their own copies, so the copies cannot differ again. The team makes this change in the prompt nodes, with no code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.6: "Design complex prompt systems to handle sophisticated tasks with FMs"
Example: "reusable prompt components"

Sources:

  • Node types for your flow
  • Construct and store reusable prompts with Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock
  • Deploy a flow to your application using versions and aliases

INCORRECT: Store the prompt text in an Amazon S3 object, and add an S3 retrieval node to each flow that passes the text to the inline prompt node.
An S3 retrieval node reads an object from a bucket and passes its content to the next node. It fits shared text that many flows need, such as a long policy document. Here the last fix also changed the model and the temperature. An inline prompt node still holds its own model and inference settings, so these would still differ from flow to flow.

INCORRECT: Merge the four flows into one flow with one prompt node that holds the text, model and settings, and add a condition node that sends each message to its channel's steps.
One flow with one prompt node holds one copy of the prompt, and a condition node sends data from the previous node to different nodes, depending on the conditions that are defined, for example the channel of each message. This fits channels that share one owner and one release plan. Here each channel team owns its flow and releases it when it chooses. One merged flow would make the four teams share one flow and release every change together.

INCORRECT: Keep the inline prompt node in each flow, and create a new flow version and an alias for each flow after every fix to the prompt.
A flow version is a snapshot of one flow, and an alias points to a version. They let a team release a tested flow and switch back to an earlier version quickly. They share nothing between flows. Each flow would still hold its own copy of the prompt, and a fix that reaches only some flows would again make them sort the same message in different ways.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a research agent as an AWS Step Functions workflow. In each round, an AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API and runs any tool that the model asks for. The loop goes on until the model stops asking for tools.
Some runs have looped for hours. Some tools return long documents, so the size and cost of each round vary a lot. An instruction in the system prompt to finish within ten rounds did not stop them.
Each run must stop at a cap on cost or a cap on model calls, whichever comes first, and the user must still get the latest answer.
Which change makes every run stop safely?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a research agent as an AWS Step Functions workflow. In each round, an AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API and runs any tool that the model asks for. The loop goes on until the model stops asking for tools.
Some runs have looped for hours. Some tools return long documents, so the size and cost of each round vary a lot. An instruction in the system prompt to finish within ten rounds did not stop them.
Each run must stop at a cap on cost or a cap on model calls, whichever comes first, and the user must still get the latest answer.
Which change makes every run stop safely?

options.text: Set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine to the longest time that a normal run takes, so Step Functions stops each run that goes on longer than that.
Count the rounds and the minutes in the state data, and add a Choice state that leaves the loop when the model is done or either count reaches its limit.
Set maxTokens in the inference configuration of every Converse request from the function to the run's whole token budget, so each model call stops when its response reaches that budget.
Count the rounds and the tokens in the state data, and add a Choice state that leaves the loop when the model is done or either count reaches its limit.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Count the rounds and the tokens in the state data, and add a Choice state that leaves the loop when the model is done or either count reaches its limit.
The caps must not depend on the model, because the model already ignored its instruction. So the workflow counts for itself. On-demand use of a model is charged by input and output tokens, and the Converse response reports the tokens of each call in its usage field. The function returns these numbers after each round. The workflow adds one to the round count, which is also the count of model calls, and it adds the round's tokens to the token total. The States.MathAdd intrinsic function can add these values inside the loop with no extra Lambda function. A Choice state then checks three conditions. The model is done when its stop reason is end_turn instead of tool_use. If the model is done, or if either count reaches its limit, the workflow leaves the loop and returns the latest answer to the user.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.3: "Develop safeguarded AI workflows to ensure controlled FM behavior"
Example: "Step Functions to implement stopping conditions"

Sources:

  • Choice workflow state

  • Converse (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • InferenceConfiguration (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

INCORRECT: Set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine to the longest time that a normal run takes, so Step Functions stops each run that goes on longer than that.
TimeoutSeconds sets the longest time that one execution can run, and it is a good last limit for a run that never ends. When the time runs out, Step Functions reports a States.Timeout error, and the execution fails. The run stops, but the user gets no answer, and the user must still get the latest answer. Time also does not measure cost. A short run with very long documents can still go past the cap on cost.

INCORRECT: Count the rounds and the minutes in the state data, and add a Choice state that leaves the loop when the model is done or either count reaches its limit.
A time limit is a real stopping condition. It fits a loop where each round costs about the same and users wait for the result. The function can report how long each round took, and the workflow adds the minutes to its count. Here the cap is on cost, and some tools return long documents. A round with long documents can finish quickly and still cost a lot. So a run can stay under the round limit and the time limit and still go past the cap on cost.

INCORRECT: Set maxTokens in the inference configuration of every Converse request from the function to the run's whole token budget, so each model call stops when its response reaches that budget.
maxTokens sets the largest number of tokens that the model may generate in one response. It is a good way to limit the length, and so the cost, of each answer. Here the cap covers the cost of the whole run. The long documents that tools return go into the model's input, and maxTokens limits only the generated response. The setting also acts on one call at a time and does not count the rounds, so the loop can still go on for hours.

questions.promptHtml:
A support agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime uses a tool in an AWS Lambda function. The tool calls a partner's shipping API, and the call waits for as long as the partner takes to answer. The function timeout is a few seconds, as long as users will wait.
Sometimes the partner API accepts the connection and then sends nothing. Lambda then stops the function at its timeout. The agent can still answer if the tool reports a failure in time.
How should the team change the tool function?
questions.promptText:
A support agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime uses a tool in an AWS Lambda function. The tool calls a partner's shipping API, and the call waits for as long as the partner takes to answer. The function timeout is a few seconds, as long as users will wait.
Sometimes the partner API accepts the connection and then sends nothing. Lambda then stops the function at its timeout. The agent can still answer if the tool reports a failure in time.
How should the team change the tool function?

options.text: Wrap the partner call in a try block, and return a clear error result to the agent from the except block when the call fails.
Raise the function timeout to its maximum value, so the partner API has more time to send its answer before Lambda stops the function.
Set the HTTP client timeout from the remaining time in the Lambda context object, minus a short margin, and return a timed-out result to the agent.
Add retries with exponential backoff and jitter around the partner call, so the function sends each failed call again after a short wait.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the HTTP client timeout from the remaining time in the Lambda context object, minus a short margin, and return a timed-out result to the agent.
The Lambda context object has a method, get_remaining_time_in_millis in Python, that returns the number of milliseconds left before the invocation times out. The function reads it before the partner call and sets the HTTP client timeout a little shorter. When the partner API sends nothing, the client stops waiting for the answer while the function still runs. The function then returns a result that says the shipping lookup timed out. The agent gets this result in time, and it answers without the shipping data.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.3: "Develop safeguarded AI workflows to ensure controlled FM behavior"
Example: "Lambda functions to implement timeout mechanisms"

Sources:

  • Using the Lambda context object to retrieve Python function information

  • Understanding the Lambda execution environment lifecycle

  • Best practices for working with AWS Lambda functions

INCORRECT: Wrap the partner call in a try block, and return a clear error result to the agent from the except block when the call fails.
A try and except block is the usual way to turn an error into a clear result for the agent, and it works when the partner API returns an error. Here the API sends nothing, and the call has no time limit, so it raises no error. It waits until the function times out. At that point, Lambda shuts down the runtime and resets the execution environment, so the code in the except block never runs.

INCORRECT: Raise the function timeout to its maximum value, so the partner API has more time to send its answer before Lambda stops the function.
A longer function timeout helps when the partner API is slow but always answers. Here the API sometimes sends nothing at all, so a longer timeout only makes the wait longer. The function timeout is already the longest time that users will wait.

INCORRECT: Add retries with exponential backoff and jitter around the partner call, so the function sends each failed call again after a short wait.
Retries with backoff and jitter help with short errors, such as throttling, where the next try often works. A retry starts only after a call fails. This call does not fail. It waits with no time limit until Lambda stops the function, so the retry never runs.

questions.promptHtml:
In an AWS Step Functions workflow, a model in Amazon Bedrock labels each insurance claim as low, medium, or high severity. Sometimes the model labels a serious claim as low, and this mistake is costly.

The team moved to a larger model of the same family and added examples of serious claims to the prompt. These mistakes now happen less often, but they still happen. The same model gives the same wrong label every time the team resends such a claim. In tests, two models from other providers labeled many of these claims correctly.

The claims experts have time to review only the few claims where no two models give the same label.

How should the workflow label each claim?
questions.promptText:
In an AWS Step Functions workflow, a model in Amazon Bedrock labels each insurance claim as low, medium, or high severity. Sometimes the model labels a serious claim as low, and this mistake is costly.
The team moved to a larger model of the same family and added examples of serious claims to the prompt. These mistakes now happen less often, but they still happen. The same model gives the same wrong label every time the team resends such a claim. In tests, two models from other providers labeled many of these claims correctly.
The claims experts have time to review only the few claims where no two models give the same label.
How should the workflow label each claim?

options.text: The workflow sends each claim to the larger model. A Lambda function puts each claim that the model labels low on an Amazon SQS queue for review.
The workflow sends each claim to the larger model. A second model call asks the smaller model that the team used before to check the label and fix any mistake that it finds.
The workflow sends each claim to the larger model and two models from other providers. A Lambda function keeps the label that at least two models give, or queues the claim for review.
The workflow sends each claim to the larger model. A second model call asks the same model to check the label and fix any mistake that it finds.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The workflow sends each claim to the larger model and two models from other providers. A Lambda function keeps the label that at least two models give, or queues the claim for review.
This design is a model ensemble with a vote. In Step Functions, a Parallel state runs its branches at the same time and gives each branch a copy of the same input. Here the three branches send the claim to the larger model and to two models from other providers in Amazon Bedrock, which offers foundation models from many providers.

The Parallel state returns an array with one label from each branch. The Lambda function keeps the label that at least two models give. When all three labels differ, the function puts the claim on an Amazon SQS queue for the claims experts. In the tests, these two models gave the right label to many of the claims that the larger model labeled wrong. So the two models can agree on the right label, even when the larger model repeats its mistake.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.4: "Create sophisticated model coordination systems to optimize performance across multiple capabilities"
Example: "custom aggregation logic for model ensembles"

Sources:

  • Parallel workflow state

  • Overview (Amazon Bedrock User Guide)

INCORRECT: The workflow sends each claim to the larger model. A Lambda function puts each claim that the model labels low on an Amazon SQS queue for review.
Human review of each claim with a risky label is a common way to catch a mistake that costs a lot. This design sends the experts every claim that the model labels low, whether the label is right or wrong. The claims experts have time to review only the few claims where no two models give the same label. With one model, the workflow has no other labels to compare, so the workflow cannot find those few claims.

INCORRECT: The workflow sends each claim to the larger model. A second model call asks the smaller model that the team used before to check the label and fix any mistake that it finds.
Checking a label with a second model can catch mistakes when the second model does not make the same mistakes as the first model. Here the checker is the smaller model that the team used before. These mistakes happened less often after the team moved to the larger model, so the smaller model makes them more often. The smaller model tends to accept the wrong label. This design also sends no claim to the claims experts, even when the two models disagree.

INCORRECT: The workflow sends each claim to the larger model. A second model call asks the same model to check the label and fix any mistake that it finds.
A second call that reviews the first answer can find a small mistake, such as a missed instruction or a wrong format. Here the model gives the same wrong label every time it reads such a claim. When the same model checks its own label, the model reads the claim in the same way and tends to keep the wrong label.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's agents are built with different frameworks, such as Strands Agents and LangGraph. They all reach the company's tools through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Each team wrote its own code to send requests to the gateway, and each agent's code lists every tool and its input fields.
Last week, the platform team renamed an input field of one tool, and three agents broke until their teams released new code. Every tool call must pass the gateway's authorization check. The platform team wants all agents to connect in one standard way.
How should each agent connect to the tools?
questions.promptText:
A company's agents are built with different frameworks, such as Strands Agents and LangGraph. They all reach the company's tools through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Each team wrote its own code to send requests to the gateway, and each agent's code lists every tool and its input fields.
Last week, the platform team renamed an input field of one tool, and three agents broke until their teams released new code. Every tool call must pass the gateway's authorization check. The platform team wants all agents to connect in one standard way.
How should each agent connect to the tools?

options.text: Each agent uses an MCP client library for its framework, keeps a copy of the tool definitions in its code, and calls tools by name.
Each agent keeps the team's own HTTP code, gets the tool list from the gateway when each session starts, and calls tools by name.
Each agent uses the AWS SDK for its language, keeps a copy of the tool definitions in its code, and calls the AWS Lambda function behind each tool.
Each agent uses an MCP client library for its framework, gets the tool list from the gateway when each session starts, and calls tools by name.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Each agent uses an MCP client library for its framework, gets the tool list from the gateway when each session starts, and calls tools by name.
The gateway works as one MCP server that combines the tools of all its MCP targets, such as Lambda functions and APIs. A client that asks for the tool list gets the tools of every target, in one list or in several pages. MCP client libraries exist for many frameworks, such as the MCP Python SDK, Strands Agents and LangGraph, so every agent connects in the same standard way.

At the start of a session, the client lists the tools with their current names and input fields. Then it calls each tool by name through the gateway. A renamed field reaches every agent at its next session, with no new release. Every call still goes through the gateway, so it passes the authorization check.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.7: "Develop model extension frameworks to enhance FM capabilities"
Example: "MCP client libraries to ensure consistent access patterns"

Sources:

  • Using MCP Client Libraries

  • Core concepts for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

  • Set up inbound authorization for your gateway

INCORRECT: Each agent uses an MCP client library for its framework, keeps a copy of the tool definitions in its code, and calls tools by name.
An MCP client library gives every agent the same standard connection, and a copy of the tool definitions in the code saves one request at the start of a session. That fits tools that do not change. Here the platform team renames fields, and a copy in the code keeps the old field name until the team releases new code. That is how three agents broke last week.

INCORRECT: Each agent keeps the team's own HTTP code, gets the tool list from the gateway when each session starts, and calls tools by name.
Getting the tool list at the start of each session fixes the problem with renamed fields. A team can also write its own HTTP code when no MCP client library exists for its language. But every team keeps connection code of its own, so the agents still do not connect in one standard way. Each team must also update its code when the protocol changes.

INCORRECT: Each agent uses the AWS SDK for its language, keeps a copy of the tool definitions in its code, and calls the AWS Lambda function behind each tool.
Calling a Lambda function directly with the AWS SDK fits an agent on AWS that has an IAM role and needs no gateway. Here every tool call must pass the gateway's authorization check. A direct call never reaches the gateway, so the check never runs. The copy of the tool definitions in the code also keeps the problem with renamed fields.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's pricing tool calls a text model a few times an hour. The team hosts an open-weight model, which it never changed, on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The endpoint runs one GPU instance all day, because the model needs a GPU to answer in seconds. Amazon Bedrock also offers this same model and bills it per input and output token.
Users wait in the tool for each answer. The company wants to pay only for requests, not for idle time, and to manage no servers.
How should the team host and call the model?
questions.promptText:
A company's pricing tool calls a text model a few times an hour. The team hosts an open-weight model, which it never changed, on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The endpoint runs one GPU instance all day, because the model needs a GPU to answer in seconds. Amazon Bedrock also offers this same model and bills it per input and output token.
Users wait in the tool for each answer. The company wants to pay only for requests, not for idle time, and to manage no servers.
How should the team host and call the model?

options.text: Host the model on a SageMaker AI serverless endpoint, which scales with the requests, and have the tool call the endpoint through an AWS Lambda function.
Host the model as an inference component on a SageMaker AI endpoint that scales to zero instances when idle, and have the tool call it through an AWS Lambda function.
Create Provisioned Throughput for the same model in Amazon Bedrock, and have the tool call it through an AWS Lambda function with the Converse API.
Use the same model in Amazon Bedrock with on-demand inference, and have the tool call it through an AWS Lambda function with the Converse API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use the same model in Amazon Bedrock with on-demand inference, and have the tool call it through an AWS Lambda function with the Converse API.
The question says that Amazon Bedrock offers the same model and bills it per input and output token. That is on-demand inference: Amazon Bedrock runs the model, and the company pays for the input and output tokens of each request, with no charge by the hour. The team never changed the model, so the model in Amazon Bedrock is the same model that the team hosts today, and the team does not need to import any model files. The team has no endpoint and no instance to manage, and nothing runs for the company while the tool is idle. When a user asks a question, the tool calls a Lambda function. Lambda runs code without servers to manage, and the company pays only for the resources that each call uses. The function sends the request with the Converse API and returns the answer while the user waits. The team then deletes the SageMaker AI endpoint, which stops the charge for the GPU instance.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.1: "Deploy FMs based on specific application needs and performance requirements"
Example: "Lambda functions for on-demand invocation"

Sources:

  • Amazon Bedrock pricing
  • Deploy models with Amazon SageMaker Serverless Inference
  • Scale an endpoint to zero instances

INCORRECT: Host the model on a SageMaker AI serverless endpoint, which scales with the requests, and have the tool call the endpoint through an AWS Lambda function.
Serverless Inference fits a model with infrequent or unpredictable traffic. It scales the endpoint down to zero when no requests come, so the team pays for the compute that the requests use. But Serverless Inference does not support GPUs, and this model needs a GPU to answer in seconds.

INCORRECT: Host the model as an inference component on a SageMaker AI endpoint that scales to zero instances when idle, and have the tool call it through an AWS Lambda function.
An endpoint that hosts inference components can scale to zero instances, which saves costs while the endpoint serves no requests. This fits a model that gets no requests for long periods and whose callers can wait. After the endpoint scales in to zero, it cannot answer until it provisions an instance again, and each call in that time returns an error. Provisioning takes several minutes. The tool gets only a few calls an hour, so the endpoint would often have zero instances when a call arrives, and users expect an answer in seconds.

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput for the same model in Amazon Bedrock, and have the tool call it through an AWS Lambda function with the Converse API.
Provisioned Throughput reserves a level of throughput for a model, measured in model units. It fits a steady, heavy load that needs that capacity every hour. Billing is hourly, and it continues until the team deletes the Provisioned Throughput, even when no request runs. The tool gets a few calls an hour, and the company wants to pay for the requests, not for idle time.

questions.promptHtml:
A company adds AI summaries to its ticketing service, a vendor product that runs outside AWS. For each new ticket, the service sends a webhook to an AWS Lambda function URL and signs it with a shared secret, the one signing method it supports. It waits a few seconds for a reply, sends the webhook again when no reply arrives, and turns off endpoints that keep timing out.
The function calls an Amazon Bedrock model before it replies. Every invocation finishes and writes a summary, but tickets now get two or three summaries. The resent webhooks often arrive while the first model call is still running.
Which changes stop the duplicates and keep the endpoint safe?
Select THREE.
questions.promptText:
A company adds AI summaries to its ticketing service, a vendor product that runs outside AWS. For each new ticket, the service sends a webhook to an AWS Lambda function URL and signs it with a shared secret, the one signing method it supports. It waits a few seconds for a reply, sends the webhook again when no reply arrives, and turns off endpoints that keep timing out.
The function calls an Amazon Bedrock model before it replies. Every invocation finishes and writes a summary, but tickets now get two or three summaries. The resent webhooks often arrive while the first model call is still running.
Which changes stop the duplicates and keep the endpoint safe?
Select THREE.

options.text: Make the function check the signature header of each request with the shared secret, which it reads from AWS Secrets Manager, and reject each request that fails the check.
Make the function URL use the AWS_IAM auth type, and grant the ticketing service permission to invoke it, so Lambda rejects each request without a valid signature.
Make the function timeout longer than the longest model call, so each invocation has enough time to finish the summary before Lambda stops it.
Make the function put each ticket event on the default Amazon EventBridge event bus and reply immediately, and let a rule invoke a second function that calls the model.
Make the second function look up the ticket ID in an Amazon DynamoDB table with GetItem, skip the model call when the item exists, and write the item after the summary.
Make the second function write the ticket ID to an Amazon DynamoDB table with an attribute_not_exists condition before the model call, and skip the call when the write fails.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Make the function check the signature header of each request with the shared secret, which it reads from AWS Secrets Manager, and reject each request that fails the check.
The ticketing service cannot sign its requests with AWS credentials, so this function URL uses the NONE auth type. With NONE, Lambda does not check who the caller is before it runs the function. Anyone who has the URL can call it. So the function itself must prove that each request came from the ticketing service. The service computes a signature from the message and the shared secret and sends it in a header. The function computes the same signature with the same secret and compares the two. Secrets Manager keeps the secret out of the code, and the function can read it through the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension.

CORRECT: Make the function put each ticket event on the default Amazon EventBridge event bus and reply immediately, and let a rule invoke a second function that calls the model.
The duplicates start with the slow reply. The model call takes longer than the few seconds that the service waits, so the service sends the webhook again. With this change, the first function only checks the signature, puts the event on the default event bus and replies. The reply now arrives in time. A rule on the default event bus matches the ticket events and invokes a second function, which makes the slow model call. So the service stops sending the same webhook and keeps the endpoint turned on.

CORRECT: Make the second function write the ticket ID to an Amazon DynamoDB table with an attribute_not_exists condition before the model call, and skip the call when the write fails.
Resends can still happen, for example after a network error, and in rare cases EventBridge invokes the same target more than once for one event. So the second function must handle a repeated ticket in a safe way. The condition lets the write succeed only when no item with that ticket ID exists yet. The first event writes the item and gets its summary. A repeated event fails the condition, and the function stops before it calls the model. This works even when two copies arrive at the same moment, because DynamoDB checks the condition as part of the write.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.2: "Develop integrated AI capabilities to enhance existing applications with GenAI functionality"
Example: "Lambda functions for webhook handlers"

Sources:

  • Tutorial: Creating a webhook endpoint using a Lambda function URL

  • DynamoDB condition expression CLI example

  • Troubleshooting Amazon EventBridge

INCORRECT: Make the function URL use the AWS_IAM auth type, and grant the ticketing service permission to invoke it, so Lambda rejects each request without a valid signature.
With AWS_IAM, every caller must sign each HTTP request with AWS Signature Version 4, using an AWS identity, and Lambda checks that signature before it runs the function. This is the right choice when the caller is an AWS service or an application with AWS credentials. The ticketing service runs outside AWS and signs its requests with the shared secret alone. Lambda would reject every webhook.

INCORRECT: Make the function timeout longer than the longest model call, so each invocation has enough time to finish the summary before Lambda stops it.
The function timeout is the longest time that Lambda lets one invocation run. Raising it is the right fix when Lambda stops a function before its work is done. That does not happen here, because every invocation finishes and writes its summary. The problem is in the ticketing service. It stops waiting after a few seconds, whatever the function timeout is, and sends the webhook again.

INCORRECT: Make the second function look up the ticket ID in an Amazon DynamoDB table with GetItem, skip the model call when the item exists, and write the item after the summary.
This check reads first and writes later. It works when repeated events arrive one after the other. The scenario says that resent webhooks often arrive while the first model call is still running. At that moment no item exists yet, because the first copy writes its item after the summary. Both copies find no item, both call the model, and the ticket still gets two summaries. A conditional write prevents this, because DynamoDB checks the condition and writes the item in one step.

The technicians work in several cities on one carrier's 5G network. Tests show that any path from the carrier network to the Region is too slow. The carrier hosts AWS compute inside its 5G network there. The company has no sites there and will not install hardware.
Where should the company run the model?
questions.promptText:
A company's phone app helps field technicians. When a technician points the camera at a machine part, the company's own fine-tuned vision model describes it. The model runs on Amazon EC2 in an AWS Region.
The technicians work in several cities on one carrier's 5G network. Tests show that any path from the carrier network to the Region is too slow. The carrier hosts AWS compute inside its 5G network there. The company has no sites there and will not install hardware.
Where should the company run the model?

options.text: Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances in the Region, and put AWS Global Accelerator in front, so each image enters the AWS network close to the technician.
Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances on AWS Outposts servers at a site in each city, and have the app send each image to the closest site.
Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances in the Region, and put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front, so each image goes through a nearby edge location.
Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances in AWS Wavelength Zones, and have the app send each image to the zone that is closest to the technician.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances in AWS Wavelength Zones, and have the app send each image to the zone that is closest to the technician.
Wavelength Zones put AWS compute and storage inside the data centers of a telecom carrier, at the edge of its 5G network, so they are the AWS compute that the carrier hosts in its network. Traffic from a phone on that network reaches an application server in a Wavelength Zone without leaving the carrier's network, so it avoids the path to the Region. The company runs its own model on EC2 instances there, and it installs no hardware. The app finds the closest zone, for example with a latency test from the phone, and sends each image there.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.4: "Develop cross-environment AI solutions to ensure data compliance across jurisdictions while enabling FM access"
Example: "AWS Wavelength to perform edge deployments"

Sources:

  • Compute (Overview of Amazon Web Services)
  • Architect apps for Wavelength
  • What is AWS Global Accelerator?

INCORRECT: Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances in the Region, and put AWS Global Accelerator in front, so each image enters the AWS network close to the technician.
Global Accelerator sends traffic into the AWS global network at the edge location closest to the user, and then to an endpoint in the nearest Region. It fits users around the world who reach one application in a Region. Here the model still runs in the Region, and tests show that any path from the carrier network to the Region is too slow.

INCORRECT: Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances on AWS Outposts servers at a site in each city, and have the app send each image to the closest site.
Outposts bring AWS infrastructure to a data center, a co-location space or an on-premises site. They fit workloads that must stay on premises for low latency or local data processing. Here the company has no sites in these cities, and it will not install hardware of its own.

INCORRECT: Run the model on Amazon EC2 instances in the Region, and put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front, so each image goes through a nearby edge location.
CloudFront serves copies of content from edge locations. When the object that a user asks for is not in the cache, CloudFront forwards the request to the origin. It fits content that many users ask for again and again, such as the images of a web page. Each camera image here is new, so every request goes on to the model in the Region, and that path is too slow.

questions.promptText:
A company offers a REST API in Amazon API Gateway that partners call to summarize documents. Behind it, an AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock.
Many partner requests have missing fields or wrong types in the JSON body. Each one reaches the model and wastes tokens. Outside the JSON body, these requests are correct. Most mistakes come from request code that partners wrote by hand in Java. The team wants bad requests stopped before any function runs. Partners send a normal number of requests.
Which changes should the company make?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add a request validator that validates query string parameters and headers to each method, and mark every parameter that partners must send as required.
Generate a Java SDK for the API from the deployed stage, and give it to the partner developers in place of their own client code.
Check the body against a JSON schema at the start of the Lambda function, and return an error to the partner before the function calls the model.
Add a request validator that validates the body of each request against a model, which holds the JSON schema that the request body must follow.
Create a usage plan for each partner with an API key, throttling and a quota, and require the API key on every method of the API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Generate a Java SDK for the API from the deployed stage, and give it to the partner developers in place of their own client code.
After a REST API is deployed to a stage, API Gateway can generate an SDK for it, and Java is one of the supported platforms. The SDK gives the partners a simple way to call each method of the API from Java. They no longer write the request code by hand, and most of the mistakes came from that code.

CORRECT: Add a request validator that validates the body of each request against a model, which holds the JSON schema that the request body must follow.
A request validator makes API Gateway check each request before it calls the backend. With body validation, API Gateway compares the JSON body of each request with a model. In API Gateway, a model is a JSON schema that names the fields of the body, which fields are required, and the type of each one. When a request does not match, API Gateway rejects it immediately with a 400 error. The Lambda function never runs, so no tokens are spent on the bad request.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.1: "Create flexible model interaction systems"
Example: "API Gateway to provide custom API clients with request validation"

Sources:

  • Request validation for REST APIs in API Gateway

  • Generate SDKs for REST APIs in API Gateway

  • Set up basic request validation in API Gateway

INCORRECT: Add a request validator that validates query string parameters and headers to each method, and mark every parameter that partners must send as required.
This validator checks that the required parameters in the URI, the query string and the headers are present and not blank. It fits APIs where partners forget a header or a query parameter. Here the requests are correct outside the JSON body. The mistakes are in the body, and this validator does not check the body.

INCORRECT: Check the body against a JSON schema at the start of the Lambda function, and return an error to the partner before the function calls the model.
A check in the function fits rules that need business logic, such as a lookup in a database. It stops the model call, so it saves the tokens. But the team wants bad requests stopped before any function runs, and this check runs inside the function.

INCORRECT: Create a usage plan for each partner with an API key, throttling and a quota, and require the API key on every method of the API.
A usage plan sets throttling and quota limits for an API, and the clients send an API key with their requests. It fits partners who send too many requests. Here partners send a normal number of requests. The problem is what each request contains, and a usage plan does not check the body.

A company's report tool calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. A Lambda proxy integration runs a Node.js function that asks a model in Amazon Bedrock for a long report. Every report arrives in full, but users see nothing until the whole report is done.
Every client calls this REST API with an API key from a usage plan, and the company wants to keep it that way. Client firewalls allow standard HTTPS requests and responses only, and they block any connection that stays open for two-way messages.
How can users see each report while the model writes it?
questions.promptText:
A company's report tool calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. A Lambda proxy integration runs a Node.js function that asks a model in Amazon Bedrock for a long report. Every report arrives in full, but users see nothing until the whole report is done.
Every client calls this REST API with an API key from a usage plan, and the company wants to keep it that way. Client firewalls allow standard HTTPS requests and responses only, and they block any connection that stays open for two-way messages.
How can users see each report while the model writes it?

options.text: Keep the REST API, set the response transfer mode of its Lambda proxy integration to STREAM, and have the function stream the ConverseStream output as it arrives.
Keep the REST API, request a higher integration timeout for the report method, and have the function return the whole report when the model finishes writing it.
Add a WebSocket API in API Gateway, and have the function post each part of the ConverseStream output to the client's connection as it arrives.
Keep the REST API for other calls, add a Lambda function URL in the RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode for reports, and have the function stream the ConverseStream output as it arrives.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Keep the REST API, set the response transfer mode of its Lambda proxy integration to STREAM, and have the function stream the ConverseStream output as it arrives.
With response streaming for REST APIs, API Gateway does not wait until the whole response is ready. It starts to send the response to the client while the backend still writes it. The default response transfer mode is BUFFERED, so the team changes it to STREAM on the Lambda proxy integration. API Gateway then invokes the function with the InvokeWithResponseStream API. Lambda supports response streaming on Node.js managed runtimes, and this function runs on Node.js. The function calls the model with ConverseStream, which returns the response in a stream, and it writes each part of the report to its own response stream as the part arrives. If the function sets neither a Content-Length header nor a Transfer-Encoding header, API Gateway adds Transfer-Encoding: chunked. The report then reaches the client in chunks over a normal HTTPS response, which the client firewalls allow. The REST API stays in place, so every client keeps calling it with an API key from its usage plan.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.2: "Develop real-time AI interaction systems to provide immediate feedback from FM"
Example: "API Gateway to implement chunked transfer encoding"

Sources:

  • Stream the integration response for your proxy integrations in API Gateway

  • Set up a Lambda proxy integration with payload response streaming in API Gateway

  • Response streaming for Lambda functions

INCORRECT: Keep the REST API, request a higher integration timeout for the report method, and have the function return the whole report when the model finishes writing it.
The integration timeout is the longest time that API Gateway waits for the backend to answer. A team can raise it for Regional and private REST APIs, and that is the right fix when long reports fail with a timeout error. Here every report already arrives in full, so no request times out. The problem is the wait before users see any text. In the default BUFFERED mode, the client gets the response only when it is complete, so users still see nothing until the model finishes the report.

INCORRECT: Add a WebSocket API in API Gateway, and have the function post each part of the ConverseStream output to the client's connection as it arrives.
A WebSocket API keeps a connection open between the client and the backend, and messages can travel both ways. The backend sends each message to a connected client with the @connections API. This fits a chat app that pushes each part of an answer to the user while the model writes it. Here the client firewalls block any connection that stays open for two-way messages, so the clients cannot use a WebSocket API.

INCORRECT: Keep the REST API for other calls, add a Lambda function URL in the RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode for reports, and have the function stream the ConverseStream output as it arrives.
A function URL in the RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode streams the function's response as it becomes available. A team can add one beside an existing API for a single streaming call, when the clients may call the function directly. But a function URL has its own auth type, AWS_IAM or NONE, and it sits outside the REST API and its usage plans. Report requests would skip the API keys, and the company wants every client to keep calling this REST API with an API key from a usage plan.
