A company offers an AI writing API to business tenants through a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. A model in Amazon Bedrock writes the text. Each tenant chooses a Basic or a Premium plan, and each plan sets its own request rate and its own number of requests each month.
Last week, one Basic tenant sent a burst of requests, and the API slowed down for every tenant. Many tenants reach the API through the same shared proxy addresses of a reseller.
Each tenant must get the limits of its own plan, and a burst from one tenant must not use up the limits of other tenants.
How should the company limit the requests of each tenant?
questions.promptText:
A company offers an AI writing API to business tenants through a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. A model in Amazon Bedrock writes the text. Each tenant chooses a Basic or a Premium plan, and each plan sets its own request rate and its own number of requests each month.
Last week, one Basic tenant sent a burst of requests, and the API slowed down for every tenant. Many tenants reach the API through the same shared proxy addresses of a reseller.
Each tenant must get the limits of its own plan, and a burst from one tenant must not use up the limits of other tenants.
How should the company limit the requests of each tenant?

options.text: Set throttling on the API stage at the total rate that the model can handle, so API Gateway rejects requests above that rate for the whole stage.
Set throttling for the POST method in the stage settings at the rate of the Premium plan, so API Gateway rejects requests above that rate for that method.
Create a usage plan for each plan tier with throttling and a monthly quota, give each tenant its own API key in the usage plan of its tier, and require API keys.
Add an AWS WAF web ACL to the API stage with a rate-based rule that counts the requests from each source IP address and blocks each address that sends too many requests.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a usage plan for each plan tier with throttling and a monthly quota, give each tenant its own API key in the usage plan of its tier, and require API keys.
A usage plan sets throttling, the target request rate, and a quota, the target number of requests in a period such as a month. It uses API keys to identify each client. The company creates one usage plan for Basic and one for Premium, each with the limits of that plan.

Each tenant gets its own API key in the usage plan of its tier. Throttling and quota limits apply to the requests of each API key, so each tenant has its own limits, and a burst from one tenant uses up only that tenant's limits. The methods require an API key, so every request counts against one tenant. These limits are applied on a best-effort basis. They reduce the effect of one tenant's burst on the others, but they are not hard limits and not a hard cost control.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.3: "Create resilient FM systems to ensure reliable operations"
Example: "API Gateway to manage rate limiting"

Sources:

  • Usage plans and API keys for REST APIs in API Gateway

  • Throttle requests to your REST APIs for better throughput in API Gateway

  • Aggregating rate-based rules in AWS WAF

INCORRECT: Set throttling on the API stage at the total rate that the model can handle, so API Gateway rejects requests above that rate for the whole stage.
Stage throttling protects the backend from more requests than it can handle. The limit is set for the methods of the stage, not for each client. Only the limits in a usage plan apply to each client, by its API key. So one tenant's burst could still use up the stage limit for everyone, and Basic and Premium tenants would get the same limit. Stage throttling also has no monthly count of requests.

INCORRECT: Set throttling for the POST method in the stage settings at the rate of the Premium plan, so API Gateway rejects requests above that rate for that method.
API Gateway can set a different throttle limit for each method in a stage. A method limit fits one method that needs a limit of its own, for example a costly method that calls a model. But the limit belongs to the method, and the requests of every tenant count against it together. One Basic tenant's burst could still use up the limit for everyone, and every Basic tenant would get the Premium rate. A method limit also has no monthly count of requests.

INCORRECT: Add an AWS WAF web ACL to the API stage with a rate-based rule that counts the requests from each source IP address and blocks each address that sends too many requests.
A rate-based rule counts requests and limits the ones that come too fast. Grouping the requests by source IP address stops a flood from one address, such as a bot. Here many tenants reach the API through the same shared proxy addresses. When a request goes through a proxy, its source IP address is the address of the last proxy, so the rule counts these tenants as one client. The rule also does not know the plan of each tenant.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's writing product has three API endpoints: grammar fixes, email drafts and contract summaries. Each endpoint calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. For each endpoint, tests found a different lowest-cost model that reaches the minimum quality for that endpoint. The compliance team approved each model for its own endpoint only.
Auditors must be able to name the model behind each endpoint before any request arrives.
How should the application choose the model for each request?
questions.promptText:
A company's writing product has three API endpoints: grammar fixes, email drafts and contract summaries. Each endpoint calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. For each endpoint, tests found a different lowest-cost model that reaches the minimum quality for that endpoint. The compliance team approved each model for its own endpoint only.
Auditors must be able to name the model behind each endpoint before any request arrives.
How should the application choose the model for each request?

options.text: Send each request first to a small classifier model that reads it and picks one of the three approved models, and then send the request to that model.
Keep a routing table in the application's configuration that maps each endpoint to its approved model, and send each request to the model for its endpoint.
Compare an embedding of each request with example requests for each task, and send the request to the approved model of the task with the closest examples.
Send every request to one model that reached the minimum quality for each endpoint in the tests, and give the auditors the ID of that model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Keep a routing table in the application's configuration that maps each endpoint to its approved model, and send each request to the model for its endpoint.
This is static routing. Each task maps to one model in advance, and no step reads the request to choose a model. Static routing works well when each task has its own entry point, and here each endpoint is one task. The routing table maps each endpoint to the model ID that the compliance team approved for it. The code reads the table and sends each request to that model, for example in the modelId field of a Converse request. Auditors can read the table and name the model behind each endpoint before any request arrives. Each endpoint also keeps the lowest-cost model that reached its minimum quality.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.4: "Develop intelligent model routing systems to optimize model selection"
Example: "application code to implement static routing configurations"

Sources:

  • Multi-LLM routing strategies for generative AI applications on AWS
  • Converse (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

INCORRECT: Send each request first to a small classifier model that reads it and picks one of the three approved models, and then send the request to that model.
A classifier model that reads each request and picks a model is LLM-assisted routing. It fits one entry point that gets many kinds of requests, where the application cannot tell the task in advance, and it adds cost and latency. Here each endpoint already tells the task. The classifier decides for each request, so it can send a grammar request to the contract model, which the compliance team approved for contract summaries only. Auditors could not name the model behind an endpoint in advance.

INCORRECT: Compare an embedding of each request with example requests for each task, and send the request to the approved model of the task with the closest examples.
Comparing an embedding of the request with example requests for each task is semantic routing. It fits one entry point that gets broad categories of requests. Here the endpoint already tells the task. The closest examples can belong to another task, so a request can reach a model that is not approved for its endpoint, and nobody can name the model behind an endpoint before the request arrives.

INCORRECT: Send every request to one model that reached the minimum quality for each endpoint in the tests, and give the auditors the ID of that model.
One model for every endpoint is the simplest design to run and to audit, and it fits when simple operations matter more than the lowest cost. Here the tests found a different lowest-cost model for each endpoint, so at least two endpoints would pay for a model that costs more than the one that the tests found for them. The compliance team also approved each model for its own endpoint only, so one model cannot serve the other endpoints.

A company's assistant gets three kinds of requests in one chat box: code questions, questions about contract clauses and general chat. Each request runs through an AWS Step Functions workflow. Tests showed that each kind is best answered by a model from a different company in Amazon Bedrock.
The app sends only the text that the user typed. To control cost, only one model may write the answer to each request.
How should the workflow send each request to the right model?
questions.promptText:
A company's assistant gets three kinds of requests in one chat box: code questions, questions about contract clauses and general chat. Each request runs through an AWS Step Functions workflow. Tests showed that each kind is best answered by a model from a different company in Amazon Bedrock.
The app sends only the text that the user typed. To control cost, only one model may write the answer to each request.
How should the workflow send each request to the right model?

options.text: A Choice state checks a request type field in the workflow input, and it passes the request to the Task state that calls the model for that type.
A Task state sends the request to the lowest-cost of the three models, and a Choice state passes it to a stronger model when the answer fails a check.
A Task state has a small model label the request as code, contract or chat, and a Choice state passes it to the Task state for that label.
A Parallel state sends the request to the three models at the same time, and a final Task state asks a judge model to keep the best answer.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A Task state has a small model label the request as code, contract or chat, and a Choice state passes it to the Task state for that label.
This is content-based routing: a model reads the request, decides what kind it is, and the workflow routes it to a specialized model. The first Task state calls a small, fast model through the Step Functions integration with Amazon Bedrock, which runs InvokeModel, and asks it for one label. A Choice state compares the label with its rules and moves to the Task state for that label. That Task state calls the model from the company that did best for that kind of request. Only that one model writes the answer, and the label call is short. The app does not need to send the kind of request, because the workflow reads the text itself.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.4: "Develop intelligent model routing systems to optimize model selection"
Example: "Step Functions for dynamic content-based routing to specialized FMs"

Sources:

  • Workflow for routing (AWS Prescriptive Guidance)

  • AGENTPERF02-BP02 Implement task-appropriate model selection strategies

  • Choice workflow state

INCORRECT: A Choice state checks a request type field in the workflow input, and it passes the request to the Task state that calls the model for that type.
A Choice state that reads a type field is the simplest way to route. It fits apps where the user picks the kind of request, for example from a menu, and the app puts it in the input. Here the app sends only the text that the user typed, so the input holds no type field for the Choice state to read.

INCORRECT: A Task state sends the request to the lowest-cost of the three models, and a Choice state passes it to a stronger model when the answer fails a check.
Sending each request to a low-cost model first, and to a stronger model only when the answer fails a check, is a cascading fallback. It fits workloads where most requests are simple and a small model answers them well. Here every request that fails the check gets two answers, and the company allows only one model to write the answer to each request. The stronger model is also one model for every kind of request, but tests showed that each kind is best answered by a model from a different company.

INCORRECT: A Parallel state sends the request to the three models at the same time, and a final Task state asks a judge model to keep the best answer.
A Parallel state runs its branches at the same time and returns an array with the output of each branch, and a judge model can then keep the best answer. This fits work where the quality of each answer matters more than its cost. Here three models would write an answer to every request, and to control cost, only one model may write the answer to each request.

questions.promptText:
A company's mobile app calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. The POST method on the /v1 resource uses a Lambda custom integration, not a proxy integration, and the function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. The team moved POST /v1 to a new function version that expects renamed fields in the JSON body of each request. The responses did not change.
Old app versions still send the old fields to POST /v1, and the company cannot make their users update. Those requests now fail. The team will not change the new function.
How should the team keep the old app versions working?

options.text: On the POST /v1 method, add a mapping template to the integration response that rewrites the function's response into the format that old app versions expect.
On the POST /v1 method, add a mapping template to the integration request that rewrites the old request into the new format before API Gateway calls the function.
On the POST /v1 method, add parameter mapping to the integration request that maps the old query string and header names to the new names before API Gateway calls the function.
On the POST /v1 method, add parameter mapping to the integration response that maps the function's response headers to the header names that old app versions expect.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: On the POST /v1 method, add a mapping template to the integration request that rewrites the old request into the new format before API Gateway calls the function.
A mapping template changes the body of the integration request before API Gateway sends it to the backend. It works here because POST /v1 uses a Lambda custom integration, where the team sets up the integration request and the integration response. With a Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway would pass the request to the function as it is. The template, written in Velocity Template Language, reads each old field, for example with $input.path, and writes a new JSON body with the new field names. The new function version receives the format that it expects, and its code does not change. The change runs inside API Gateway, so the team adds no new function to run.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.1: "Create enterprise connectivity solutions to seamlessly incorporate FM capabilities into existing enterprise environments"

Sources:

  • Mapping template transformations for REST APIs in API Gateway

  • Data transformations for REST APIs in API Gateway

  • Choose an API Gateway API integration type

INCORRECT: On the POST /v1 method, add a mapping template to the integration response that rewrites the function's response into the format that old app versions expect.
A mapping template on the integration response rewrites the body that the backend returns before API Gateway sends it to the client. It fits a backend whose response format changed. Here the responses did not change. The requests fail because old app versions send the old field names in the request body.

INCORRECT: On the POST /v1 method, add parameter mapping to the integration request that maps the old query string and header names to the new names before API Gateway calls the function.
Parameter mapping can change URL path parameters, query string parameters and header values in the integration request. It fits old clients that send a renamed value in a query string or a header. It cannot change the request payload, and the renamed fields here are in the JSON body of each request.

INCORRECT: On the POST /v1 method, add parameter mapping to the integration response that maps the function's response headers to the header names that old app versions expect.
Parameter mapping on the integration response can set the headers of the response, for example from a header that the backend returns under another name, and it needs a non-proxy integration. It fits clients that read a header under an older name. Here the responses did not change, and the problem is the request body.

questions.promptText:
A company's chat assistant calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. Each request sends the whole chat history, and Amazon Bedrock supports token counting for this model. Long chats now fail with an error that says the input is too long.
Users paste code and switch between English and Japanese in the same chat. The assistant must keep as many past turns as the model can take.
Which change should the team make before each call?

options.text: Send the request to the CountTokens API first, and remove the oldest turns one at a time until the count fits the model's input limit.
Estimate the tokens from the number of characters in the request, and remove the oldest turns one at a time until the estimate fits the model's input limit.
Send the request to the CountTokens API first, and when the count is over the model's input limit, cut the history to the last three turns.
Estimate the tokens from the number of characters in the request, and when the estimate is over the model's input limit, cut the history to the last three turns.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Send the request to the CountTokens API first, and remove the oldest turns one at a time until the count fits the model's input limit.
The CountTokens API returns the number of input tokens that the model would process if the same request were sent for inference. The count follows the model's own tokenization, and it matches the count that the model would be charged for. The call itself has no charge. Before each Converse call, the application sends the same messages and system prompt to CountTokens. When the count is over the limit, it removes the oldest turn and counts again, until the request fits. So each request keeps as many past turns as the model can take.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.1: "Create FM API interfaces to address the specific requirements of GenAI workloads"
Example: "token limit management"

Sources:

  • Monitor your token usage by counting tokens before running inference

  • CountTokens (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Key terminology (Amazon Bedrock User Guide)

INCORRECT: Estimate the tokens from the number of characters in the request, and remove the oldest turns one at a time until the estimate fits the model's input limit.
An estimate from the number of characters is quick and needs no extra call. It fits rough planning, such as a first cost forecast. But a token can be a word, a part of a word, a punctuation mark or a common phrase, so the number of characters in a token changes with the text. Token counting is also model-specific. These chats mix code, English and Japanese, so a count from characters is too low for some chats, which still fail, and too high for others, which lose turns that would have fit.

INCORRECT: Send the request to the CountTokens API first, and when the count is over the model's input limit, cut the history to the last three turns.
A short, fixed window of recent turns is a simple way to control the size of each request, and it fits an assistant where the latest turns are the ones that matter. The count here is exact, so the cut comes at the right time. But the assistant must keep as many past turns as the model can take. A cut to three turns drops older turns that would still fit in the request.

INCORRECT: Estimate the tokens from the number of characters in the request, and when the estimate is over the model's input limit, cut the history to the last three turns.
A character estimate with a short, fixed window is a quick guard for a prototype. It misses both needs here. A token can be a word, a part of a word or a punctuation mark, so an estimate from characters is not reliable for chats that mix code, English and Japanese. The cut can come too early or too late. When it comes, the three turns that stay leave out history that would still fit.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a nightly job that writes long analysis reports with Amazon Bedrock. The job calls the Converse API with Amazon Nova Pro through an AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) client that uses the default settings. It sends one call at a time from one thread, and it does not stream responses.
Many calls now fail in the client. Each call connects without delay, and the error comes later, while the model is still writing the report. Amazon Bedrock rejects no call for too many requests. The SDK retries each failed call, every retry starts the long report again, and token use has doubled.
Which change stops these failures and the repeated token use?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a nightly job that writes long analysis reports with Amazon Bedrock. The job calls the Converse API with Amazon Nova Pro through an AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) client that uses the default settings. It sends one call at a time from one thread, and it does not stream responses.
Many calls now fail in the client. Each call connects without delay, and the error comes later, while the model is still writing the report. Amazon Bedrock rejects no call for too many requests. The SDK retries each failed call, every retry starts the long report again, and token use has doubled.
Which change stops these failures and the repeated token use?

options.text: Set retries in the Config object of the Boto3 client to standard mode with more attempts, so the client tries short errors again after a growing wait.
Set retries in the Config object of the Boto3 client to adaptive mode with more attempts, so the client also slows its own request rate after errors.
Set read_timeout in the Config object of the Boto3 client to a value longer than the longest call, so the client keeps waiting for the answer.
Set max_pool_connections in the Config object of the Boto3 client to a higher value, so more calls can use open connections at the same time.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set read_timeout in the Config object of the Boto3 client to a value longer than the longest call, so the client keeps waiting for the answer.
The read timeout is the time that the client waits for data from an open connection before it throws an error. A long report can take more time than the default value. The model is still writing when the client stops waiting, so the call fails, although Amazon Bedrock is still working on it. With a read timeout longer than the longest call, the client waits until the report is complete. The call succeeds the first time, so the SDK has nothing to retry, and the repeated token use stops.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.1: "Create FM API interfaces to address the specific requirements of GenAI workloads"
Example: "retry strategies to handle model timeouts"

Sources:

  • Config Reference (Botocore)
  • Scaling and throughput best practices (Amazon Bedrock User Guide)
  • Retries (Boto3 Developer Guide)

INCORRECT: Set retries in the Config object of the Boto3 client to standard mode with more attempts, so the client tries short errors again after a growing wait.
Standard mode retries short errors, such as a dropped connection or throttling, with an exponential backoff between tries. More attempts help when the next try often works. Here every try fails in the same way, because the client stops waiting before a long report is done. Each retry sends the whole request again, starts the long report again and meets the same limit, so more attempts only add token use.

INCORRECT: Set retries in the Config object of the Boto3 client to adaptive mode with more attempts, so the client also slows its own request rate after errors.
Adaptive mode builds on standard mode and adds rate limiting on the client side. It slows the client down when AWS returns throttling errors, which helps a job that sends many requests at the same time. The scenario says that Amazon Bedrock rejects no call for too many requests, so there is nothing to slow down. The retries would still start the long report again and fail at the same point.

INCORRECT: Set max_pool_connections in the Config object of the Boto3 client to a higher value, so more calls can use open connections at the same time.
The connection pool keeps open connections that the client can reuse. Its size matters when many threads share one client, because the pool limits how many connections stay open at the same time. This job sends one call at a time from one thread, so one connection is enough. A bigger pool does not change how long the client waits for the answer.

questions.promptHtml:
A company plans a new AI feature. A web page will send a support question to an API in Amazon API Gateway, and an AWS Lambda function will call a model in Amazon Bedrock. A front-end team and a back-end team start on the same day, but the Lambda function will not be ready for several weeks. The teams disagree about the request and response fields.
They want one contract file that both teams review in the code repository. From the first week, the front-end team wants to call a working endpoint that sends back sample answers. The back-end team will write no function code before both teams approve the contract.
Which steps should the teams take first?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company plans a new AI feature. A web page will send a support question to an API in Amazon API Gateway, and an AWS Lambda function will call a model in Amazon Bedrock. A front-end team and a back-end team start on the same day, but the Lambda function will not be ready for several weeks. The teams disagree about the request and response fields.
They want one contract file that both teams review in the code repository. From the first week, the front-end team wants to call a working endpoint that sends back sample answers. The back-end team will write no function code before both teams approve the contract.
Which steps should the teams take first?
Select TWO.

options.text: Build the Lambda function first, deploy a REST API that uses it, and export the OpenAPI definition from the stage as the contract for the front-end team.
Write the contract as an OpenAPI definition file, and import the definition into API Gateway to create a REST API that has a method for each operation.
Deploy the imported REST API to a stage, generate a JavaScript SDK from the stage, and give the SDK to the front-end team to call the API.
Set a mock integration that returns example responses on each method of the REST API, and replace it with a Lambda integration when the function is ready.
Put a small Lambda function behind each method that returns example responses, and replace the function code with the model call when the back end is ready.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Write the contract as an OpenAPI definition file, and import the definition into API Gateway to create a REST API that has a method for each operation.
In an API-first approach, the contract comes before any code. An OpenAPI definition is a file that describes each path, method, request and response, so both teams can review and change it in the repository. API Gateway can import an OpenAPI definition file to create a REST API. Later, it can overwrite or merge the API with a new version of the file. So the API always matches the contract that both teams approved.

CORRECT: Set a mock integration that returns example responses on each method of the REST API, and replace it with a Lambda integration when the function is ready.
A mock integration makes API Gateway return a response itself, without calling any backend. The team sets the response body for each method in an integration response mapping template. Mock integrations exist for this case: they let dependent teams work with an API before the backend is complete. When the Lambda function is ready, the back-end team changes each integration, and the front-end code keeps calling the same methods.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.2: "Develop accessible AI interfaces to accelerate adoption and integration of FMs"
Example: "OpenAPI specifications for API-first development approaches"

Sources:

  • Develop REST APIs using OpenAPI in API Gateway

  • Mock integrations for REST APIs in API Gateway

  • Generate SDKs for REST APIs in API Gateway

INCORRECT: Build the Lambda function first, deploy a REST API that uses it, and export the OpenAPI definition from the stage as the contract for the front-end team.
Exporting an OpenAPI definition from a deployed stage is a good way to document an API that already runs. Here the order is wrong. The back-end team will write no function code before both teams approve the contract, and the function will not be ready for several weeks. With this plan, the contract comes last, and the front-end team waits for weeks.

INCORRECT: Deploy the imported REST API to a stage, generate a JavaScript SDK from the stage, and give the SDK to the front-end team to call the API.
After a REST API is deployed to a stage, API Gateway can generate an SDK for it, for example in JavaScript. The SDK gives the front-end code a simple way to call each method, and it helps when the API already sends back real answers. An SDK changes how the front end calls the API. It does not change what the API sends back. In the first week there is no backend, and the front-end team wants a working endpoint that sends back sample answers.

INCORRECT: Put a small Lambda function behind each method that returns example responses, and replace the function code with the model call when the back end is ready.
A stub function that returns fixed responses is a real way to fake a backend, and it helps when the fake answers need some logic. Here, the back-end team will write no function code before both teams approve the contract. A mock integration gives the same sample answers from API Gateway itself, with no code to write and remove later.

A test page asks a model in Amazon Bedrock for JSON as plain text, and parsing fails when the model adds extra words. The team will write no backend function code.
What should the team add to the app?

options.text: Define a conversation route with a.conversation() in the Amplify data schema, with a system prompt that asks for the order fields, and call it with the useAIConversation hook.
Define a generation route with a.generation() in the Amplify data schema, with a.string() as its return type and a prompt that asks for JSON, and call it with the useAIGeneration hook.
Define a generation route with a.generation() in the Amplify data schema, with a return type that holds the order fields, and call it from the button with the useAIGeneration hook.
Add the AIConversation component to the page with a conversation route, and have the system prompt ask the model to reply with the order fields as JSON.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Define a generation route with a.generation() in the Amplify data schema, with a return type that holds the order fields, and call it from the button with the useAIGeneration hook.
The Amplify AI kit offers two kinds of AI routes. A generation route is an AWS AppSync query that generates structured data according to the team's definition. The team defines it in the data schema with a.generation(), with the note as an argument and a return type, a custom type that holds the order fields. The button calls the route with the useAIGeneration hook and gets the typed fields back, so the browser parses no free text. Each click is one request and one response. Unlike a conversation route, it does not save messages to a conversation history. The team defines the route in the data schema, so it writes no backend function code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.2: "Develop accessible AI interfaces to accelerate adoption and integration of FMs"

Sources:

  • Generation (AWS Amplify Gen 2 Documentation)
  • Architecture (AWS Amplify Gen 2 Documentation)
  • Build fullstack AI apps in minutes with the new Amplify AI Kit

INCORRECT: Define a conversation route with a.conversation() in the Amplify data schema, with a system prompt that asks for the order fields, and call it with the useAIConversation hook.
A conversation route is a real-time API for chats with many turns. Amplify stores the conversations and messages in Amazon DynamoDB and streams the responses to the client. It fits a chat assistant that must remember earlier turns. Here each click is one request, and the app must not store the notes or a chat history. A chat reply is also text, so the browser would still parse JSON from it.

INCORRECT: Define a generation route with a.generation() in the Amplify data schema, with a.string() as its return type and a prompt that asks for JSON, and call it with the useAIGeneration hook.
A generation route can return a custom type or a scalar type, such as a string. A string return type fits free text that the page shows as it is, for example a short product description. Here the button must turn the note into typed fields. With a string, the model's JSON comes back as text again, and the browser must parse it. The test page already showed that parsing fails when the model adds extra words.

INCORRECT: Add the AIConversation component to the page with a conversation route, and have the system prompt ask the model to reply with the order fields as JSON.
The AIConversation component gives a page a ready chat interface that uses a conversation route. It fits a help panel where users talk with an assistant. Because it uses a conversation route, the notes would be stored as messages in DynamoDB. The reply is chat text, so parsing can fail again when the model adds extra words.

Sales managers read these summaries in a review call that often starts a few minutes after a deal closes.

A company's sales staff work in Salesforce, and its integration code runs in AWS Lambda. When a deal closes, the company wants a short summary of the deal notes, written by a model in Amazon Bedrock, in a field on the deal record. Sales managers read these summaries in a review call that often starts a few minutes after a deal closes.
The CRM team protects the Salesforce API limits. It does not allow any job that queries Salesforce at set times to look for new or changed records.
Which integration should the company build?

options.text: Salesforce sends closed deals to an Amazon EventBridge partner event source, and a rule invokes a Lambda function that writes each summary immediately and updates the deal record.
An Amazon AppFlow flow copies closed deals to Amazon S3 on a schedule, and an S3 event invokes a Lambda function that writes each summary immediately and updates the deal record.

Salesforce sends closed deals to an Amazon EventBridge partner event source, and a rule queues them in Amazon SQS for a Lambda function that writes the summaries each night and updates the deal records.
An Amazon AppFlow flow copies closed deals to Amazon S3 on a schedule, and a Lambda function reads the new files each night, writes the summaries and updates the deal records.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Salesforce sends closed deals to an Amazon EventBridge partner event source, and a rule invokes a Lambda function that writes each summary immediately and updates the deal record.
Salesforce can send events directly to Amazon EventBridge. An admin sets up an event relay in Salesforce, and Salesforce creates a partner event source in EventBridge. A rule matches the events for closed deals and sends each one to its target, here a Lambda function. The function asks the model for the summary and writes it to the deal record through the Salesforce API. It reads the Salesforce credentials from AWS Secrets Manager, not from its code or its environment variables. Nothing queries Salesforce at set times, because Salesforce sends each change itself. The summary is on the record within minutes, before the review call starts.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.3: "Create business system enhancements"
Example: "Lambda functions to implement customer relationship management [CRM] enhancements"

Sources:

  • Receiving events from Salesforce in Amazon EventBridge

  • Flow triggers (Amazon AppFlow User Guide)

  • Use Secrets Manager secrets in Lambda functions

INCORRECT: An Amazon AppFlow flow copies closed deals to Amazon S3 on a schedule, and an S3 event invokes a Lambda function that writes each summary immediately and updates the deal record.
Amazon AppFlow can copy Salesforce records to Amazon S3, and a schedule-triggered flow runs at the times that the team sets. This fits teams that want regular copies of CRM data, for example for reports, when the CRM owners allow it. The S3 event and the function would work here. But each run of the flow reads records from Salesforce at a set time, and the CRM team does not allow any job like that.

INCORRECT: Salesforce sends closed deals to an Amazon EventBridge partner event source, and a rule queues them in Amazon SQS for a Lambda function that writes the summaries each night and updates the deal records.
Sending closed deals to EventBridge as they happen meets the CRM team's rule, and a queue holds the events until a function reads them. A nightly run fits summaries that people read the next day, such as a daily report. Here sales managers read the summaries in a review call that often starts a few minutes after a deal closes. A summary written that night comes too late for the call.

INCORRECT: An Amazon AppFlow flow copies closed deals to Amazon S3 on a schedule, and a Lambda function reads the new files each night, writes the summaries and updates the deal records.
A scheduled copy with a nightly run is a common way to build a daily report from CRM data. It does not meet either need here. The flow reads records from Salesforce at set times, which the CRM team does not allow. The summaries are also written each night, so they miss the review call that starts a few minutes after a deal closes.

Code that Kiro writes keeps breaking these rules. Developers now paste the rules into the chat for each task, and the unit tests still pass when a rule is broken. The team will run no new AWS resources for this.
Kiro must follow the rules in all future work in the project and check each handler again whenever it changes one.
Which Kiro features should the team set up?

questions.promptText:
A team builds AWS Lambda functions in Node.js that call models in Amazon Bedrock, and its developers write the code with Kiro. The team keeps one page of performance rules. For example, each function creates its Amazon Bedrock client outside the handler, and long answers use response streaming.
Code that Kiro writes keeps breaking these rules. Developers now paste the rules into the chat for each task, and the unit tests still pass when a rule is broken. The team will run no new AWS resources for this.
Kiro must follow the rules in all future work in the project and check each handler again whenever it changes one.
Which Kiro features should the team set up?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add a steering file that holds the team's performance rules, so Kiro includes the rules in every chat and task in the project.
Add a spec for each new handler file that lists the team's performance rules in its requirements, so Kiro plans that handler with the rules.
Set up an agent hook that runs when Kiro saves a handler file and runs the team's unit tests for that handler.
Set up an agent hook that runs when Kiro saves a handler file and asks Kiro to review the change against the team's performance rules.
Connect Kiro to an MCP server backed by an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that holds the team's performance rules, so Kiro can search them.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a steering file that holds the team's performance rules, so Kiro includes the rules in every chat and task in the project.
A steering file is a markdown file in the project that gives Kiro lasting knowledge about the project, such as its patterns, libraries and standards. By default, Kiro loads it into every interaction, so developers no longer paste the rules into each chat. The team writes its page of performance rules in one steering file, and code that Kiro writes for any later task starts from these rules. For example, the function creates its Amazon Bedrock client outside the handler, so later invocations in the same execution environment can reuse the client.

CORRECT: Set up an agent hook that runs when Kiro saves a handler file and asks Kiro to review the change against the team's performance rules.
An agent hook is an automated trigger that runs a set action when an event happens in the project, such as a file save. This hook runs when Kiro saves a handler file. Its action sends Kiro a prompt to review the change against the performance rules, for example that the function creates its Amazon Bedrock client outside the handler. The code that breaks the rules is code that Kiro writes, so each handler that Kiro changes gets a review right after the change. The unit tests cannot do this job, because they pass when a rule is broken.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.4: "Enhance developer productivity to accelerate development workflows for GenAI applications"
Example: "performance optimization"

Sources:

  • Steering (Kiro documentation)

  • Hooks (Kiro documentation)

  • Scaling organizational knowledge in Kiro with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, LangChain, and MCP

INCORRECT: Add a spec for each new handler file that lists the team's performance rules in its requirements, so Kiro plans that handler with the rules.
A spec turns the plan for new work into requirements, a design and tasks, and rules in its requirements help Kiro plan that work. A steering file holds context for the whole project, while a spec covers the work that is being built. The team would copy the rules into every new spec, as developers now paste them into every chat. A change to an existing handler has no new spec, so it would not get the rules at all, and Kiro must follow the rules in all future work.

INCORRECT: Set up an agent hook that runs when Kiro saves a handler file and runs the team's unit tests for that handler.
A hook that runs the unit tests each time Kiro saves a handler is a good way to catch code that stops working, and a hook can run a shell command, such as a test run, with no one asking. Here the unit tests pass even when a rule is broken. A handler that creates its client inside the handler still returns the right answer, so the tests find nothing wrong.

INCORRECT: Connect Kiro to an MCP server backed by an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that holds the team's performance rules, so Kiro can search them.
An MCP server can connect Kiro to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and Kiro sends a query to it when it needs an answer. This fits a company with hundreds of documents, such as architecture decisions, API specs and runbooks. The team has one page of rules and will run no new AWS resources, and a knowledge base is a new resource. For a short list of rules that every change must follow, a steering file keeps them in Kiro's context with no search.

A research assistant compares the companies that a user names in each request. Users name a different number of companies each time, from two to twenty. Today one agent in an AWS Lambda function studies the companies one after another with a model in Amazon Bedrock, with all its notes in one conversation.
Requests with many companies take many minutes, and the answers mix up facts between companies. A model with a larger context window did not fix this.
A new worker function studies one company and returns short notes. Each answer must arrive in about the time that one company takes.
How should the team orchestrate the work in AWS Step Functions?
questions.promptText:
A research assistant compares the companies that a user names in each request. Users name a different number of companies each time, from two to twenty. Today one agent in an AWS Lambda function studies the companies one after another with a model in Amazon Bedrock, with all its notes in one conversation.
Requests with many companies take many minutes, and the answers mix up facts between companies. A model with a larger context window did not fix this.
A new worker function studies one company and returns short notes. Each answer must arrive in about the time that one company takes.
How should the team orchestrate the work in AWS Step Functions?

options.text: A model lists the companies in a first state, a Map state runs the worker function for every company in the list at the same time, and a last state combines the notes.
A model lists the companies in a first state, a Map state with MaxConcurrency set to 1 runs the worker function for one company at a time, and a last state combines the notes.
A model lists the companies in a first state, a Parallel state runs the worker function at the same time in its branches, one branch for each company, and a last state combines the notes.
A model lists the companies in a first state, a Choice state loops back to the worker function for one company at a time until all have notes, and a last state combines the notes.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A model lists the companies in a first state, a Map state runs the worker function for every company in the list at the same time, and a last state combines the notes.
This is the orchestrator and workers pattern. In the first state, a model reads the request and returns the list of companies, and the list can have a different length each time. A Map state runs the same steps for each item of an array that a previous state passes to it, so it runs the worker function once for each company in the list. With no limit on concurrency, Step Functions runs the iterations as concurrently as possible, so the answer takes about as long as the slowest company. Each worker sees one company only, so facts from other companies cannot mix into its notes. The Map state returns an array with the output of each iteration, and the last state combines the notes into one answer.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.5: "Develop advanced GenAI applications to implement sophisticated AI capabilities"
Example: "Step Functions to orchestrate agent design patterns"

Sources:

  • Using Map state in Inline mode in Step Functions workflows

  • Workflow for parallelization (AWS Prescriptive Guidance)

  • Parallel workflow state

INCORRECT: A model lists the companies in a first state, a Map state with MaxConcurrency set to 1 runs the worker function for one company at a time, and a last state combines the notes.
A MaxConcurrency value of 1 makes the Map state run one iteration at a time, in the order of the list. Step Functions starts the next iteration only when the previous one is complete. This fits work where a downstream system takes one request at a time, or where the order matters. Each worker still sees one company, so the facts no longer mix. But the companies run one after another, so a request with twenty companies still takes many times longer than one company.

INCORRECT: A model lists the companies in a first state, a Parallel state runs the worker function at the same time in its branches, one branch for each company, and a last state combines the notes.
A Parallel state runs its branches at the same time, and each branch gets a copy of the input. It fits a fixed set of different tasks, for example a security check, a cost estimate and a compliance check on the same input. The branches are written into the state machine definition, so their number is the same in every run. Users name a different number of companies each time, so a fixed set of branches cannot match each request.

INCORRECT: A model lists the companies in a first state, a Choice state loops back to the worker function for one company at a time until all have notes, and a last state combines the notes.
A Choice state that sends the workflow back to a task is a known way to repeat work, and it fits steps where each pass needs the result of the pass before it. Each pass here studies one company, so the facts no longer mix. But the loop runs the companies one after another, and each answer must arrive in about the time that one company takes.

The company must also stop users who are on its own list of suspended accounts, which it keeps in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Company policy says that harmful input must never reach the model. A company's assistant accepts a photo and a short text request in English from each user. The app stores each photo in Amazon S3, and an AWS Step Functions workflow handles each request before a model in Amazon Bedrock answers it. Last month, harmful photos and abusive text reached the model.
The company must also stop users who are on its own list of suspended accounts, which it keeps in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Company policy says that harmful input must never reach the model. The security team wants Step Functions itself to keep the input and the result of every check for each request, with no logging setup.
Which workflow design meets these needs?

options.text: A Standard workflow checks the photo with Amazon Rekognition, the text with Amazon Comprehend and the user with a Lambda function in a Parallel state, and a Choice state sends clean requests to the model.

An Express workflow checks the photo with Amazon Rekognition, the text with Amazon Comprehend and the user with a Lambda function in a Parallel state, and a Choice state sends clean requests to the model.
A Standard workflow calls the model in the same Parallel state as the Rekognition, Comprehend and Lambda checks, and a Choice state returns the answer when every check passes.
An Express workflow sends each request to the model with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that filters harmful text and images, and a Choice state stops each request that the guardrail blocks.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A Standard workflow checks the photo with Amazon Rekognition, the text with Amazon Comprehend and the user with a Lambda function in a Parallel state, and a Choice state sends clean requests to the model.
The Parallel state runs the three checks at the same time, and each branch gets a copy of the request. Amazon Rekognition DetectModerationLabels detects unsafe content in the photo, which it reads from Amazon S3. Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection scores the text for toxic content. A Lambda function looks up the user in the DynamoDB table of suspended accounts. A Choice state then sends the request to the model only when all three checks pass, so harmful input never reaches the model. Step Functions keeps the execution history of a Standard workflow, and the console shows the input and the output of each state, so the security team can see every check for each request with no logging setup.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.1: "Develop comprehensive content safety systems to protect against harmful user inputs to FMs"
Example: "Step Functions and Lambda functions to implement custom moderation workflows"

Sources:

  • Choosing workflow type in Step Functions

  • DetectModerationLabels (Amazon Rekognition API Reference)

  • Trust and safety (Amazon Comprehend Developer Guide)

INCORRECT: An Express workflow checks the photo with Amazon Rekognition, the text with Amazon Comprehend and the user with a Lambda function in a Parallel state, and a Choice state sends clean requests to the model.
An Express workflow runs the same checks, and it fits high-volume, short event processing, such as mobile app backends. But Step Functions does not capture the execution history of an Express workflow. The team would have to turn on logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs to see each check, and the security team wants Step Functions itself to keep each check with no logging setup.

INCORRECT: A Standard workflow calls the model in the same Parallel state as the Rekognition, Comprehend and Lambda checks, and a Choice state returns the answer when every check passes.
Running the model call next to the checks saves time, because the model does not wait for the checks to finish. It fits a service where only the answer must be held back until the checks pass. Here company policy says that harmful input must never reach the model. In this design, the model reads the photo and the text before any check finishes.

INCORRECT: An Express workflow sends each request to the model with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that filters harmful text and images, and a Choice state stops each request that the guardrail blocks.
A guardrail with content filters checks the text and the images in a request for harmful content, and it can block a request that holds it. It fits harmful content in general. But a guardrail checks the content of the request, not who sent it. It cannot look up the user in the company's own table of suspended accounts, so suspended users would still reach the model. This is also an Express workflow, so Step Functions keeps no execution history of the checks.

Before launch, leadership wants one score for each candidate model that shows how much offensive text the model writes when prompts try to provoke it. The team has no prompt set of its own yet. It wants the same test for every model, with no person reading the outputs.
How should the team measure this for each candidate model?

options.text: Run an automatic model evaluation job with the general text generation task and the Robustness metric on the built-in WikiText2 dataset, and compare the scores of the models.
Run an automatic model evaluation job with the text summarization task and the Robustness metric on the built-in Gigaword dataset, and compare the scores of the models.
Run an automatic model evaluation job with the general text generation task and the Toxicity metric on the built-in RealToxicityPrompts dataset, and compare the scores of the models.
Run an automatic model evaluation job with the text summarization task and the Toxicity metric on the built-in Gigaword dataset, and compare the scores of the models.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run an automatic model evaluation job with the general text generation task and the Toxicity metric on the built-in RealToxicityPrompts dataset, and compare the scores of the models.
An automatic model evaluation job scores a model on one task type with a built-in or a custom prompt dataset, and no person reads the outputs. For general text generation, the Toxicity metric uses the detoxify algorithm, and a low value means that the model writes little toxic content. The built-in RealToxicityPrompts dataset holds prompts that try to get the model to write toxic language, like the users that leadership expects. The team runs one job for each candidate model with the same task, metric and dataset, so every model gets the same test. Then it compares the four scores.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.2: "Create content safety frameworks to prevent harmful outputs"
Example: "specialized FM evaluations for content moderation and toxicity detection"

Sources:

  • General text generation for model evaluation in Amazon Bedrock
  • Review metrics for an automated model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock (console)
  • Text summarization for model evaluation in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Run an automatic model evaluation job with the general text generation task and the Robustness metric on the built-in WikiText2 dataset, and compare the scores of the models.
Robustness measures how much the output changes after small changes to the input that keep its meaning, such as typing mistakes, upper case letters and extra spaces. A low score means that the model handles such changes well. This is a good test for a feature where users often make typing mistakes. It says nothing about offensive text.

INCORRECT: Run an automatic model evaluation job with the text summarization task and the Robustness metric on the built-in Gigaword dataset, and compare the scores of the models.
This job measures how much a model's summaries change after small changes to the input, on Gigaword, a dataset of news article headlines. It fits a summarizer that must give the same summary for slightly different input. This feature writes a paragraph from a short prompt, and leadership wants a score for offensive text, not for stable output.

INCORRECT: Run an automatic model evaluation job with the text summarization task and the Toxicity metric on the built-in Gigaword dataset, and compare the scores of the models.
The Toxicity metric is the right measure, and a toxicity score on a summarization task fits a feature that summarizes text. Here the prompts are news article headlines for the model to summarize, and nothing in them tries to provoke offensive text. Leadership wants to know what each model writes when a prompt tries to make it offensive, as the feature's public users will.

The JSON body holds the answer and two internal fields: the Amazon S3 paths of the source documents and the ID of the prompt template. Partners must never receive these internal fields. The service team will not change the service this year. The API team may change only API Gateway settings, with no new compute to run.
How should the API team keep the internal fields away from partners?
questions.promptText:
A company gives partners a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. The POST /answers method uses an HTTP integration, not a proxy integration, with an internal service on Amazon ECS that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. Each response arrives in full as one JSON object.
The JSON body holds the answer and two internal fields: the Amazon S3 paths of the source documents and the ID of the prompt template. Partners must never receive these internal fields. The service team will not change the service this year. The API team may change only API Gateway settings, with no new compute to run.
How should the API team keep the internal fields away from partners?

options.text: Add a mapping template to the integration response of the POST /answers method that builds a new JSON body with the answer and without the internal fields.
Add parameter mapping to the integration response of the POST /answers method that maps the answer, and none of the internal fields, to the method response.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, with a rule that matches the names of the internal fields and blocks each message that contains them.
Add parameter mapping to the integration response of the POST /answers method that maps the service's headers, and none of its internal headers, to the method response.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a mapping template to the integration response of the POST /answers method that builds a new JSON body with the answer and without the internal fields.
The method uses an HTTP custom integration, so the team sets up the integration request and the integration response itself. A mapping template on the integration response is a script in Velocity Template Language (VTL) that turns the backend's response body into the body that the client gets. The template reads the answer, for example with $input.path('$.answer'), and writes a new JSON body that holds only that field. The internal fields are not in the new body, so partners never receive them. The change is an API Gateway setting, so the service and the compute stay as they are. With a proxy integration, API Gateway would pass the backend response to the client as it is.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.4: "Create defense-in-depth safety systems to provide comprehensive protection against FM misuse"
Example: "API Gateway to implement API response filtering"

Sources:

  • Set up an integration response in API Gateway

  • Data transformations for REST APIs in API Gateway

  • Using rule actions in AWS WAF

INCORRECT: Add parameter mapping to the integration response of the POST /answers method that maps the answer, and none of the internal fields, to the method response.
Parameter mapping on an integration response fills the headers of the method response. Its source can be a backend header or a field of the backend's JSON body, for example to give the client one value in a header. It fits a client that needs a backend value in a header. But its targets are headers only, and it does not change the response body. The JSON body still reaches partners with the answer and both internal fields. To change the body, API Gateway uses a mapping template.

INCORRECT: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, with a rule that matches the names of the internal fields and blocks each message that contains them.
AWS WAF inspects the web requests that clients send to the API stage. Its rules allow, block or count those requests, and a rule that matches strings fits requests that carry known attack text. The internal fields are in the responses that the backend sends. For a web ACL on an API stage, the rule actions are Allow, Block, Count, CAPTCHA and Challenge. None of them rewrites the body of a response, so partners would still get the fields.

INCORRECT: Add parameter mapping to the integration response of the POST /answers method that maps the service's headers, and none of its internal headers, to the method response.
Method response parameters define which headers the client receives, and parameter mapping on the integration response fills them from the headers that the backend returns. Mapping some headers and leaving out others fits a backend that sends internal headers, such as a server name, that clients must not see. Here the internal fields are not headers. They sit in the JSON body next to the answer, and parameter mapping does not rewrite the body. To change the body, API Gateway uses a mapping template.

Another team serves this endpoint to other apps, and all apps must call the model through it.
The security team wants the same guardrail on a new app that calls this endpoint. Each user prompt must be checked before the model reads it, and each answer must be checked before the user sees it. The app must act on the guardrail's decision each time.
How should the team apply the guardrail in the new app?
questions.promptText:
A company's apps on Amazon Bedrock use one Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters and denied topics. The company also fine-tuned an open-weight model and hosts it on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Another team serves this endpoint to other apps, and all apps must call the model through it.
The security team wants the same guardrail on a new app that calls this endpoint. Each user prompt must be checked before the model reads it, and each answer must be checked before the user sees it. The app must act on the guardrail's decision each time.
How should the team apply the guardrail in the new app?

options.text: Register the endpoint with Amazon Bedrock Marketplace, and call it with the Converse API and the guardrail ID and version in each request.
Call the ApplyGuardrail API with the source INPUT on each prompt before the endpoint call, and with the source OUTPUT on each answer from the endpoint.
Call the ApplyGuardrail API with the source INPUT on each prompt before the endpoint call, and send the answer to the user when the prompt passes the check.
Import the fine-tuned model into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import, and call it with the guardrail ID and version in each InvokeModel request.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call the ApplyGuardrail API with the source INPUT on each prompt before the endpoint call, and with the source OUTPUT on each answer from the endpoint.
The ApplyGuardrail API checks text with a guardrail that already exists, without calling a foundation model. So it works with a model that Amazon Bedrock does not run, such as a model on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The app first calls ApplyGuardrail with the source INPUT on the user's prompt. If the action in the response is GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED, the app stops, and the prompt never reaches the endpoint. If the action is NONE, the app calls the endpoint. Then it calls ApplyGuardrail again with the source OUTPUT on the answer, and it acts on that result before the user sees the answer. The apps on Amazon Bedrock and the new app now use the same guardrail.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.5: "Implement advanced threat detection to protect against adversarial inputs and security vulnerabilities"
Example: "input sanitization and content filters"

Sources:

  • Use the ApplyGuardrail API in your application

  • Bring your own endpoint (Amazon Bedrock User Guide)

  • Implement model-independent safety measures with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

INCORRECT: Register the endpoint with Amazon Bedrock Marketplace, and call it with the Converse API and the guardrail ID and version in each request.
Amazon Bedrock Marketplace can register a SageMaker AI endpoint that hosts a model from the Marketplace. The team then calls the endpoint through Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API, and it can add a guardrail to each request. This fits a Marketplace model that the team uses as the provider supplied it. A registered endpoint must keep the provider's model artifacts, and this company fine-tuned its model, so the endpoint cannot be registered.

INCORRECT: Call the ApplyGuardrail API with the source INPUT on each prompt before the endpoint call, and send the answer to the user when the prompt passes the check.
This is the right API for the prompt, and a check on the input alone fits a design where another step already checks the answers. Here nothing else checks the answers, and the security team wants each answer checked before the user sees it. Without a second call with the source OUTPUT, a harmful answer from the model reaches the user.

INCORRECT: Import the fine-tuned model into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import, and call it with the guardrail ID and version in each InvokeModel request.
Custom Model Import brings a model that a team customized in another environment, such as SageMaker AI, into Amazon Bedrock. The import job reads the model files from Amazon S3, and the team then calls the imported model in Amazon Bedrock with a guardrail in each request. It fits a team that wants to run its customized model in Amazon Bedrock. Here the imported model would be a second copy of the model, and the new app would call that copy, not the endpoint. The scenario says that all apps must call the model through the endpoint.

After the last release, testers found by hand a prompt that overrode the assistant's instructions and a prompt that made it reveal its system prompt. The team fixed both, but each new release brings new weak points.
The testers have time for a manual review once each quarter. The team wants every release tested against all known attacks, including each new one that anyone finds. No release with a working attack may reach users.
Which steps should the team take?
Select THREE.
questions.promptText:
A company's support assistant runs on Amazon Bedrock. A pipeline in AWS CodePipeline ships a new version every week, first to a staging endpoint and then to production. After the last release, testers found by hand a prompt that overrode the assistant's instructions and a prompt that made it reveal its system prompt. The team fixed both, but each new release brings new weak points.
The testers have time for a manual review once each quarter. The team wants every release tested against all known attacks, including each new one that anyone finds. No release with a working attack may reach users.
Which steps should the team take?
Select THREE.

options.text: Store the attack prompts as a test suite in a versioned Amazon S3 bucket, and add each new attack that testers or users report.
Run the suite each night in an AWS CodeBuild project that an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts, against the production endpoint.
Run the suite in an AWS CodeBuild test action in a new CodePipeline stage, against the staging endpoint of each release.
Make the test action fail when any attack in the suite succeeds, so the pipeline stops the release before it reaches production.
Make the nightly run send an alert through Amazon SNS for each attack that succeeds, so the team fixes it in the next release.
Add AWS WAF rules to the assistant's API that block requests with the text of each attack that the testers found.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Store the attack prompts as a test suite in a versioned Amazon S3 bucket, and add each new attack that testers or users report.
A suite of attack prompts turns each finding into a test that runs again and again. It covers known kinds of attack, such as prompt injection, system prompt extraction and requests for personal data. The team keeps the suite in an S3 bucket with versioning, so each change keeps the earlier version of the suite. Each new attack that testers or users find goes into the suite, so every later release is tested against it.

CORRECT: Run the suite in an AWS CodeBuild test action in a new CodePipeline stage, against the staging endpoint of each release.
Automated adversarial tests belong in the CI/CD pipeline, so that every new version is tested for these weak points before it reaches production. A CodeBuild action in CodePipeline runs the commands in its buildspec inside a CodeBuild container, and it can be a test action. The new stage runs after the release reaches the staging endpoint, so the test sends each attack prompt to the version that is about to go to production.

CORRECT: Make the test action fail when any attack in the suite succeeds, so the pipeline stops the release before it reaches production.
A test protects users only when its result can stop the release. The test script fails the action when any attack in the suite succeeds. When an action does not complete successfully, the revision does not move on to the next stage. So a release with a working attack stays in staging and never reaches production, and the team fixes it first.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.5: "Implement advanced threat detection to protect against adversarial inputs and security vulnerabilities"
Example: "automated adversarial testing workflows"

Sources:

  • Hardening the generative AI application through a GenAIOps framework

  • How pipeline executions work

  • AGENTSEC07-BP05 Regular security assessments and red teaming

INCORRECT: Run the suite each night in an AWS CodeBuild project that an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts, against the production endpoint.
Running the suite on a schedule against production is a good extra check, because it finds weak points that appear between releases. But it runs after a release is already live. A release with a working attack would reach users before the nightly run finds it, and no release with a working attack may reach users.

INCORRECT: Make the nightly run send an alert through Amazon SNS for each attack that succeeds, so the team fixes it in the next release.
An alert for each successful attack keeps the team informed, and the team should use findings like these to plan the fixes of the next release. Here the alert comes from the nightly run on production. When the alert arrives, users can already reach the weak point.

INCORRECT: Add AWS WAF rules to the assistant's API that block requests with the text of each attack that the testers found.
AWS WAF rules that match known attack text add a layer of input checks in front of the API, for example against known malicious strings. They block only the text that the rules name. Each new release brings new weak points, and an attack in new words passes the rules. WAF rules also do not test a release before it reaches users.

A company keeps its HR policy documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. The bucket is the data source of a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and only the knowledge base's service role may read the documents. The knowledge base reads new and changed documents when it syncs, several times a day.
Last quarter, a developer's IAM role read several documents. The security team found out weeks later in a manual review. The account's only AWS CloudTrail trail uses the default event settings and delivers to another S3 bucket.
The security team wants an Amazon CloudWatch alarm within minutes after anyone else reads a document, and no alarm for normal reads.
Which settings should the team add?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company keeps its HR policy documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. The bucket is the data source of a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and only the knowledge base's service role may read the documents. The knowledge base reads new and changed documents when it syncs, several times a day.
Last quarter, a developer's IAM role read several documents. The security team found out weeks later in a manual review. The account's only AWS CloudTrail trail uses the default event settings and delivers to another S3 bucket.
The security team wants an Amazon CloudWatch alarm within minutes after anyone else reads a document, and no alarm for normal reads.
Which settings should the team add?
Select TWO.

options.text: Turn on S3 request metrics for the documents bucket, and add a CloudWatch alarm that uses anomaly detection on the GetRequests metric of the bucket.
Change the trail to also log data events for object reads in the documents bucket, so the trail records each read and the principal that made it.
Send the trail's events to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and add a metric filter for every read of the documents bucket, with an alarm on each match.
Turn on Amazon Macie for the account, and have an Amazon EventBridge rule send each Macie policy finding for the documents bucket to the security team.
Send the trail's events to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and add a metric filter for reads by any principal except the knowledge base role, with an alarm.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Change the trail to also log data events for object reads in the documents bucket, so the trail records each read and the principal that made it.
Object reads, such as GetObject, are data events in CloudTrail. By default, a trail does not log data events, so the current trail never recorded the developer's reads. The team adds data events for the documents bucket to the trail, and it can limit them to read operations with an advanced event selector. Each read then becomes a CloudTrail event that names the principal that made it, including the reads of the knowledge base's own role.

CORRECT: Send the trail's events to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and add a metric filter for reads by any principal except the knowledge base role, with an alarm.
A trail can send its events to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and it sends only the events that match its settings. CloudTrail typically delivers events a few minutes after the call. A metric filter turns the log events that match its pattern into a metric, and a CloudWatch alarm watches that metric. The pattern matches reads in the documents bucket where the principal is not the knowledge base's service role. The syncs are the normal reads, and they do not match, so they raise no alarm. A read by any other role matches, so the alarm fires within minutes, not weeks later.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"
Example: "CloudWatch to monitor data access"

Sources:

  • Logging data events (AWS CloudTrail User Guide)

  • Creating CloudWatch alarms for CloudTrail events: examples

  • Types of Macie findings

INCORRECT: Turn on S3 request metrics for the documents bucket, and add a CloudWatch alarm that uses anomaly detection on the GetRequests metric of the bucket.
S3 request metrics count the requests to a bucket, and GetRequests counts the GET requests for objects. An alarm with anomaly detection on this count fits a bucket where a sudden rise in reads is the risk. But the metric has no dimension for the principal that sent a request. The knowledge base reads documents several times a day, so a few reads by another role look like the normal reads, and the alarm cannot separate the two.

INCORRECT: Send the trail's events to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and add a metric filter for every read of the documents bucket, with an alarm on each match.
A metric filter that matches every read fits a bucket that no one should read at all, such as a locked archive. Here the knowledge base reads new and changed documents each time it syncs, several times a day, and these are the normal reads. The security team wants no alarm for normal reads. This filter matches every sync, so the alarm fires several times a day, and a read by another role looks like one more alarm among many.

INCORRECT: Turn on Amazon Macie for the account, and have an Amazon EventBridge rule send each Macie policy finding for the documents bucket to the security team.
Amazon Macie monitors the S3 buckets in an account for security and access control. It creates a policy finding when a bucket's settings change in a risky way, for example when a bucket becomes public or is shared with an account outside the organization. Macie publishes new policy findings to EventBridge, so a rule can alert a team. This fits a team that must hear about risky changes to its buckets. Here the developer's role read documents, and nothing about the bucket changed. A policy finding reports the settings of a bucket, not each read of an object, so this setup sends no alert after the read that the security team wants to catch.
