The legal team stopped the project over two concerns. First, it believes that the records will help improve the provider's model that other companies also use. Second, it wants the company, not AWS, to control the encryption of the fine-tuned model, so that the company decides who can use it. The company will run no model infrastructure of its own.
Which actions answer both concerns?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company wants to fine-tune a third-party model in Amazon Bedrock on its customer support records, which it keeps in Amazon S3. In tests, only this model reached the company's minimum quality.
The legal team stopped the project over two concerns. First, it believes that the records will help improve the provider's model that other companies also use. Second, it wants the company, not AWS, to control the encryption of the fine-tuned model, so that the company decides who can use it. The company will run no model infrastructure of its own.
Which actions answer both concerns?
Select TWO.

options.text: Fine-tune an Amazon Nova model in Amazon Bedrock instead of the chosen model, so no third-party model provider receives the training records.
Fine-tune an open-weight model on Amazon SageMaker AI instead, and host it on an endpoint that the company runs itself.
Fine-tune the chosen model in Amazon Bedrock, which trains a private copy of it and shares the training records with no model provider.
Fine-tune the chosen model in Amazon Bedrock with a customer managed AWS KMS key set for the custom model when the team creates the job.
Fine-tune the chosen model in Amazon Bedrock with a customer managed AWS KMS key set on the Amazon S3 bucket that holds the training records.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Fine-tune the chosen model in Amazon Bedrock, which trains a private copy of it and shares the training records with no model provider.
Fine-tuning in Amazon Bedrock does not change the provider's model. Amazon Bedrock makes a separate copy of the base model and trains this private copy with the company's records. It uses the records only for this fine-tuning job. They do not improve the base model, and Amazon Bedrock does not share them with the model provider. So the model that other companies use learns nothing from these records, which answers the first concern. The company also keeps the model that it chose, the only one that reached its minimum quality.

CORRECT: Fine-tune the chosen model in Amazon Bedrock with a customer managed AWS KMS key set for the custom model when the team creates the job.
By default, Amazon Bedrock encrypts a custom model with an AWS owned key. When the team creates the fine-tuning job, it can name a customer managed key in AWS KMS for the custom model instead. The company owns this key, and the key policy decides which roles can use it. A role that calls the custom model needs permission to decrypt with the key. So the company controls the encryption of the fine-tuned model and decides who can use it, which answers the second concern.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.2: "Develop privacy-preserving systems to protect sensitive information during FM interactions"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock native data privacy features"

Sources:

  • Encryption of custom models

  • Amazon Bedrock FAQs

INCORRECT: Fine-tune an Amazon Nova model in Amazon Bedrock instead of the chosen model, so no third-party model provider receives the training records.
Amazon Nova models are built by Amazon, and fine-tuning one in Amazon Bedrock is a good choice for a team that has no preferred model. Here, only the chosen third-party model reached the company's minimum quality in the tests. The switch is also not needed for the first concern, because Amazon Bedrock shares the training records with no model provider, whichever model the team fine-tunes. And it does nothing for the second concern, the key that protects the fine-tuned model.

INCORRECT: Fine-tune an open-weight model on Amazon SageMaker AI instead, and host it on an endpoint that the company runs itself.
Fine-tuning an open-weight model on SageMaker AI and hosting it on the company's own endpoint gives the company full control of the model files and of the instances that serve the model. It fits a company that is ready to run its own model hosting. Here the company will run no model infrastructure of its own, and only the chosen model reached the minimum quality in the tests.

INCORRECT: Fine-tune the chosen model in Amazon Bedrock with a customer managed AWS KMS key set on the Amazon S3 bucket that holds the training records.
A customer managed key on the bucket protects the training records while they sit in Amazon S3, and this is good practice for sensitive data. But the second concern is about the fine-tuned model, not the records. The key on the bucket does not encrypt the custom model. Unless the team names a customer managed key for the custom model when it creates the job, Amazon Bedrock encrypts the model with an AWS owned key.

The privacy team has used Amazon Macie only for one-time checks. The account holds thousands of buckets, and the privacy budget covers only a small sample of objects each day. Use the Macie bucket inventory, and have each team check the bucket's public access and encryption settings before it connects the bucket.

CORRECT: Turn on automated sensitive data discovery for the account, and have each team check the bucket's sensitivity score before it connects the bucket.
Automated sensitive data discovery gives broad visibility into where sensitive data might be in Amazon S3. Macie keeps evaluating the bucket inventory, selects representative objects with sampling, and inspects them each day. By default, it covers all the general purpose buckets in the account, so it also analyzes new buckets, and no one has to keep a list of buckets. For each bucket, Macie keeps a sensitivity score, a number that shows how much sensitive data the bucket might contain, and it updates the score each day as the analysis continues. A new bucket starts with the label Not yet analyzed, so a team waits for a real score before it connects the bucket. The analysis inspects only a fraction of the data, which fits a small daily budget.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.2: "Develop privacy-preserving systems to protect sensitive information during FM interactions"
Example: "Amazon Comprehend and Amazon Macie to detect personally identifiable information [PII]"

Sources:

  • Performing automated sensitive data discovery
  • Sensitivity scoring for S3 buckets
  • What is Amazon Macie?

INCORRECT: Run a one-time sensitive data discovery job that inspects every object in every current bucket, and share the job's findings with the teams.
A one-time job with full sampling fits a single assessment of data that already exists, such as an archive before its first use. Here teams create new buckets every week, and a one-time job does not analyze them. A job that inspects every object in thousands of buckets also costs much more than a budget that covers a small sample each day.

INCORRECT: Run a daily sensitive data discovery job on a list of the buckets that exist today, with a low sampling depth, and send its findings to the teams.
A recurring job on chosen buckets fits a fixed set of buckets that need regular checks, and a low sampling depth keeps its cost down. But this job analyzes only the buckets on its list. Teams create new buckets every week, and someone would have to add each one by hand. The privacy team wants new buckets covered with no manual step.

INCORRECT: Use the Macie bucket inventory, and have each team check the bucket's public access and encryption settings before it connects the bucket.
Macie keeps an inventory of the S3 buckets and evaluates their security and access control, such as public access and encryption settings. This fits a check that a bucket is not open to the public. But these settings say nothing about the data inside the objects. The privacy team wants a rating of how much personal data a bucket may hold.

The company's retention policy says that each log must be deleted a fixed number of days after it is written. Until then, auditors must be able to read any log. One year later, no log has ever been deleted, and the bucket keeps growing. The team will run no custom code for this.
Which change enforces the retention policy?
questions.promptText:
A company turned on model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock and sends the logs to an Amazon S3 bucket under one prefix. Each log holds the full prompt and response, and many prompts contain customer details. The bucket does not use versioning, and nothing else writes to the prefix.
The company's retention policy says that each log must be deleted a fixed number of days after it is written. Until then, auditors must be able to read any log. One year later, no log has ever been deleted, and the bucket keeps growing. The team will run no custom code for this.
Which change enforces the retention policy?

options.text: Add an S3 Lifecycle rule on the log prefix with an Expiration action at the policy's number of days, so each log expires at that age.
Add an S3 Lifecycle rule on the log prefix that moves each log to S3 Glacier Deep Archive at the policy's number of days, for long-term storage.
Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket with a default retention period of the policy's number of days, so S3 keeps each log for that time.
Add an S3 Lifecycle rule on the log prefix that moves each log to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so S3 moves logs that nobody reads to cheaper tiers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an S3 Lifecycle rule on the log prefix with an Expiration action at the policy's number of days, so each log expires at that age.
Amazon Bedrock stores invocation logs until the logging configuration is deleted, and nothing in this setup removes old logs from the bucket. That is why no log has ever been deleted. An S3 Lifecycle rule acts on the objects that match its filter, here the log prefix. The Expiration action acts when an object reaches the age that the rule sets. The bucket does not use versioning, so S3 queues each expired log for removal and removes it permanently, with no code to run. Until that age, the logs stay where they are, and auditors can read any of them.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.2: "Develop privacy-preserving systems to protect sensitive information during FM interactions"
Example: "Amazon S3 Lifecycle configurations to implement data retention policies"

Sources:

  • Expiring objects (Amazon S3 User Guide)
  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
  • Locking objects with Object Lock

INCORRECT: Add an S3 Lifecycle rule on the log prefix that moves each log to S3 Glacier Deep Archive at the policy's number of days, for long-term storage.
A transition moves objects to another storage class. S3 Glacier Deep Archive fits data that a company must keep for years, for example for compliance, and rarely reads. But a transition only moves each log, and it deletes nothing. The logs with customer details would stay after the policy's date, in an archive where each read first needs a restore.

INCORRECT: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket with a default retention period of the policy's number of days, so S3 keeps each log for that time.
S3 Object Lock stores objects in a write-once-read-many model. A retention period keeps an object version locked until the period ends, which fits records that must be kept for a set time. The policy here asks for the opposite: each log must be deleted at a set age. When the retention period ends, the log can be deleted, but Object Lock does not delete it. Object Lock also works only in buckets with versioning, and this bucket has none.

INCORRECT: Add an S3 Lifecycle rule on the log prefix that moves each log to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so S3 moves logs that nobody reads to cheaper tiers.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors how often objects are read and moves the objects that nobody reads to lower-cost access tiers. It fits data with changing or unknown access patterns. It moves objects between tiers and does not delete them, so the logs with customer details would stay in the bucket, only in another tier.

But by default, CloudWatch Logs keeps log data indefinitely, so entries stay after the policy's number of years. Without a KMS key on the log group, CloudWatch Logs still encrypts the data, but not with the company's own key.

INCORRECT: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging writes each model request and response to a log group that keeps its default settings, with no expiry date and the default encryption.
This log shows each model call, which helps a team that studies prompts and answers. It fails both needs here. Each request holds only the prompt, with no record ID and no document IDs, and the log group keeps data indefinitely without the company's own KMS key.

Support engineers read this log group every day to fix errors, and they must keep that access. A small fraud team must still see the original values in the same log events when it investigates a case. The log group keeps events for two weeks.

questions.promptText:
A company's support assistant runs in AWS Lambda, and the function writes each user prompt to its log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The prompts now contain customer names, card numbers and email addresses.
Support engineers read this log group every day to fix errors, and they must keep that access. A small fraud team must still see the original values in the same log events when it investigates a case. The log group keeps events for two weeks.
The team will write no new code and will not change the application code for this.
Which changes hide the values from the support engineers and keep them readable for the fraud team?
Select TWO.

options.text: Grant the logs:Unmask permission to the fraud team's IAM role, and do not grant it to the IAM role that the support engineers use.
Change the function to remove names, card numbers and email addresses from each prompt before it writes the prompt to the log group.
Add a data protection policy to the log group with managed data identifiers for names, credit card numbers and email addresses in each event.
Give the support engineers a saved CloudWatch Logs Insights query that masks names, card numbers and email addresses, and keep the fraud team's access as it is.
Add a subscription filter that sends each log event to a new Lambda function, which masks the values and writes the events to a second log group.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Grant the logs:Unmask permission to the fraud team's IAM role, and do not grant it to the IAM role that the support engineers use.
Masked data stays readable for the people who need it. Only users who have the logs:Unmask IAM permission can view unmasked data. The fraud team's role gets this permission, so its members can see the original values in the same log events. The support engineers' role does not get it, so they keep reading the log group every day and see masks where the values were.

CORRECT: Add a data protection policy to the log group with managed data identifiers for names, credit card numbers and email addresses in each event.
A data protection policy finds sensitive data in log events as they arrive in the log group. Managed data identifiers are ready-made data types, and CloudWatch Logs has identifiers for names, credit card numbers and email addresses. By default, the matching data is masked at all egress points, such as Logs Insights queries, metric filters and subscription filters. The policy is a setting, so no code changes. Events that arrived before the policy stay unmasked, and the two-week retention removes them.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.4: "Implement continuous monitoring and advanced governance controls to support safety audits and regulatory readiness"
Example: "token-level redaction"

Sources:

  • Help protect sensitive log data with masking

  • CloudWatch Logs managed data identifiers for sensitive data types

INCORRECT: Change the function to remove names, card numbers and email addresses from each prompt before it writes the prompt to the log group.
Removing sensitive values in code before they reach a log is a good practice when nobody needs them later. Here the fraud team must see the original values in the log events, and the function cannot restore values that it removed. The team will also not change the application code for this.

INCORRECT: Give the support engineers a saved CloudWatch Logs Insights query that masks names, card numbers and email addresses, and keep the fraud team's access as it is.
A Logs Insights query can replace text in the fields that it returns, which helps a person who wants query results without these values. But the query changes only its own results. The stored log events still hold the values. The support engineers keep their access to the log group, so they can run any other query or open the events and see the values. Keeping the fraud team's access meets only the fraud team's need.

INCORRECT: Add a subscription filter that sends each log event to a new Lambda function, which masks the values and writes the events to a second log group.
A subscription filter sends log events to another service as they arrive, and a Lambda function can then change them and write them to another place. This fits a change that no built-in feature offers. Here the team will write no new code, and this design needs a new function. The support engineers would also keep their access to the original log group, where the values stay.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's assistant runs in an AWS Lambda function and serves four features, such as billing help and returns. An Amazon Bedrock guardrail checks each answer for grounding, and the assistant shows the grounding score next to the answer. Managers call an answer low confidence when its score is at or under a threshold that they chose.
Last month, low-confidence answers in the returns feature became three times as common. They are still a small share, and most answers in that feature still score high. The other three features stayed normal. Managers now want an alarm for each feature when its share of low-confidence answers rises above a limit.
How should the team publish the scores and set the alarm?
questions.promptText:
A company's assistant runs in an AWS Lambda function and serves four features, such as billing help and returns. An Amazon Bedrock guardrail checks each answer for grounding, and the assistant shows the grounding score next to the answer. Managers call an answer low confidence when its score is at or under a threshold that they chose.
Last month, low-confidence answers in the returns feature became three times as common. They are still a small share, and most answers in that feature still score high. The other three features stayed normal. Managers now want an alarm for each feature when its share of low-confidence answers rises above a limit.
How should the team publish the scores and set the alarm?

options.text: Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and a Feature dimension, and alarm on the percentile rank of scores at or under the threshold for each feature.
Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and a Feature dimension, and alarm on the average score of each feature when it falls under the threshold.
Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and no Feature dimension, and alarm on the percentile rank of scores at or under the threshold for all answers.
Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and no Feature dimension, and alarm on the average score of all answers when it falls under the threshold.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and a Feature dimension, and alarm on the percentile rank of scores at or under the threshold for each feature.
PutMetricData publishes custom metrics to CloudWatch. The function sends each grounding score as its own data point, and it adds the name of the feature as a Feature dimension. A dimension is part of the identity of a metric, so each feature gets its own metric. CloudWatch calculates percentile statistics for a custom metric only when the function publishes the raw data points. A statistic set is not enough, because it holds only the minimum, maximum, sum and sample count of many data points. The percentile rank statistic, PR, gives the percentage of data points that meet a fixed threshold. For example, PR(:0.4) returns the percentage of scores that are 0.4 or less. When PR uses the managers' threshold, it gives the share of low-confidence answers in each feature, and a CloudWatch alarm can use this statistic. The alarm for the returns feature goes into the ALARM state when its share rises above the limit, even when its average score changes very little.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.1: "Develop transparent AI systems in FM outputs"
Example: "CloudWatch to collect confidence metrics and quantify uncertainty"

Sources:

  • CloudWatch statistics definitions
  • Metrics concepts
  • PutMetricAlarm (Amazon CloudWatch API Reference)

INCORRECT: Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and a Feature dimension, and alarm on the average score of each feature when it falls under the threshold.
An alarm on the average score of each feature fits a problem where all answers in a feature slowly become less grounded. Here most answers in the returns feature still score high, and the low-confidence answers are still a small share, even after that share tripled. A few more low scores among many high scores move the average very little, so this alarm does not go into the ALARM state while the share rises.

INCORRECT: Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and no Feature dimension, and alarm on the percentile rank of scores at or under the threshold for all answers.
The percentile rank is the right statistic for the share of answers at or under a threshold, and one metric with no dimension fits an assistant with a single feature. Here the four features share one metric, so the alarm watches the share of low scores across all answers. The other three features stayed normal, so the rise in the returns feature moves the combined share only a little. Managers also asked for an alarm for each feature, and one metric gives them only one alarm.

INCORRECT: Publish each score as a raw data point with PutMetricData and no Feature dimension, and alarm on the average score of all answers when it falls under the threshold.
One average of all scores gives a simple view of the whole assistant. It fails both needs here. An average changes very little when a small share of scores is low, and one metric for all four features does not show which feature changed.

For each of the two applicant groups that the fairness policy names, an AWS Lambda function publishes two custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch: the number of recommendations and the number of approvals.
The number of requests changes a lot from week to week, and the approval rates of both groups rise and fall together with the season. The policy measures one thing: the approval rate of one group must stay close to the rate of the other group. The team must show this every week and get an alert when the gap grows past the policy's limit.
Which alarm should the team create?
questions.promptText:
A lender's assistant recommends whether to approve each loan request, and staff make the final decision. For each of the two applicant groups that the fairness policy names, an AWS Lambda function publishes two custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch: the number of recommendations and the number of approvals.
The number of requests changes a lot from week to week, and the approval rates of both groups rise and fall together with the season. The policy measures one thing: the approval rate of one group must stay close to the rate of the other group. The team must show this every week and get an alert when the gap grows past the policy's limit.
Which alarm should the team create?

options.text: One alarm for each group on its approvals metric, when the number of approvals in a week falls under a fixed value.
An alarm on a metric math expression that divides approvals by recommendations for each group and takes the absolute difference between the two rates.
One alarm for each group on a metric math expression that divides approvals by recommendations, when the group's rate leaves a fixed range.
A composite alarm that combines one approval rate alarm for each group with an OR rule, so that one alarm covers both groups.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An alarm on a metric math expression that divides approvals by recommendations for each group and takes the absolute difference between the two rates.
Metric math queries several CloudWatch metrics and uses math expressions to create a new time series. Here the expression divides approvals by recommendations for each group, which gives each group's approval rate. Then ABS of the difference between the two rates gives the gap, whichever group is higher. A CloudWatch alarm can watch the result of a math expression, so it fires when the gap passes the policy's limit. A rate is a share of the requests, so a busy week and a quiet week compare fairly, and a seasonal change that moves both rates together leaves the gap the same. The same expression on a CloudWatch graph shows the gap each week.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.2: "Apply fairness evaluations to ensure unbiased FM outputs"
Example: "pre-defined fairness metrics in CloudWatch"

Sources:

  • Math expressions with metrics

  • Create a CloudWatch alarm based on a metric math expression

  • Composite alarms

INCORRECT: One alarm for each group on its approvals metric, when the number of approvals in a week falls under a fixed value.
An alarm on the number of approvals fits a goal about volume, for example a minimum number of approved requests each week. Here the number of requests changes a lot from week to week, so the number of approvals moves with it. A drop can mean fewer requests, not a larger gap, and a gap can grow while both counts stay above the fixed value.

INCORRECT: One alarm for each group on a metric math expression that divides approvals by recommendations, when the group's rate leaves a fixed range.
A rate for each group is the right measure, and a fixed range fits a group whose own rate must stay inside set limits. Here the rates of both groups rise and fall together with the season. Both alarms can fire when the season moves both rates while the gap stays small. A gap can also grow while each rate stays inside its range. The policy is about the gap, and an alarm on one group's rate does not measure it.

INCORRECT: A composite alarm that combines one approval rate alarm for each group with an OR rule, so that one alarm covers both groups.
A composite alarm watches the states of other alarms and combines them with a rule, such as OR or AND. It fits a team that wants one notification instead of many. But it works on alarm states, not on metric values. It cannot compute the difference between two rates, so it can only combine the states of the two group alarms, and neither of those alarms measures the gap.

A company runs a loan letter writer as a flow in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows. The prompt node in the flow uses a prompt version from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. The team wrote a new prompt version that reduces biased wording in the letters.
Before the new version replaces the old one, both versions must write letters for real customers during the same weeks. A customer who gets a letter from the new version must get every later letter from the new version too. The team then compares the bias scores of the two versions.
How should the team run this comparison?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a loan letter writer as a flow in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows. The prompt node in the flow uses a prompt version from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. The team wrote a new prompt version that reduces biased wording in the letters.
Before the new version replaces the old one, both versions must write letters for real customers during the same weeks. A customer who gets a letter from the new version must get every later letter from the new version too. The team then compares the bias scores of the two versions.
How should the team run this comparison?

options.text: Run both prompt versions through two flow versions with one flow alias each, and let the application choose the alias from a hash of the customer ID.
Run both prompt versions through two Lambda function versions that each call one flow alias, and let a weighted Lambda alias choose a version for each customer request.
Run both prompt versions as variants in the Prompt Management compare mode, with test values from recent loan requests, and save the better variant as the draft.
Run both prompt versions in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with an LLM-as-a-judge model, on a dataset of recent loan requests, and keep the version that scores better.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run both prompt versions through two flow versions with one flow alias each, and let the application choose the alias from a hash of the customer ID.
A flow version is a snapshot of the flow, and a prompt node can point to one prompt version by its ARN. So one flow version runs the old prompt and the other runs the new prompt. Each alias points to one flow version, and the application calls InvokeFlow with an alias ID. The application decides which alias each customer gets. A hash of the customer ID gives the same result for the same customer every time, so each customer stays on one version for every letter. The application logs the alias with each letter, and the team compares the bias scores for each alias.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.2: "Apply fairness evaluations to ensure unbiased FM outputs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management and Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows to perform systematic A/B testing"

Sources:

  • Deploy a flow to your application using versions and aliases

  • Implement Lambda canary deployments using a weighted alias

  • Create a prompt using Prompt management

INCORRECT: Run both prompt versions through two Lambda function versions that each call one flow alias, and let a weighted Lambda alias choose a version for each customer request.
A weighted Lambda alias is the standard way to send a share of requests to a new function version, known as a canary deployment. Lambda chooses the version for each request with a simple probabilistic model, and it does not use the customer ID to choose. So one customer can get the old wording in one letter and the new wording in the next. The scenario requires that a customer who got the new version keeps getting it.

INCORRECT: Run both prompt versions as variants in the Prompt Management compare mode, with test values from recent loan requests, and save the better variant as the draft.
Compare mode in the Prompt Management console runs variants of a prompt side by side on test values. It is a good way to choose a prompt before a release. When the team saves one variant as the draft, the other variants are deleted. The scenario asks for both versions to write letters for real customers during the same weeks, and a console test sends no letters to anyone.

INCORRECT: Run both prompt versions in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with an LLM-as-a-judge model, on a dataset of recent loan requests, and keep the version that scores better.
An evaluation job with a judge model scores the responses to the prompts in a dataset. It is a good step before any live test, because it compares both versions on the same prompts. But this job runs on a dataset of past requests, not on letters for real customers. The scenario asks for both versions to serve real customers during the same weeks, with each customer kept on one version.

Teams change their working drafts many times a day during tests, and create a new version for each release. Policy says every guardrail version must keep its sensitive information filter and its denied topics. Last month, a team removed a filter during a test and released a version without it. The account has an AWS CloudTrail trail that logs management events.
The governance team needs an alert within minutes of such a release, and no alert for test changes. Teams must still edit and release their own guardrails.
Which solution meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
A company uses Amazon Bedrock Guardrails in production. Each application calls a numbered version of its own team's guardrail on every request. Teams change their working drafts many times a day during tests, and create a new version for each release. Policy says every guardrail version must keep its sensitive information filter and its denied topics. Last month, a team removed a filter during a test and released a version without it. The account has an AWS CloudTrail trail that logs management events.
The governance team needs an alert within minutes of such a release, and no alert for test changes. Teams must still edit and release their own guardrails.
Which solution meets these needs?

options.text: An IAM policy that denies UpdateGuardrail and CreateGuardrailVersion to the teams, and lets the governance team make every guardrail change and every new version.
An IAM policy with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key on the application roles, so each model call must apply the guardrail of the team that owns the application.

An Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for UpdateGuardrail events from CloudTrail that invokes an AWS Lambda function, which checks the guardrail with GetGuardrail and alerts through Amazon SNS.

An Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for CreateGuardrailVersion events from CloudTrail that invokes an AWS Lambda function, which checks the version with GetGuardrail and alerts through Amazon SNS.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for CreateGuardrailVersion events from CloudTrail that invokes an AWS Lambda function, which checks the version with GetGuardrail and alerts through Amazon SNS.
Creating a version is the step that releases a guardrail, because applications call numbered versions. CloudTrail records each CreateGuardrailVersion call as a management event, and EventBridge receives these API call events on the default event bus when the account has a trail with logging. The rule starts the check when EventBridge receives the event, so the check does not wait for a schedule. The Lambda function reads that version with GetGuardrail. The response includes the sensitive information policy and the topic policy, so the function can see if either one is missing and send the alert. Teams keep full control of their guardrails, and test changes to a draft cause no alert.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.3: "Develop policy-compliant AI systems to ensure adherence to responsible AI practices"
Example: "Lambda functions to perform automated compliance checks"

Sources:

  • Deploy your guardrail

  • GetGuardrail (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • AWS service events delivered via AWS CloudTrail

INCORRECT: An IAM policy that denies UpdateGuardrail and CreateGuardrailVersion to the teams, and lets the governance team make every guardrail change and every new version.
Central control of guardrail changes is a valid choice in some companies, and this policy does prevent a release without the filter. But the teams can no longer edit or release their own guardrails, and the question requires that they can.

INCORRECT: An IAM policy with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key on the application roles, so each model call must apply the guardrail of the team that owns the application.
This condition key denies a model call that does not include the guardrail named in the policy. It is the right control when some applications skip their guardrail. Here, every application already applies its team's guardrail on every request. The missing filter is in the guardrail version itself: a version without the filter is still the same guardrail, so the call passes. The policy also sends no alert.

INCORRECT: An Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for UpdateGuardrail events from CloudTrail that invokes an AWS Lambda function, which checks the guardrail with GetGuardrail and alerts through Amazon SNS.
UpdateGuardrail is the call that changes the working draft of a guardrail. A rule on this event is the right choice when applications use the draft directly. Here, applications call numbered versions, and teams change their drafts many times a day during tests. Every test change would start a check, and a draft with a filter removed for a test would send an alert. The governance team wants no alert for test changes.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A support team uses Claude Haiku in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API to summarize each closed ticket. The case screen shows three parts of each ticket, each on its own line: what went wrong, how it was fixed and what happens next.
The first summaries were several paragraphs long, so the team set a low limit on the number of tokens that the model may generate. The summaries are now short, but some end in the middle of a sentence, and agents cannot tell a cut summary from a complete one.
Each summary must come from one model call, and the screen must never show a cut summary.
Which changes keep each summary short and complete?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A support team uses Claude Haiku in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API to summarize each closed ticket. The case screen shows three parts of each ticket, each on its own line: what went wrong, how it was fixed and what happens next.
The first summaries were several paragraphs long, so the team set a low limit on the number of tokens that the model may generate. The summaries are now short, but some end in the middle of a sentence, and agents cannot tell a cut summary from a complete one.
Each summary must come from one model call, and the screen must never show a cut summary.
Which changes keep each summary short and complete?
Select TWO.

options.text: Lower the maxTokens value further, so each summary has less room and the model writes fewer tokens for each ticket.
Add a newline character to stopSequences, so the model stops at the end of its first line of output.
Raise maxTokens well above the length of three short bullets, and do not show any summary whose stop reason is max_tokens.
When a summary stops at the limit, send it back in a second call that asks the model to rewrite it as three bullets.
State in the system prompt that each summary has three bullets of one sentence each, and name the topic of each bullet.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Raise maxTokens well above the length of three short bullets, and do not show any summary whose stop reason is max_tokens.
maxTokens sets the largest number of tokens that the model may generate in one response. It does not tell the model how long its answer should be. When the model reaches the limit, it stops where it is, and the stop reason in the response is max_tokens. That is how the summaries ended in the middle of a sentence. With the length set in the prompt, the team can set maxTokens well above the length of three short bullets, and it stays as an upper limit in case the model writes far more than expected. The application reads the stop reason of each response. A summary that ends with end_turn is complete. The application does not show a summary with max_tokens, so a cut summary never reaches the screen.

CORRECT: State in the system prompt that each summary has three bullets of one sentence each, and name the topic of each bullet.
A prompt can set constraints on the output, such as how many sentences to write and what each one covers. The model then writes its answer to fit them. Here the system prompt asks for three bullets of one sentence each and names the topic of each bullet: what went wrong, how it was fixed and what happens next. These are the three parts that the case screen shows. The model writes a short summary that still covers all three parts. The summary is short because the prompt asks for three one-sentence bullets, not because a limit stopped the model in the middle of a sentence.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.1: "Develop token efficiency systems to reduce FM costs while maintaining effectiveness"
Example: "response size controls"

Sources:

  • InferenceConfiguration (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Converse (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • Design a prompt

INCORRECT: Lower the maxTokens value further, so each summary has less room and the model writes fewer tokens for each ticket.
A low maxTokens value limits the length and the cost of each response. It fits tasks that need only a very short answer, such as a label for sentiment, where the model finishes well inside the limit. Here the limit already cuts summaries in the middle of a sentence. maxTokens only sets the point where generation stops, so a lower value cuts more summaries, not fewer.

INCORRECT: Add a newline character to stopSequences, so the model stops at the end of its first line of output.
A stop sequence is a sequence of characters that makes the model stop generating. A newline as a stop sequence fits output that must be a single line, such as a title, when the model sometimes adds more lines after it. Here each summary has three parts, and the screen shows each part on its own line. The model would stop after the first line, so every summary would lose the other two parts.

INCORRECT: When a summary stops at the limit, send it back in a second call that asks the model to rewrite it as three bullets.
A second call that shortens or reformats an answer is a real repair step when extra model calls are acceptable. Here each summary must come from one model call. This design adds a second call for every summary that stops at the limit.

questions.promptHtml:
A company summarizes insurance claims with Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock. The first version called InvokeModel with the Nova request body, which set maxTokens, temperature, topP and topK. The team tuned the topK value over weeks of tests, and reviewers approved the summaries at that value.
The company now moves every model call to the Converse API, so that all features share one request format. Another team already moved its Claude Haiku calls to Converse and shared its code as an example. The team copied its four settings into the Converse field for inference settings, and the call now fails with a validation error.
How should the team pass the tuned value?
questions.promptText:
A company summarizes insurance claims with Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock. The first version called InvokeModel with the Nova request body, which set maxTokens, temperature, topP and topK. The team tuned the topK value over weeks of tests, and reviewers approved the summaries at that value.
The company now moves every model call to the Converse API, so that all features share one request format. Another team already moved its Claude Haiku calls to Converse and shared its code as an example. The team copied its four settings into the Converse field for inference settings, and the call now fails with a validation error.
How should the team pass the tuned value?

options.text: Call the Converse API, keep the base settings in inferenceConfig, and send the tuned value as top_k at the top level of additionalModelRequestFields.
Keep this call on InvokeModel, and send the tuned value as topK in the inferenceConfig object of the Amazon Nova request body.
Call the Converse API, keep the base settings in inferenceConfig, and send the tuned value as topK in an inferenceConfig object in additionalModelRequestFields.
Keep this call on InvokeModel, and send the tuned value as top_k at the top level of the Amazon Nova request body.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call the Converse API, keep the base settings in inferenceConfig, and send the tuned value as topK in an inferenceConfig object in additionalModelRequestFields.
The Converse API has one base set of inference settings in its inferenceConfig field: maxTokens, stopSequences, temperature and topP. topK is not in that set, so the copied settings fail. A setting that only some models support goes in the additionalModelRequestFields field, as JSON in the form that the model expects. Amazon Nova expects topK inside its own inferenceConfig object. So the team puts that object, with the tuned topK value, in additionalModelRequestFields, and it keeps maxTokens, temperature and topP in the base inferenceConfig field. The model gets the same four values as before, and the call uses the Converse API like every other call.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.4: "Enhance FM performance to achieve optimal results for specific GenAI use cases"
Example: "model-specific parameter configurations"

Sources:

  • Using the Converse API (Amazon Nova User Guide)

  • Inference using Converse API

  • Complete request schema (Amazon Nova User Guide)

INCORRECT: Call the Converse API, keep the base settings in inferenceConfig, and send the tuned value as top_k at the top level of additionalModelRequestFields.
A top_k field at the top level of additionalModelRequestFields is the right form for Anthropic Claude models. That is why the other team's code works for its Claude Haiku calls. This company calls Amazon Nova Pro, and Nova names and places this setting in a different way: topK, with a capital K, inside an inferenceConfig object in additionalModelRequestFields. A top-level top_k is the field name that Claude models use, and it is not the Nova setting that the team tuned.

INCORRECT: Keep this call on InvokeModel, and send the tuned value as topK in the inferenceConfig object of the Amazon Nova request body.
This is the request that worked before. In the Nova request body for InvokeModel, topK is in the inferenceConfig object next to maxTokens, temperature and topP. Keeping a call on InvokeModel fits a feature that needs a request body for one model. Here the company moves every model call to the Converse API, so that all features share one request format.

INCORRECT: Keep this call on InvokeModel, and send the tuned value as top_k at the top level of the Amazon Nova request body.
In the InvokeModel request body of Anthropic Claude models, top_k is a field at the top level, so this form fits a Claude call on InvokeModel. It is wrong for two reasons here. The Nova request body takes topK inside its inferenceConfig object, not at the top level. And the company moves every model call to the Converse API.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A retail company uses Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock for two features. The first reads customer emails and extracts order fields, such as the order number and the delivery date. The second writes five slogans for each marketing campaign. Both features send the same sampling settings with each request.
The extractor sometimes returns different values when it reads the same email twice, although its replies always use the right fields and layout. Finance needs the same values on every run. The slogan writer returns almost the same five slogans each time a marketer asks again, although its prompt already includes clear sample slogans. Marketers want new ideas on every request.
Which setup should the team give each feature?
questions.promptText:
A retail company uses Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock for two features. The first reads customer emails and extracts order fields, such as the order number and the delivery date. The second writes five slogans for each marketing campaign. Both features send the same sampling settings with each request.
The extractor sometimes returns different values when it reads the same email twice, although its replies always use the right fields and layout. Finance needs the same values on every run. The slogan writer returns almost the same five slogans each time a marketer asks again, although its prompt already includes clear sample slogans. Marketers want new ideas on every request.
Which setup should the team give each feature?

options.text: Extractor: a low temperature and its current prompt. Slogan writer: a high temperature and its current prompt.
Extractor: a high temperature and a stricter output format. Slogan writer: a low temperature and more example slogans.
Extractor: a low temperature and its current prompt. Slogan writer: a low temperature and more example slogans.
Extractor: a high temperature and a stricter output format. Slogan writer: a high temperature and its current prompt.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Extractor: a low temperature and its current prompt. Slogan writer: a high temperature and its current prompt.
Temperature changes how the model picks each next token. A lower temperature makes the model more likely to choose the most likely tokens, which leads to more deterministic replies. A higher temperature makes the model more likely to choose less likely tokens, which leads to more varied replies. The extractor needs the same values each time it reads the same email, so it gets a low temperature, and its prompt does not change, because its replies already use the right fields and layout. The slogan writer needs new ideas on every request, so it gets a high temperature, and its prompt does not change, because it already holds clear sample slogans. Each feature sends its own settings with its requests, although both use the same model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.4: "Enhance FM performance to achieve optimal results for specific GenAI use cases"
Example: "appropriate temperature and top-k/top-p selection based on requirements"

Sources:

  • Influence response generation with inference parameters
  • InferenceConfiguration (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

INCORRECT: Extractor: a high temperature and a stricter output format. Slogan writer: a low temperature and more example slogans.
This setup fits the opposite case: a feature that may use different words each time inside a fixed format, and a writer that must follow one approved writing style. Here it makes both problems worse. A high temperature makes the extractor's values vary even more, and its replies already use the right fields and layout. A low temperature makes the slogan writer choose the most likely words again and again, and its prompt already holds clear sample slogans.

INCORRECT: Extractor: a low temperature and its current prompt. Slogan writer: a low temperature and more example slogans.
A low temperature for both features fits two features that must each give the same reply every time, and more examples guide the style of a writer. The extractor part is right. But a low temperature is why the slogan writer repeats itself: it keeps choosing the most likely words. Its prompt already holds clear sample slogans, so more examples change the style of the slogans, not how different they are from each other.

INCORRECT: Extractor: a high temperature and a stricter output format. Slogan writer: a high temperature and its current prompt.
A high temperature with a strict output format fits a feature that may use different words each time inside a fixed layout, such as varied product descriptions in one template. The slogan writer part is right. But the extractor's replies already use the right fields and layout, and the problem is the values. A high temperature makes the model choose less likely tokens, so the values change even more between runs.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company runs four features on one model in Amazon Bedrock: a chat assistant, a summarizer, an email writer and a search helper. Each feature runs in its own AWS Lambda function. All four functions share one IAM role and call the model on demand, in one AWS Region, with the same model ID. The four features are busy during the same office hours. Summarizer requests are far longer than the others.
Token use doubled last month. Capacity planners must now see, for each feature and each hour, how many tokens go into the model and how many come back. The four functions must keep sharing their one IAM role.
How can the team see token use for each feature?
questions.promptText:
A company runs four features on one model in Amazon Bedrock: a chat assistant, a summarizer, an email writer and a search helper. Each feature runs in its own AWS Lambda function. All four functions share one IAM role and call the model on demand, in one AWS Region, with the same model ID. The four features are busy during the same office hours. Summarizer requests are far longer than the others.
Token use doubled last month. Capacity planners must now see, for each feature and each hour, how many tokens go into the model and how many come back. The four functions must keep sharing their one IAM role.
How can the team see token use for each feature?

options.text: Graph the InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics of the model ID in CloudWatch, and match their peaks with the busy hours of each feature.
Create an application inference profile for each feature from the foundation model, have each feature call its own profile ARN, and graph each profile's token metrics.
Graph the InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics of the model ID in CloudWatch, and split the tokens of each hour by the Invocations of each function.
Tag each Lambda function with its feature as a cost allocation tag, and compare Amazon Bedrock token usage by tag in AWS Cost Explorer.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an application inference profile for each feature from the foundation model, have each feature call its own profile ARN, and graph each profile's token metrics.
An application inference profile is a resource that a team creates to track the usage and costs of a model. When the team creates it from the foundation model, the profile sends requests to that model in the same Region. Here the team creates one profile for each feature, and each function calls the model with the ARN of its own profile in place of the model ID.

The functions keep their shared IAM role, and the role's policy must allow calls to the new profiles. In CloudWatch, the team can then graph the Bedrock runtime metrics, such as InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount, for each profile. So the planners see the tokens in and the tokens out of each feature, hour by hour.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.5: "Create efficient resource allocation systems specifically for FM workloads"
Example: "utilization monitoring for prompt and completion patterns"

Sources:

  • Set up a model invocation resource using inference profiles

  • Track, allocate, and manage your generative AI cost and usage with Amazon Bedrock

  • Monitor bedrock-runtime inference using CloudWatch metrics

INCORRECT: Graph the InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics of the model ID in CloudWatch, and match their peaks with the busy hours of each feature.
InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount count the tokens that go into the model and the tokens that it returns, and a graph of them is the right view when one application uses a model. These metrics are reported for the model ID, and all four features call the same model ID, so each metric shows one line for all of them. Matching peaks with busy hours works only when the features are busy at different times, and these four are busy during the same office hours.

INCORRECT: Graph the InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics of the model ID in CloudWatch, and split the tokens of each hour by the Invocations of each function.
The Invocations metric of a Lambda function counts how many times the function code runs. Dividing a total by the number of calls from each caller is a quick estimate when the calls are about the same size. Here they are not. Summarizer requests are far longer than the others, so one summarizer call has many more tokens than a chat message. A split by the number of calls gives each feature the wrong share of the tokens.

INCORRECT: Tag each Lambda function with its feature as a cost allocation tag, and compare Amazon Bedrock token usage by tag in AWS Cost Explorer.
A cost allocation tag on a resource organizes the costs of that resource, so tags on the functions split the Lambda charges by feature. The token charges belong to Amazon Bedrock, not to the functions. For on-demand model calls, Amazon Bedrock tracks costs by tag through the tags on an application inference profile, and these functions call the model ID directly. The planners also need the tokens in and out for each hour, not only the cost.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company's writing service runs in an AWS Lambda function. For each user request, the function first runs a product search that sometimes takes several seconds. Then it builds a prompt from one of twelve templates and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API, with the same model ID for every template.
Latency and token cost vary widely between requests, and the team must find which templates cause the slow, long model calls. The slow calls appear only with real user requests, never in tests, and every template is in use all day.
How should the team profile the model calls by template?
questions.promptText:
A company's writing service runs in an AWS Lambda function. For each user request, the function first runs a product search that sometimes takes several seconds. Then it builds a prompt from one of twelve templates and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API, with the same model ID for every template.
Latency and token cost vary widely between requests, and the team must find which templates cause the slow, long model calls. The slow calls appear only with real user requests, never in tests, and every template is in use all day.
How should the team profile the model calls by template?

options.text: Graph InvocationLatency, InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount for the model ID in CloudWatch, and compare the lines with the hours when each template is most in use.
Replay a sample of past requests for each template against the model with the Converse API from a script, and compare the average latency and token counts of each template.
Graph the Duration metric of the Lambda function and the token metrics of the model ID in CloudWatch, and compare the lines with the hours when each template is most in use.
Log the template ID, the token counts and latencyMs from each Converse response at the end of each request, and group the entries by template in a Logs Insights query.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Log the template ID, the token counts and latencyMs from each Converse response at the end of each request, and group the entries by template in a Logs Insights query.
Each Converse response reports the token counts and the latency of that one model call. Its usage field holds the input tokens and the output tokens, and its metrics field holds latencyMs, the latency of the call in milliseconds. The function already knows which template it used. So at the end of each request, it writes one log entry with the template ID and these numbers, for example as JSON. The entries come from real user requests, where the problem appears. A CloudWatch Logs Insights query with the stats command then groups the entries by template, for example the average latencyMs and the average output tokens of each template. The latency comes from the model call alone, so the slow product search cannot make a template look slow.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.6: "Optimize FM system performance for GenAI workflows"
Example: "API call profiling for prompt-completion patterns"

Sources:

  • Converse (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • ConverseMetrics (Amazon Bedrock API Reference)

  • stats (Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide)

INCORRECT: Graph InvocationLatency, InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount for the model ID in CloudWatch, and compare the lines with the hours when each template is most in use.
InvocationLatency, InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount show the latency and the token use of a model. Comparing them with the busy hours of each prompt works when different prompts run at different times. These metrics have no dimension for a prompt template, and every template uses the same model ID. Every template is also in use all day, so the hours cannot show which template caused a slow call.

INCORRECT: Replay a sample of past requests for each template against the model with the Converse API from a script, and compare the average latency and token counts of each template.
Replaying past requests from a script measures each template under the same conditions, and it is a good way to compare templates before a release, as a performance benchmark. Here the slow calls appear only with real user requests, never in tests. A replay of past requests is a test of that kind, so it can show normal times for every template while real users still get the slow, long calls.

INCORRECT: Graph the Duration metric of the Lambda function and the token metrics of the model ID in CloudWatch, and compare the lines with the hours when each template is most in use.
The Duration metric of a Lambda function is the time that its code spends on one event, and the token metrics of the model show the tokens in and out. A graph of these metrics next to the busy hours of each prompt works when different prompts run at different times, and when the model call is the only slow step. Neither is true here. Every template is in use all day, and neither metric has a dimension for the template. The Duration of each invocation also includes the product search, which sometimes takes several seconds, so a slow search looks the same as a slow model call.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a document assistant on one Amazon Bedrock model. The team set an Amazon CloudWatch alarm with a fixed threshold on the token use of this model. The alarm fires every weekday morning during normal peak use, so the team ignores it.
Last week, during several short periods at night, users pasted very long documents into the assistant. The answers stayed as short as usual, and the number of requests stayed at its normal night level. Each burst was still smaller than a normal weekday morning, so the alarm did not fire.
Which alarm fires for bursts like these and does not fire during the normal daily cycle?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a document assistant on one Amazon Bedrock model. The team set an Amazon CloudWatch alarm with a fixed threshold on the token use of this model. The alarm fires every weekday morning during normal peak use, so the team ignores it.
Last week, during several short periods at night, users pasted very long documents into the assistant. The answers stayed as short as usual, and the number of requests stayed at its normal night level. Each burst was still smaller than a normal weekday morning, so the alarm did not fire.
Which alarm fires for bursts like these and does not fire during the normal daily cycle?

options.text: A CloudWatch alarm on the OutputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
A CloudWatch alarm on the InputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses a static threshold and fires when the value goes above the highest value of a normal day.
A CloudWatch alarm on the InputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
A CloudWatch alarm on the OutputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses a static threshold and fires when the value goes above the highest value of a normal day.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A CloudWatch alarm on the InputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
Start with what the users did. A pasted document becomes part of the prompt, so a very long document means many more tokens in the input of each request. InputTokenCount counts the tokens in the input, so it rises during each burst, even when the number of requests stays the same. Now look at the timing. An anomaly detection model learns the trend of a metric and its hourly, daily and weekly patterns from past data, and it draws a band of expected values for each point in time. The busy weekday morning is part of that pattern, so it stays inside the band. At night the expected value is low, so a burst of long documents goes above the band and the alarm fires.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.2: "Implement comprehensive GenAI monitoring systems to proactively identify issues and evaluate key performance indicators specific to FM implementations"
Example: "anomaly detection for token burst patterns and response drift"

Sources:

  • Using CloudWatch anomaly detection
  • Create a CloudWatch alarm based on anomaly detection
  • Monitor bedrock-runtime inference using CloudWatch metrics

INCORRECT: A CloudWatch alarm on the OutputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
OutputTokenCount counts the tokens in the model's response. An alarm like this helps when answers suddenly grow longer, for example after a change to the prompt. Here, the evidence is in the input of each call: users sent long documents, and the answers stayed as short as usual. The output did not change, so this alarm does not fire for these bursts.

INCORRECT: A CloudWatch alarm on the InputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses a static threshold and fires when the value goes above the highest value of a normal day.
This alarm watches the right metric, and a static threshold above the highest value of a normal day works well for a workload whose load is about the same at every hour. It would also stop the morning alarms. But the scenario says that each night burst was smaller than a normal weekday morning. A threshold above the highest value of a normal day is also above every night burst, so this alarm never fires for these bursts.

INCORRECT: A CloudWatch alarm on the OutputTokenCount metric for the model ID that uses a static threshold and fires when the value goes above the highest value of a normal day.
This alarm has both problems. It watches the output, which did not change during the bursts, and its static threshold is above the busy morning value, so it is also above every night burst. It fits a service whose load is about the same at every hour and where long answers are the risk. Here, neither the metric nor the threshold matches the evidence.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a generative AI application on Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock, the only Amazon Bedrock workload in its AWS account. Last quarter, a bug made the application call the model in a loop, and Bedrock spend rose for nine days before finance noticed it in the monthly bill.
Spend is higher on weekdays than on weekends, and it grows every month as more customers join, so any fixed dollar threshold stops being useful for an alarm within weeks. The on-call team wants a message in its Amazon SNS topic as soon as unusual spend is found. No one will change alarm settings or read cost reports by hand.
How should the team detect unusual Amazon Bedrock spend?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a generative AI application on Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock, the only Amazon Bedrock workload in its AWS account. Last quarter, a bug made the application call the model in a loop, and Bedrock spend rose for nine days before finance noticed it in the monthly bill.
Spend is higher on weekdays than on weekends, and it grows every month as more customers join, so any fixed dollar threshold stops being useful for an alarm within weeks. The on-call team wants a message in its Amazon SNS topic as soon as unusual spend is found. No one will change alarm settings or read cost reports by hand.
How should the team detect unusual Amazon Bedrock spend?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch billing alarm on the EstimatedCharges metric with a fixed threshold above this month's expected spend, and send it to the SNS topic.
Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services, and add an alert subscription that sends a weekly summary of anomalies by email.
Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services, and add an alert subscription that sends individual alerts to the SNS topic.
Create a CloudWatch billing alarm on the EstimatedCharges metric, have finance raise its threshold each month, and send it to the SNS topic.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services, and add an alert subscription that sends individual alerts to the SNS topic.
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning models to detect unusual spend patterns in the services that an account uses. It can take weekly or monthly patterns and natural growth into account, which keeps false alerts low. So the higher weekday spend and the growth from new customers are normal to it, while a loop that makes spend rise suddenly is not. A monitor for AWS services automatically evaluates every AWS service that the account uses, including Amazon Bedrock. An alert subscription with individual alerts notifies the team as soon as an anomaly is detected, and these alerts need an Amazon SNS topic, here the on-call team's topic. The team can then look at the root causes of the anomaly by service, account, Region and usage type. No one sets or updates a dollar amount.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.2: "Implement comprehensive GenAI monitoring systems to proactively identify issues and evaluate key performance indicators specific to FM implementations"
Example: "cost anomaly detection"

Sources:

  • Getting started with AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
  • Detecting unusual spend with AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
  • Create a billing alarm to monitor your estimated AWS charges

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch billing alarm on the EstimatedCharges metric with a fixed threshold above this month's expected spend, and send it to the SNS topic.
A billing alarm on EstimatedCharges fires when the current charges pass a threshold that the team sets. It fits an account with steady spend, where one amount stays useful for a long time. Here spend grows every month as more customers join. This month's threshold would soon be too low, the alarm would fire for normal growth, and no one will change the threshold by hand.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services, and add an alert subscription that sends a weekly summary of anomalies by email.
A weekly summary is one email each week with the anomalies that the monitor found. It fits a finance team that reviews spend once a week. Here the on-call team wants a message in its SNS topic as soon as unusual spend is found. Weekly summaries go by email, not to an SNS topic, and one can arrive days after a loop starts.

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch billing alarm on the EstimatedCharges metric, have finance raise its threshold each month, and send it to the SNS topic.
Raising the threshold of a billing alarm each month keeps the threshold close to the new level of spend, which fits a small account where someone reviews the budget every month. Here no one will change alarm settings or read cost reports by hand, so the threshold would soon be lower than the growing spend again.

A company's web assistant sends each question through a REST API in Amazon API Gateway to an AWS Lambda function that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. Under each answer, users see three buttons: thumbs-up, copy and regenerate. The thumbs-up and regenerate buttons call the API, but the copy button copies the text inside the browser and sends nothing to the backend.
The product team wants to know what real users do with each answer, and it must link every button click to the answer that it belongs to. Each answer already carries an answer ID in the page.
How should the team track these user actions?
questions.promptText:
A company's web assistant sends each question through a REST API in Amazon API Gateway to an AWS Lambda function that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. Under each answer, users see three buttons: thumbs-up, copy and regenerate. The thumbs-up and regenerate buttons call the API, but the copy button copies the text inside the browser and sends nothing to the backend.
The product team wants to know what real users do with each answer, and it must link every button click to the answer that it belongs to. Each answer already carries an answer ID in the page.
How should the team track these user actions?

options.text: Add a CloudWatch RUM app monitor to the web app with custom events turned on, and record an event with the answer ID for each click.
Turn on model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock, and query the logged requests and responses for each answer ID in CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Turn on access logging for the API Gateway stage, and count the requests that each button sends for each answer ID in CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Create a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that clicks each button on a test answer every few minutes, and record each result with the answer ID.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a CloudWatch RUM app monitor to the web app with custom events turned on, and record an event with the answer ID for each click.
CloudWatch RUM collects client-side data from real user sessions, and for web applications this includes user behavior. The team creates an app monitor, and RUM gives it a code snippet that adds the RUM web client to the page. With custom events turned on in the app monitor, the page calls the web client's recordEvent API for each click, with an event type, such as copy, and data, such as the answer ID. The event comes from the browser, so a copy click is recorded even though it sends nothing to the backend. The team can then search the events by event type in the RUM console and link each click to its answer.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.3: "Develop integrated observability solutions to provide actionable insights for FM applications"
Example: "user interaction tracking"

Sources:

  • Send custom events (Amazon CloudWatch User Guide)

  • CloudWatch RUM

  • Set up CloudWatch logging for REST APIs in API Gateway

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock, and query the logged requests and responses for each answer ID in CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Model invocation logging records the request data, the response data and the metadata of each model call. It fits a review of what the model received and returned. A thumbs-up or a copy is something that the user does after the answer arrives, and no model call records it. The copy button does not even reach the backend.

INCORRECT: Turn on access logging for the API Gateway stage, and count the requests that each button sends for each answer ID in CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Access logging on an API Gateway stage records who called the API and how. It fits user actions that reach the backend, so it would show the thumbs-up and regenerate clicks. The copy button copies the text inside the browser and sends nothing to the backend, so the access logs never record a copy.

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that clicks each button on a test answer every few minutes, and record each result with the answer ID.
A Synthetics canary is a script that runs on a schedule and performs the same actions as a customer. It fits a check that the buttons still work, even when no one uses the app. But a canary is not a real user. Its clicks show that the buttons work, not what real users do with real answers.
