Some sessions now cost far more than the rest, and users in those sessions wait much longer for each answer. These users asked about as many questions as other users. Every tool call in those sessions reports success, nothing was rejected for too many requests, and the tool functions run as fast as usual.
Which data shows the cause inside the expensive sessions?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a travel booking agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The agent calls a model in Amazon Bedrock and uses tools that run in AWS Lambda functions. AgentCore observability is turned on, and the agent code is instrumented.
Some sessions now cost far more than the rest, and users in those sessions wait much longer for each answer. These users asked about as many questions as other users. Every tool call in those sessions reports success, nothing was rejected for too many requests, and the tool functions run as fast as usual.
Which data shows the cause inside the expensive sessions?

options.text: The Duration and Errors metrics of the tool functions in AWS Lambda, for the hours when the expensive sessions ran.
The spans of each trace in the expensive sessions on the CloudWatch generative AI observability page, with each tool call's input.
The daily Amazon Bedrock cost in AWS Cost Explorer, grouped by usage type, for the days when the expensive sessions ran.
The trace count, server errors and throttles of each expensive session on the Sessions tab of the CloudWatch generative AI observability page.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The spans of each trace in the expensive sessions on the CloudWatch generative AI observability page, with each tool call's input.
A session holds the whole conversation between a user and the agent. It contains several traces, and each trace records one request from start to end. Inside a trace, spans record each step, and the trace includes each tool invocation with its input and output parameters and its run time. On the Sessions tab of the CloudWatch generative AI observability page, the team opens an expensive session and reads its traces. The Timeline shows each span and how long it took, the Events tab shows the model inputs and outputs, and the trace shows each tool call with its input and output. Only this data shows what happened step by step inside one session, for example the same tool called again and again with the same input. Each such call succeeds and runs fast, so no metric of a single call looks wrong.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.4: "Create tool performance frameworks to ensure optimal tool operation and utilization for FMs"
Example: "call pattern tracking"

Sources:

  • Agent details, Sessions
  • Modifying your chart (AWS Cost Management User Guide)
  • Understand observability for agentic resources in AgentCore

INCORRECT: The Duration and Errors metrics of the tool functions in AWS Lambda, for the hours when the expensive sessions ran.
Duration is the time that a function's code spends on one event, and Errors counts the invocations that end in a function error. These metrics are the right place to look when a tool is slow or broken. Here the tool functions run as fast as usual, and every tool call reports success. The metrics also count each invocation on its own, so they cannot show how many times one session called the same tool.

INCORRECT: The daily Amazon Bedrock cost in AWS Cost Explorer, grouped by usage type, for the days when the expensive sessions ran.
Cost Explorer shows cost over time, for example day by day, and it can group that cost by usage type. A usage type is the unit that a service uses to measure one kind of usage. This view is the right tool when the Amazon Bedrock bill rises and the team must find which kind of usage caused the rise, and on which days. Here the problem is inside single sessions. Some sessions cost far more than the rest, and the cheaper sessions ran on the same days. A daily total includes the cost of every session on that day, so it cannot separate the expensive sessions from the others, and it shows no step inside any session.

INCORRECT: The trace count, server errors and throttles of each expensive session on the Sessions tab of the CloudWatch generative AI observability page.
For each session, the Sessions tab shows its number of traces, its server errors, its client errors and its throttles. These numbers show a session with failures, throttled requests or many more requests than usual. Here every tool call reports success, nothing was rejected for too many requests, and these users asked about as many questions as other users, one trace for each question. So the numbers for the expensive sessions look normal.

A company's support assistant runs in an AWS Lambda function. For each user question, the function calls RetrieveAndGenerate on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The knowledge base keeps its vectors in an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection, which also holds the indexes of two other teams' search applications.
Since the document set doubled last month, users wait about twice as long for each answer. The answers are as long and as good as before, and each call still uses the same number of chunks. The team must now see how much of each wait comes from finding the chunks, and it wants an alarm when that part grows.
How should the team measure this part of each wait?
questions.promptText:
A company's support assistant runs in an AWS Lambda function. For each user question, the function calls RetrieveAndGenerate on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The knowledge base keeps its vectors in an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection, which also holds the indexes of two other teams' search applications.
Since the document set doubled last month, users wait about twice as long for each answer. The answers are as long and as good as before, and each call still uses the same number of chunks. The team must now see how much of each wait comes from finding the chunks, and it wants an alarm when that part grows.
How should the team measure this part of each wait?

options.text: Keep calling RetrieveAndGenerate, time each call in the function, and publish that time as a custom CloudWatch metric with an alarm on it.
Graph the SearchRequestLatency metric of the knowledge base's OpenSearch Serverless collection in Amazon CloudWatch, and add an alarm on that metric.
Call Retrieve and then Converse in the function, time the Retrieve call, and publish that time as a custom CloudWatch metric with an alarm on it.
Turn on knowledge base logging to CloudWatch Logs, and add a metric filter and an alarm on the events that it writes for each document.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call Retrieve and then Converse in the function, time the Retrieve call, and publish that time as a custom CloudWatch metric with an alarm on it.
RetrieveAndGenerate combines two steps in one call. It retrieves the chunks that are most relevant to the question, and then it calls the model to write the answer. Its response holds the answer and the citations, but no time for each step, so the function sees only the total time of the call. Retrieve does the first step alone: an embedding model turns the question into a vector, and the knowledge base searches the vector index for similar chunks. When the function calls Retrieve first, it can time that call on its own. Then it builds the prompt from the chunks and calls Converse to write the answer. The function sends the Retrieve time to CloudWatch as a custom metric, and the team sets an alarm on it. Now the team sees how much of each wait comes from finding the chunks.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.6: "Implement retrieval quality testing to evaluate and optimize information retrieval components for FM augmentation"
Example: "retrieval latency measurements"

Sources:

  • Retrieving information from data sources using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

  • Monitoring OpenSearch Serverless with Amazon CloudWatch

  • Monitor knowledge bases using CloudWatch Logs

INCORRECT: Keep calling RetrieveAndGenerate, time each call in the function, and publish that time as a custom CloudWatch metric with an alarm on it.
This metric measures the whole wait, from the question to the answer. That is the right number when a team tracks how long users wait for each answer. Here the team must split the wait. One RetrieveAndGenerate call holds both the search for the chunks and the writing of the answer, so its time mixes the two parts.

INCORRECT: Graph the SearchRequestLatency metric of the knowledge base's OpenSearch Serverless collection in Amazon CloudWatch, and add an alarm on that metric.
SearchRequestLatency is the average time that a search operation takes against an OpenSearch Serverless collection. It fits a team that watches the search time of a collection that serves its own application. Here the collection also holds the indexes of two other teams' search applications. The metric covers the whole collection and has no dimension for one index, so the other teams' searches mix with the assistant's searches. It also does not include the step where the question becomes a vector.

INCORRECT: Turn on knowledge base logging to CloudWatch Logs, and add a metric filter and an alarm on the events that it writes for each document.
Knowledge base logging sends logs to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3 or Amazon Data Firehose. The logs record data ingestion: the status of each ingestion job and of each document, for example when its embedding and its indexing start and complete. This fits a team that must see how a sync handles each document, which matters after a document set doubles. But these logs cover ingestion only, not the searches that answer user questions. An alarm on them cannot measure how long finding the chunks takes.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs an order agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The agent changes orders through tools that write to an Amazon DynamoDB table, and AgentCore observability records a trace of each session. The current release check has a model grade the answers, and every release passes it.
After the last release, some orders kept the old address. Others got a new address with the wrong house number, and the table accepted every write. Each time, the agent said the change was done and repeated the address the customer gave.
To measure task completion, the team now runs versioned test scenarios from Amazon S3 against a staging copy of the agent.
When does a test scenario count as complete?
questions.promptText:
A company runs an order agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The agent changes orders through tools that write to an Amazon DynamoDB table, and AgentCore observability records a trace of each session. The current release check has a model grade the answers, and every release passes it.
After the last release, some orders kept the old address. Others got a new address with the wrong house number, and the table accepted every write. Each time, the agent said the change was done and repeated the address the customer gave.
To measure task completion, the team now runs versioned test scenarios from Amazon S3 against a staging copy of the agent.
When does a test scenario count as complete?

options.text: When a judge model in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job reads the agent's final reply and gives it a passing score on a task success rubric.
When the order record in the Amazon DynamoDB table, read after the run, holds the values that the scenario expects for that order.
When the agent's final reply matches the expected reply that the scenario file in Amazon S3 stores as the ground truth for that scenario.
When the AgentCore observability trace of the session shows the update tool call for the order, with a success result from the tool.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: When the order record in the Amazon DynamoDB table, read after the run, holds the values that the scenario expects for that order.
To measure task completion, the team checks one thing: is the order now in the state that the customer asked for? The answer is in the DynamoDB table, not in the reply and not in the trace. Each test scenario asks for one change and states the expected result, for example the new address with the right house number. After the agent runs, an AWS Lambda function reads that order from the table and compares it with the expected values. The completion rate is the share of scenarios where the order ends in the right state. The rule for success is fixed, so an automated check can decide it with no model involved, and the release pipeline can stop a release that scores too low. This rule finds both failures from the last release: the address that never changed, and the address with the wrong house number.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.7: "Develop agent performance frameworks to ensure that agents perform tasks correctly and efficiently"
Example: "task completion rate measurements"

Sources:

  • AGENTREL05-BP02 Facilitate reliable adaptation through evaluation-driven improvement cycles

  • View observability data for your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents

  • Create a prompt dataset for a model evaluation job that uses a model as judge

INCORRECT: When a judge model in an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job reads the agent's final reply and gives it a passing score on a task success rubric.
A judge model scores the text of a response against a rubric, and it is a good tool for the quality of a reply. In both failures, the reply said that the change was done and repeated the address that the customer asked for. The text looked like a success. A judge reads only that text, so it passes the same broken releases as the current check.

INCORRECT: When the agent's final reply matches the expected reply that the scenario file in Amazon S3 stores as the ground truth for that scenario.
Comparing a reply with a stored ground truth answer is a common way to test a question and answer system, where the reply itself is the result. Here the result is the change to the order. In both failures, the agent repeated the address that the customer gave, so the reply matched the expected reply. The order in the table did not.

INCORRECT: When the AgentCore observability trace of the session shows the update tool call for the order, with a success result from the tool.
A trace records each tool invocation and its result, so this rule finds an order where the agent never called the update tool. It does not find the other failure. When the agent sent the wrong house number, the update tool ran and the table accepted the write, so the tool returned success. A success result shows that the write worked. It does not show that the new values were the ones the customer asked for.

Business stakeholders want one page that shows the newest scores and metrics of the three models side by side, with no one copying numbers by hand. The stakeholders have no access to the AWS Management Console. The platform team runs no servers of its own, and it will write no function code for this page.

Business stakeholders want one page that shows the newest scores and metrics of the three models side by side, with no one copying numbers by hand. How should the team build the comparison page?

options.text: Install Grafana on an Amazon EC2 instance with a Grafana login for each stakeholder, add an Amazon Athena data source for the result files and a CloudWatch data source, and build one dashboard.
Create an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace with IAM Identity Center sign-in, add a CloudWatch data source, and have an AWS Lambda function publish each new score as a custom metric.
Install Grafana on an Amazon EC2 instance with a Grafana login for each stakeholder, add a CloudWatch data source, and have an AWS Lambda function publish each new score as a custom metric.
Create an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace with IAM Identity Center sign-in, add an Amazon Athena data source for the result files and a CloudWatch data source, and build one dashboard.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace with IAM Identity Center sign-in, add an Amazon Athena data source for the result files and a CloudWatch data source, and build one dashboard.
Amazon Managed Grafana runs the Grafana servers for the company. AWS manages their provisioning, setup, scaling and maintenance, so the platform team runs no server. Users sign in to the workspace with single sign-on, through IAM Identity Center or another identity provider, not with IAM. So the stakeholders need no access to the AWS Management Console. An Amazon Athena data source runs SQL queries on the result files where they are stored in Amazon S3, and Athena has no infrastructure to manage. A CloudWatch data source reads the latency and token metrics. One dashboard shows the scores and the metrics of the three models side by side. Each refresh of the dashboard runs every query on it again, and the team can set the dashboard to refresh on a regular interval. So the panels show the newest result files and metrics, and no one copies numbers.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.8: "Create comprehensive reporting systems to communicate performance metrics and insights effectively to stakeholders for FM implementations"
Example: "model comparison visualizations"

Sources:

  • Use AWS data source configuration to add Amazon Athena as a data source

  • What is Amazon Managed Grafana?

  • Authenticate users in Amazon Managed Grafana workspaces

INCORRECT: Install Grafana on an Amazon EC2 instance with a Grafana login for each stakeholder, add an Amazon Athena data source for the result files and a CloudWatch data source, and build one dashboard.
Grafana that a team installs on its own EC2 instance fits a team that wants full control of its Grafana server. Here the platform team runs no servers of its own. On EC2, the team would have to provision, set up, scale and maintain the Grafana server itself. Amazon Managed Grafana does these tasks for the team.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace with IAM Identity Center sign-in, add a CloudWatch data source, and have an AWS Lambda function publish each new score as a custom metric.
Publishing each score as a custom metric puts the scores in CloudWatch next to the latency and token metrics. That fits a team that wants CloudWatch alarms on the scores. Here the platform team will write no function code for this page. A Lambda function that reads each new result file and publishes its scores is new code that the team must write and maintain. An Athena data source reads the scores from the files with a query, and no function is needed.

INCORRECT: Install Grafana on an Amazon EC2 instance with a Grafana login for each stakeholder, add a CloudWatch data source, and have an AWS Lambda function publish each new score as a custom metric.
This design fits a team that wants full control of its own Grafana server and CloudWatch alarms on each score. Here it does not meet two limits. The platform team runs no servers of its own, and the Grafana server on EC2 is one. The team will also write no function code for this page, and the Lambda function that publishes the scores is new code.

questions.promptText:
A company tracks the quality of its models in an Amazon Quick Sight Enterprise edition dashboard. The dashboard reads a SPICE dataset that refreshes every Monday at 6 AM with the quality scores of the week before.
Each Monday morning, an analyst exports the dashboard by hand and sends it to the company leaders, who read it before their 10 AM meeting. Every leader has a Quick Sight account, but the leaders rarely sign in. They want the same summary every week, whether the scores rise or fall, and the analyst's manual work must stop.
How should the team deliver the weekly summary?

options.text: Share the dashboard with the leaders' group, and keep the Monday refresh of the SPICE dataset, so each leader can open the newest scores.
Create a threshold alert on the KPI visual of the quality score, with the Weekly at most frequency, for each time the score crosses a threshold that the leaders set.
Schedule an email report of the dashboard to the leaders' group every Monday at 8 AM, after the Monday refresh of the SPICE dataset ends.
Create a threshold alert on the KPI visual of the quality score, with the Daily at most frequency, for each time the score crosses a threshold that the leaders set.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Schedule an email report of the dashboard to the leaders' group every Monday at 8 AM, after the Monday refresh of the SPICE dataset ends.
In Enterprise edition, Quick Sight can send a dashboard as a report by email, once or on a schedule, for example weekly. The recipients must be part of the company's Quick subscription, and the dashboard must be shared with them. Every leader has an account, so the team shares the dashboard with the leaders' group and schedules the report. Quick Sight builds an email snapshot of the dashboard for each recipient, based on their data permissions. The dataset refreshes at 6 AM, so a report at 8 AM includes the scores of the week that just ended. The leaders get the same summary every Monday before their meeting, whatever the scores show, and the analyst does nothing.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.8: "Create comprehensive reporting systems to communicate performance metrics and insights effectively to stakeholders for FM implementations"
Example: "automated reporting mechanisms"

Sources:

  • Scheduling and sending Quick Sight reports by email

  • Creating Alerts (Amazon Quick User Guide)

  • Refreshing SPICE data

INCORRECT: Share the dashboard with the leaders' group, and keep the Monday refresh of the SPICE dataset, so each leader can open the newest scores.
Sharing a dashboard lets each reader open the newest data whenever they sign in, and the Monday refresh keeps that data current. This fits readers who work in the dashboard often. Here the leaders rarely sign in, and they want the summary to reach them every Monday before their meeting. Sharing and refreshing keep the dashboard current, but neither one delivers the summary to the leaders, so the analyst would still have to send it.

INCORRECT: Create a threshold alert on the KPI visual of the quality score, with the Weekly at most frequency, for each time the score crosses a threshold that the leaders set.
A threshold alert sends an email when the data crosses a threshold, for example when a quality score falls under a set value. With Weekly at most, it sends at most one alert a week when the threshold is crossed. This fits readers who want to hear only about a problem. Here the leaders want the same summary every week, whether the scores rise or fall. In a week when no score crosses the threshold, Quick Sight sends no email.

INCORRECT: Create a threshold alert on the KPI visual of the quality score, with the Daily at most frequency, for each time the score crosses a threshold that the leaders set.
A threshold alert sends an email when the data crosses a threshold, and with the Daily at most setting, it sends at most one alert a day. It fits readers who want to hear about a problem within a day, for example when a quality score falls under a set value. Here the leaders want the same summary every week, whether the scores rise or fall. In a week when no score crosses the threshold, Quick Sight sends no email.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's shopping assistant runs in an AWS Lambda function behind Amazon API Gateway and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. AWS CodePipeline deploys each release. After the last model update, every pipeline action completed and health checks passed, but one flow broke. After the assistant asked a clarifying question about the size, the user's reply started a new order.
The pipeline's tests use single prompts. After the incident, the team added more of them, and all pass on the broken release. A test customer account exists for automated checks.
The team wants a broken flow found within minutes of each deployment, and the previous release restored with no person involved.
Which changes meet these needs?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company's shopping assistant runs in an AWS Lambda function behind Amazon API Gateway and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. AWS CodePipeline deploys each release. After the last model update, every pipeline action completed and health checks passed, but one flow broke. After the assistant asked a clarifying question about the size, the user's reply started a new order.
The pipeline's tests use single prompts. After the incident, the team added more of them, and all pass on the broken release. A test customer account exists for automated checks.
The team wants a broken flow found within minutes of each deployment, and the previous release restored with no person involved.
Which changes meet these needs?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add an On Failure condition to the deploy stage with a CloudWatchAlarm rule and a wait time of several minutes, with the result Rollback.
Create a CloudWatch Synthetics canary with HTTP steps that runs the whole conversation with the test account every few minutes, and add an alarm on its SuccessPercent metric.
Add more single-prompt tests to the AWS CodeBuild test action of the pipeline, and stop the release before it reaches the deploy stage when any of the tests fails.
Add an On Success condition to the deploy stage with a CloudWatchAlarm rule and a wait time of several minutes, with the result Rollback.
Add an Entry condition to the deploy stage with a CloudWatchAlarm rule and a wait time of several minutes, with the result Fail.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a CloudWatch Synthetics canary with HTTP steps that runs the whole conversation with the test account every few minutes, and add an alarm on its SuccessPercent metric.
A canary is a script that runs on a schedule and follows the same routes and actions as a customer, so it checks the service even when no customer is using it. An API canary can run several HTTP steps in one run, and each step is a separate request. Here the steps follow the broken flow: the canary asks for a product, answers the clarifying question and checks each reply, for example that the second reply completes the same order. SuccessPercent is the percentage of the canary's runs that succeed and find no failures. A CloudWatch alarm on this metric goes into the ALARM state when the runs start to fail, so a broken release is found within minutes of the deployment. The test account keeps these orders apart from real customers.

CORRECT: Add an On Success condition to the deploy stage with a CloudWatchAlarm rule and a wait time of several minutes, with the result Rollback.
A stage condition in CodePipeline runs a check at a fixed point in a stage: before the stage starts, when it fails, or when it succeeds. Stage conditions work in V2 type pipelines, the pipeline type that adds settings for release safety. An On Success condition runs its check when the stage succeeds, and its result can be Rollback or Fail. Here the check is a CloudWatchAlarm rule, which reads the state of an alarm that already exists in CloudWatch, such as the alarm on the conversation checks. The wait time gives the alarm several minutes to change its state before the rule result applies. For an On Success condition, the OK and INSUFFICIENT_DATA states meet the rule, and the ALARM state does not. When the new release breaks the conversation, the alarm goes into the ALARM state, the rule fails, and the condition rolls the deploy stage back to an earlier execution that succeeded in that stage, with no person involved.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.9: "Create deployment validation systems to maintain reliability during FM updates"
Example: "synthetic user workflows"

Sources:

  • AWS CodePipeline introduces stage level conditions to implement pipeline gates

  • Using canary blueprints

  • How do stage conditions work?

INCORRECT: Add an On Failure condition to the deploy stage with a CloudWatchAlarm rule and a wait time of several minutes, with the result Rollback.
An On Failure condition runs its check when the stage fails, and its result is Rollback. It fits a deployment that fails part of the way through, where the team wants the stage to go back to the last good release. Here every pipeline action completed, so the deploy stage did not fail. The condition never runs, and the broken release stays in production.

INCORRECT: Add more single-prompt tests to the AWS CodeBuild test action of the pipeline, and stop the release before it reaches the deploy stage when any of the tests fails.
More unit tests with single prompts find more problems in answers to one prompt, before a release deploys. That is the simple fix, and the team already tried it. After the incident, it added more single-prompt tests, and they all pass on the broken release. The failure appears only across two turns of one conversation.

INCORRECT: Add an Entry condition to the deploy stage with a CloudWatchAlarm rule and a wait time of several minutes, with the result Fail.
An Entry condition checks the state of an alarm before a release enters the stage, and it can block the change when the production environment is not healthy. It fits a team that must not deploy during an incident. Here production was healthy before the release, so the check allows the broken release to enter the stage. The problem starts only after the deployment, and an Entry condition can only fail or skip the stage. It cannot restore the previous release.

The check must block the release when any answer is about a different policy from the other answers.

How should the check compare the answers?
questions.promptText:
A human resources (HR) assistant answers policy questions with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Staff asked the same question about unused vacation days in several ways. One of the answers described the rules for working from home instead.
The assistant writes answers in free text, and two correct answers rarely use the same words. The policies change every month, and no one keeps approved answers to compare with. The team wants a check in AWS CodeBuild that runs before each release and sends five rewordings of each test question to the assistant. The check must block the release when any answer is about a different policy from the other answers.
How should the check compare the answers?

options.text: Compare the five answers to each question with each other as exact strings, and block the release when any two answers differ.
Compare each answer with a stored reference answer as exact strings, and block the release when any answer differs from it.
Embed each answer with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and block the release when the similarity between an answer and a stored reference answer is below a threshold.
Embed each answer with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and block the release when the similarity between any two answers to the same question is below a threshold.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Embed each answer with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and block the release when the similarity between any two answers to the same question is below a threshold.
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings turns a text into a vector that represents the meaning of the text, and semantic similarity is one use of these vectors. Answers about the same policy usually have vectors that are close, even when they use different words. An answer about another policy, such as the rules for working from home, usually has a lower similarity to the answers about vacation days.

Here the check embeds the five answers to each test question and computes the similarity between every pair. The check needs no stored answer, because the check compares the answers with each other. Embeddings can place two texts too close together or too far apart, so the team chooses the threshold from its own test runs. When the similarity between any two answers to a question is below the threshold, the check fails and the release stops.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.9: "Create deployment validation systems to maintain reliability during FM updates"
Example: "automated quality checks to ensure response consistency"

Sources:

  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings models

  • Evaluating quality and reliability in generated outputs

INCORRECT: Compare the five answers to each question with each other as exact strings, and block the release when any two answers differ.
An exact match fits outputs with a fixed form, such as a category label or a yes or no field, where every correct answer has the same text. Here the assistant writes free text, and two correct answers rarely use the same words. This check would block releases where the answers agree in meaning and differ only in wording.

INCORRECT: Compare each answer with a stored reference answer as exact strings, and block the release when any answer differs from it.
Comparing each answer with a stored reference as an exact string fits a golden set of fixed outputs, such as labels. This check fails here for two reasons. No one keeps approved answers to compare with, because the policies change every month. Also, the answers are free text, so a correct answer rarely matches a stored text word for word.

INCORRECT: Embed each answer with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and block the release when the similarity between an answer and a stored reference answer is below a threshold.
Embedding similarity against a stored reference answer is a common regression test for teams that keep approved answers. This test accepts different wording, because it compares meaning instead of words. Here no one keeps approved answers, because the policies change every month. The check must compare the answers with each other instead.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's travel agent runs in an AWS Lambda function and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. In each session, the agent calls tools, such as a hotel search, many times. Each tool returns a JSON document with hundreds of fields, and the function adds each document in full to the conversation.
Sessions now fail after several tool calls. The model call returns a validation error that says the input is too long, and the same call fails again. The function ends long before its time limit. The agent's replies mention a hotel's name, price and dates, and nothing else. The compliance team approved only the current model.
Which change stops these sessions from failing?
questions.promptText:
A company's travel agent runs in an AWS Lambda function and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. In each session, the agent calls tools, such as a hotel search, many times. Each tool returns a JSON document with hundreds of fields, and the function adds each document in full to the conversation.
Sessions now fail after several tool calls. The model call returns a validation error that says the input is too long, and the same call fails again. The function ends long before its time limit. The agent's replies mention a hotel's name, price and dates, and nothing else. The compliance team approved only the current model.
Which change stops these sessions from failing?

options.text: Change each tool function to return the few fields that the agent needs, so that each tool result stays small.
Retry each failed model call with exponential backoff and jitter, so that the request succeeds on a later try.
Move the agent to a model with a larger context window in Amazon Bedrock, so that the same history fits in each request.
Raise the memory and the timeout of the agent's Lambda function, so that it has room and time for the large documents.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Change each tool function to return the few fields that the agent needs, so that each tool result stays small.
To keep the context of a conversation, the application includes all the messages of the conversation in each later Converse request. Each tool result is added to the conversation as a toolResult block in a user message. So every tool call adds a document with hundreds of fields to every later request, and the input grows with each call until it no longer fits the model's context window. The replies show that the agent uses a hotel's name, price and dates. Tools built for agents return compact results with only the fields that the agent needs. Each result then stays small, and a session can run many more tool calls before its input grows too long.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.1: "Resolve content handling issues to ensure that necessary information is processed completely in FM interactions"
Example: "context window overflow diagnostics"

Sources:

  • AGENTPERF06-BP01 Design optimized tool integration strategies

  • Inference using Converse API

  • Troubleshooting Amazon Bedrock API Error Codes

INCORRECT: Retry each failed model call with exponential backoff and jitter, so that the request succeeds on a later try.
Retries with exponential backoff and jitter are the recommended answer to throttling errors, and to a service that is busy for a short time. Here the model call returns a validation error, which means that the input does not meet the constraints of the service. A retry sends the same input again, and the scenario shows that the same call fails again.

INCORRECT: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window in Amazon Bedrock, so that the same history fits in each request.
A model with a larger context window fits a task where one request must hold a long input, such as a whole contract. Here the compliance team approved only the current model, so the team cannot move the agent to another model.

INCORRECT: Raise the memory and the timeout of the agent's Lambda function, so that it has room and time for the large documents.
A longer timeout helps a function that stops at its timeout, for example when a request to another service takes longer to respond. More memory helps code that needs more memory to run. Here the function ends long before its time limit, and the model call returns the error. The model rejects the input itself, so more memory or time for the function changes nothing.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's sales assistant calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. A teammate published a new version of the prompt to improve answer quality. The teammate changed several parts of the prompt and its settings, and the version description says only "quality fixes". The teammate is now on leave.
Since then, answers no longer end with the one-line next step that the sales team requires. When the team runs both versions on the same sample requests, the new version breaks this rule and the old version does not. The other changes made the answers better, and the team must keep them.
How should the team find the change that broke the rule?
questions.promptText:
A company's sales assistant calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. A teammate published a new version of the prompt to improve answer quality. The teammate changed several parts of the prompt and its settings, and the version description says only "quality fixes". The teammate is now on leave.
Since then, answers no longer end with the one-line next step that the sales team requires. When the team runs both versions on the same sample requests, the new version breaks this rule and the old version does not. The other changes made the answers better, and the team must keep them.
How should the team find the change that broke the rule?

options.text: Change the application to call the ARN of the previous prompt version, so that the assistant uses the old prompt text and settings again.
Compare the two versions in Prompt Management to find the fields that differ, then test each changed field alone in the draft with the same test variables.
Test both versions in Prompt Management with the same test variables, and read the two outputs side by side to find the version that breaks the rule.
Compare the two versions in Prompt Management to find the fields that differ, then undo each of those changes in the draft at the same time.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Compare the two versions in Prompt Management to find the fields that differ, then test each changed field alone in the draft with the same test variables.
Prompt Management can compare two versions of a prompt. In the Versions section, the team selects both versions and chooses Compare. The JSON objects that define the two versions appear side by side, and the differences between them are marked and highlighted. This gives the team the list of changes that the version description does not give. Then the team tests one change at a time. In the prompt draft, it sets one changed field back to its old value, keeps the other changes, and runs the prompt with the same test variables. When the one-line next step appears again, that field broke the rule. The team fixes that field and keeps the other improvements.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.3: "Troubleshoot prompt engineering problems to improve FM response quality and consistency beyond basic prompt adjustments"
Example: "version comparison"

Sources:

  • Compare versions of a prompt in Prompt management

  • Test a prompt using Prompt management

  • Deploy a prompt to your application using versions in Prompt management

INCORRECT: Change the application to call the ARN of the previous prompt version, so that the assistant uses the old prompt text and settings again.
A version is a snapshot of a prompt, so an application can switch between versions, and going back to the previous version is a fast way to undo a bad release. Here the other changes made the answers better, and the team must keep them. Going back removes every change together, and it does not show which change broke the rule.

INCORRECT: Test both versions in Prompt Management with the same test variables, and read the two outputs side by side to find the version that breaks the rule.
Running two versions with the same test variables shows how their outputs differ, which is how a team finds out that a new version breaks a rule. Here the team already knows this: on the same sample requests, the new version breaks the rule and the old one does not. Running them again gives the same result. It does not show which change inside the new version caused the break.

INCORRECT: Compare the two versions in Prompt Management to find the fields that differ, then undo each of those changes in the draft at the same time.
The comparison is the right first step, because it lists the fields that changed. Undoing every change at the same time makes the draft the same as the old version, which fits when none of the changes is worth keeping. Here the other changes made the answers better, and the team must keep them. After this step, the rule works again, but the improvements are gone, and the team still does not know which change broke the rule.
